detail.abstract:
The transition from predictive Machine Learning to Generative AI and Agentic Systems represents a fundamental rupture in the history of enterprise software. For the first time, organizations are deploying systems whose outputs are not explicitly programmed but are instead stochastically derived. Traditional Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) governance models-built on the assumption of deterministic code-fail to address the probabilistic risks of this new era, leading to a paralysis known as "Pilot Purgatory."
Enterprise Anchors™ is an Augmented Intelligence Operating Model designed to bridge this "Probability Gap." It shifts governance from static, point-in-time approvals to Continuous Authority to Operate (cATO). By encapsulating AI agents within a Context-Based Mesh Architecture-creating "Anchored-Agents"-organizations can enforce safety minima, govern autonomy dynamically based on statistical yield (Six Sigma), and maintain immutable evidence trails. This standard defines the principles, charter, framework, and platform required to scale an AI agency with mathematical confidence.

title: AI Skills for Life and Work: Rapid Evidence Review

detail.title: AI Skills for Life and Work: Rapid Evidence Review
detail.abstract:
As AI-based products and services become increasingly embedded not only in people’s work but also in their everyday lives, the imperative for equipping the UK population with AI skills for life and work is becoming steadily more acute. The aim must be understanding AI in a technical and applied sense, but also the broader implications of using AI, whether that be in work or in everyday life. This rapid evidence review aims to explore the main literature on the AI skills for work and life. The specific research questions it is intended to address are as follows:
  • What AI-relevant skills are needed for life and work?
  • To what extent does the UK have or lack these skills in the labour force?
  • What can the UK learn from international counterparts about AI skills?

title: Codifying the Law of Evidence—From Stare Decisis Domination to Codification’s Innovation
affiliations: Law Society of Ontario

detail.title: Codifying the Law of Evidence—From Stare Decisis Domination to Codification’s Innovation

contentType.other: WORD copy of my written article

detail.abstract: The theme of this article is to make clear and persuasive the advantages of codification of bodies of law. I have chosen the law of evidence because: (1) it is a very necessary and frequently used body of evidentiary principles essential for almost all legal proceedings; and, (2) the Law Reform Commission of Canada (the LRCC) recommended, for very necessary reasons, that it be codified in its Report on Evidence in December, 1975 to the Honourable S.R. Basford, Minister of Justice. That Report contains the LRCC’s recommended Code of Evidence in both the English and French languages. I have reproduced them as the last section of this paper, The law of evidence is spread over many dozens of reported cases (caselaw) with little of it in statutory form. Access is made much easier by having all of the principles underlying the rules of evidence in one text, especially a text that is a code. It thereby reduces the time and cost of legal research, proceedings and, legal services. Because of their greater accessibility, the statutory rules of evidence are much more frequently used than are laws based upon caselaw. The success of the U.S. Federal Rules of Evidence (the FRE, operative from July 1, 1975), provides an excellent example of a successful codification of the law of evidence. Six months later, approximately 80% of its provisions appeared in the LRCC’s Evidence Code as part of its Report on Evidence (December, 1975). A code that was recommended to be enacted.

title: How Data Trading Platforms Enhance Corporate Innovation: Evidence from Knowledge Economies
affiliations: Northwest Normal University, Northwest Normal University, Northwest Normal University and Northwest Normal University

detail.title: How Data Trading Platforms Enhance Corporate Innovation: Evidence from Knowledge Economies
detail.abstract: In the context of the burgeoning digital economy, data factors as emerging core production factors exert an increasingly prominent impact on corporate innovation. Based on panel data from 4,011 listed companies spanning 2007-2023, this study employs the establishment of data trading platforms as a quasi-natural experiment and utilizes a difference-in-differences (DID) model to empirically examine the impact mechanism of data factor marketization on corporate innovation quality. The results indicate that data factor marketization increase company innovation quality. Mechanism analysis reveals that data factor marketization primarily promotes corporate innovation quality through two pathways: reducing agency costs and enhancing media attention. The establishment of data trading platforms significantly reduces firms’ administrative expense ratios while simultaneously increasing media attention, thereby driving improvements in innovation quality. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the promotion impact of data factor marketization on enterprise innovation quality shows regional differences, differences in the nature of property rights and differences in the quality of information disclosure. The research of this paper provides micro-level evidence for the innovation-driven effect of data factor marketization and provides policy implications for deepening the reform of factor marketization.

title: A Response to "How AI Destroys Institutions"
affiliations: Suffolk University Law School

detail.title: A Response to "How AI Destroys Institutions"
detail.abstract:
In “How AI Destroys Institutions,”  Professors Woodrow Hartzog and Jessica Silbey argue that Generative AI (GenAI) systems—by their very design—undermine expertise, short-circuit decision-making, and isolate humans from one another.  These aren't bugs to be fixed with better governance. They're features, baked into the technology's core affordances.  The conclusion is stark: GenAI constitutes "a death sentence for civic institutions,"  like higher education, the rule of law, journalism, and democracy itself.

Hartzog and Silbey offer a provocative argument. In this response, I focus on one methodological issue that would sharpen their analysis and make the likely institutional effects appear more contingent: the baseline question—relative to what? 

Every claim about GenAI's destructive effects implicitly invokes a baseline. GenAI destroys institutions compared to... what? They never quite say, and the ambiguity does a lot of work.

The unstated comparison seems to be institutions as they ought to function: repositories of legitimate knowledge, sites of transparent deliberation, communities bound by shared purpose. The rule of law as guarantor of accountability. Universities as engines of free inquiry. Journalism as democracy's watchdog. These are noble aspirations. They're also not how these institutions operate in practice.

This isn't a minor oversight. The "relative to what" problem pervades the analysis of each institution, with the flagged risks either overstated or failing to recognize potential benefits to these institutions from the use of GenAI. Although Hartzog and Silbey do recognize that our institutions are currently fragile and sometimes ineffective,  their analysis would be strengthened by engaging more directly with the extent of those problems—and by analyzing when GenAI might mitigate rather than worsen them.

The reality is that any predictions about GenAI’s institutional impact—whether a “death sentence” or utopia—are simplifications. The future is much likely to unfold in ways that we cannot even begin to imagine.

title: When Should a Sharing Platform Adopt the Bilateral Review System?
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management, Peking University and University of Science and Technology of China - School of Management

detail.title: When Should a Sharing Platform Adopt the Bilateral Review System?
detail.abstract: The sharing economy and platforms have gained popularity in recent years, raising concerns about the lack of information on the demand side: the cost of serving specific buyers is typically unknown to sellers. To mitigate this concern, some platforms, such as Airbnb, have adopted the bilateral review system (BRS), allowing buyers and sellers to rate each other. This differs from the traditional unilateral review system (URS), which allows only buyers to rate sellers. In this study, we examine how these two review systems impact the operation of a peer-to-peer (P2P) sharing platform, where sellers with different qualities are matched with buyers with different serving costs. Our analysis reveals that under URS, even with perfect seller information, high-quality sellers can still be driven out of the market, owing to unknown information about the buyer and the ``co-production'' nature of the serving cost. This differs from the adverse selection problem often observed in the used car market, where sellers of high-quality products withdraw due to generally unknown product quality. Additionally, we highlight the critical role of the expected buyer cost: When this cost is high, BRS can benefit the platform by alleviating the adverse selection problem; however, when this cost is low, BRS becomes detrimental to the platform. Our analysis also shows that BRS helps buyers but can hurt sellers. Moreover, BRS has the potential to generate a favorable outcome for all parties involved, resulting in a win-win-win situation benefiting the platform, buyers, and sellers. Our results not only shed light on review system design but also provide a plausible explanation for the widespread use of BRS by sharing platforms such as Airbnb, Fiverr, and Turo.

title: Cool AI-ed Persists: The Overhyped Integration Trap in Consumer Electronics

detail.title: Cool AI-ed Persists: The Overhyped Integration Trap in Consumer Electronics
detail.abstract: The cooling of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, as diagnosed in prior analyses, extends beyond financial valuations to pervasive marketing practices in consumer electronics. This paper examines the persistent overhype of AI integration at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) 2026, where exhibitors from Samsung, LG, Bosch, and others showcased "AI-powered" features across appliances, televisions, and gadgets, often at the expense of core product quality and user experience. Drawing from firsthand observations, aggregated media reviews, sentiment analysis, and historical parallels, we argue that this overemphasis on superficial AI elements-such as predictive algorithms and voice interfaces-dilutes traditional strengths in hardware reliability, design innovation, and usability, leading to increasingly compromised products. While conceding that targeted AI applications can enhance functionality, the paper demonstrates through case studies and quantitative evidence (e.g., declining consumer satisfaction scores and elevated return rates) that the current "AI everything" trend risks brand erosion and market backlash. By framing this as an extension of bubble dynamics, the analysis contributes to critical scholarship on technology adoption, urging restrained integration strategies to preserve excellence amid hype. Implications for manufacturers, consumers, and regulators are discussed, emphasizing the need for balanced innovation in the "Cool AI-ed" era.

detail.abstract: Designers shape far more than products or interfaces. They shape how people act, decide, and relate to the world around them. detail.abstract: Organisations increasingly rely on AI-based reasoning systems to support synthesis, decision-making, and coordination. Despite rapid improvements in model capability, many such systems exhibit growing incoherence over time: decisions conflict, rationales are lost, and organisational intent drifts. This paper argues that these failures are structural rather than algorithmic. Organisational coherence is a system-level property that depends on durable, authoritative memory, and therefore cannot be provided by stateless or probabilistic reasoning components such as large language models. Treating reasoning systems as systems of record constitutes a category error that cannot be corrected through scale, optimisation, or improved prompting. We formalise the distinction between reasoning and record, and outline the architectural consequences of enforcing this separation in AI-mediated organisational systems.

title: Integrated Policies for AI Skills, Shared Compute, and Governance Infrastructure: A Comparative Review and Implementation Pathways for Japan
affiliations: Hiroshima University and Hiroshima University

detail.title: Integrated Policies for AI Skills, Shared Compute, and Governance Infrastructure: A Comparative Review and Implementation Pathways for Japan
detail.abstract: Generative AI and foundation models are reshaping AI workforce policy. In leading jurisdictions, the policy problem is no longer framed as "training" alone, but as an integrated package that links: (1) institutionalised AI literacy (clarified responsibility, learning outcomes, and auditable training records); (2) access regimes for computational resources (compute), data, models, and evaluation environments (shared infrastructure, linkage programs, and user support); and (3) governance mechanisms (standards, audits, safety evaluation, and incident response). This article conducts a scoping review of international principles and standards (OECD, UNESCO, the G7 Hiroshima Process, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) and compares three core cases: the European Union (AI Act and EuroHPC AI Factories), the United States (NIST frameworks and the National AI Research Resource, NAIRR), and the United Kingdom (Compute Roadmap and the AI Safety Institute). We then analyse Japan as an implementation case, decomposing its current policy toolkit into four levers: soft law (industry guidelines), public procurement, higher-education accreditation, and shared compute (e.g., ABCI). We argue that Japan's main challenge is not the absence of instruments but the lack of linkage across instruments through operational evidence that enables accountability and auditability (training records, risk assessments, logs, and corrective actions). Building on the comparative analysis, we propose a Japan-oriented linkage model that connects application, review, support, execution, and evaluation in a single operational circuit, and we specify a minimal operational evidence set and a staged roadmap for implementation.

title: Geospatial Inequality in the Green Transition: Pollution Redistribution from Electric Vehicles
affiliations: Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management,  and Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.title: Geospatial Inequality in the Green Transition: Pollution Redistribution from Electric Vehicles

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) are widely recognized to deliver environmental benefits by replacing tailpipe emissions with electricity. This paper shows that when electricity generation remains coal-intensive, EV adoption reduces urban air pollution but also redistributes it across space. Using monthly city-level comprehensive vehicle registration data and satellite-based pollution measures around power plants in China, we find that EV adoption reduces urban pollution while increasing pollution exposure near coal-fired power plants. The results are robust to extensive controls and instrumental-variable estimates based on charging-station expansion. We further use a new method that incorporates interregional electricity transmission, addressing a major challenge in identifying the causal environmental impacts of electrification. Pollution displacement generates both intra-city and inter-city environmental inequality, with roughly two-thirds arising across cities and one-third within cities, highlighting the importance of power-sector decarbonization in evaluating the environmental justice implications of EV adoption.

title: Creativity in Auditing: Is there a "dark side"?
affiliations: ESCP Business School and ESCP Business School, Department of Financial Reporting & Audit

detail.title: Creativity in Auditing: Is there a "dark side"?

publicationDetails.journalName: ESCP Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This pre-registered experiment examines the effect of creativity on auditor justification and acceptance of a judgmental accounting treatment. Forty-two experienced auditors from different German audit firms ranging from seniors to partners completed a case that asked them to develop arguments in favor of a less appropriate judgmental revenue recognition accounting treatment. The case varied whether or not the client expresses a preference for that specific accounting treatment. We measure creativity using Gough (1979)'s creative personality scale. We predict and find, first, that more creative auditors develop more and stronger arguments in support of the specific accounting treatment and, second, that auditors are more likely to accept the accounting treatment when they have developed more and stronger supporting arguments. Auditors' domain-specific expertise moderates the effect of creativity. More creative auditors only develop more and stronger arguments when they have low to medium levels of domain-specific expertise, but for high levels of domain-specific expertise, the effect of creativity reverses. Our path analysis confirms these findings. Overall, our results suggest that creativity in auditing also has a "dark side" and can negatively impact audit quality. Our results imply that audit practitioners and researchers, along with audit regulators and standard setters, should consider the dual nature of creativity in staffing, training, quality control, and should develop mechanisms to identify and mitigate bias arising from creative rationalization.

detail.abstract: The architectural integrity of contemporary enterprise systems is fundamentally predicated on the sophistication of their abstraction layers. As global technological landscapes transition from rigid, monolithic legacies toward fluid, cloud-native environments, the strategic implementation of these layers-as explored in the foundational work of my research at Twilio Inc.-becomes the primary mechanism for mitigating the inherent complexity of distributed systems. Abstraction is not merely a technical convenience but a strategic imperative that enables organizations to decouple business logic from the volatile particulars of hardware, network protocols, and data storage engines. By providing a simplified interface to complex underlying operations, these layers facilitate organic growth, enhance system resilience, and provide a defense against the compounding interest of technical debt.

title: Fanmarks
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University School of Law

detail.title: Fanmarks

publicationDetails.detailsText: Research Handbook on the Law and Economics of Trademark Law (Glynn S. Lunney, ed., Edward Elgar, 2023)

detail.abstract: This book chapter argues that companies should not, as a matter of trademark policy, be able to challenge "fanmarks"--marks that identify goods or services as referring to copyrighted works, rather than as originating from the sources of that work. In the fan context, for example, companies should not be able to challenge marks that describe their fan endeavors using words and symbols associated with the objects of their fandom. These would be, for example, the names of fan clubs and convention events dedicated to the copyrighted works, purveyors of products that express the love (or hate) for the copyrighted work, and the like. It argues that, like all descriptive marks, fanmarks are capable of achieving secondary meaning that identifies a particular fan group as the source of a good or service, and distinguish one fan source from another fan source or from the publisher, studio, etc. that produced the underlying work on which the fan good or service is based.  The chapter argues that under trademark doctrine and according to an economic approach, this result is both correct and appropriate, even when the products or services produced under them compete with products or services protected by the copyright owner of the copyrighted work.

title: IP Law in the Shadow of Norms
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University School of Law

detail.title: IP Law in the Shadow of Norms
detail.abstract: Although much research regarding intellectual property law and its relationship with the norms of creative communities paints a rosy picture of norms both as governance mechanisms and motivational frameworks for creators and innovators, it also helps identify where norms falter and may inhibit progress, or where law is necessary to resolve disputes over what copying and imitation behaviors are allowed and when permission is required. Even when norms govern intra-community behavior well, they cannot resolve disputes among communities with conflicting norms. Further, there might be circumstances when norms are harmful for reasons unrelated to innovation governance, such as when they inspire violence or other social harms. While law and norms scholarship typically characterizes norms as existing "in the shadow of" law, this Article considers why and how formal intellectual doctrine might benefit from situating itself conceptually in the shadow of diverse norms that can inform the operation of law and its interpretation, particularly in circumstances when norms conflict.

title: Considering the Role of Fairness in Copyright Fair Use
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University School of Law

detail.title: Considering the Role of Fairness in Copyright Fair Use
detail.abstract: Moral intuitions regarding when it is "fair" to engage in unauthorized copying or derivation from a copyrighted work may often take into account factors that the fair use statute, 17 U.S.C. § 107, does not enumerate among fair use considerations. This project examines one extralegal factor that may weigh in a moral equation: a contrast in relative status between the copyright owner of the underlying work and the accused infringer. Is it more or less "fair" for a teen to sell unauthorized fanfiction based on their favorite movie or for a movie studio to turn a kid's fiction into a blockbuster movie without permission? A number of scholars have observed that copyright law has the potential to promote social justice or, conversely, to establish or reinforce stubborn social, racial, or economic hierarchies. The fair use doctrine provides an example of this duality: it can allow less privileged speakers to "talk back" to dominant culture, to find voices and audiences, and to forge paths to success; it can also allow more privileged speakers to engage in cultural appropriation and exploitation with impunity. The differences between these scenarios may have more to do with who is on which side of the fair use coin than with any of the doctrinally prescribed fair use factors. This thought experiment considers whether and how the fair use doctrine might better promote progress if it took considerations, such as party resources and cultural market share, into account.

detail.abstract: This study examines how legal texts function as instruments of knowledge and information governance through an analysis of North Korean legislative revisions after July 1, 2013. While intellectual property and security are often treated as separate legal or technical domains, this paper argues that they are components of a unified governance structure over knowledge and information embedded within legal systems. Using a legal-text coding methodology applied to constitutional amendments, criminal statutes, enterprise regulations, publication laws, and the Law on Legislation, the research identifies consistent patterns through which law defines what constitutes knowledge, regulates the movement of information, assigns ownership over intellectual and technical assets, and enforces protection through sanctions and security mechanisms. The findings demonstrate that North Korean law constructs a layered architecture in which intellectual property logic, information security practices, and legal authority converge into an integrated system of knowledge governance. The 2016 constitutional revision and the intensification of legislative activity after 2013 provide empirical evidence of deliberate regulatory densification aimed at strengthening state control over knowledge and information.

detail.title: A Scalable Web-Based Tool for Wind and Solar Energy Potential Assessment and Generation Forecasting
detail.abstract: Ukraine's energy sector is undergoing rapid transformation due to both the need to restore generation capacity following large-scale infrastructure damage and the accelerated transition to renewable energy sources (RES). Accurate forecasting of electricity production from solar and wind power plants is a key factor for balancing the energy system and reducing investment risks associated with the development of distributed generation. This paper presents GreenPowerAtlasa software-information platform that integrates long-term satellite climatic datasets from NASA POWER with short-term weather forecasts from Open Meteo. The system implements advanced forecasting algorithms, including statistical models (ARIMA), neural networks (LSTM), and stochastic wind speed distributions (Weibull, Gamma). This ensures both long-term potential assessment and short-term generation forecasting. The architecture of GreenPowerAtlas provides scalability, high performance, and secure user access, while interactive visualization tools support decision-making for investors, engineers, and energy network operators. The platform has been successfully tested on real projects in Ukraine, particularly in assessing the solar energy potential of the Novyi Rozdil Industrial Park, confirming its practical value and readiness for large-scale implementation.

title: Influence of Rheological, Ionic-Electrostatic, and Van Der Waals Forces on the Flow Structure of Water-Coal Fuel in Pipeline

detail.title: Influence of Rheological, Ionic-Electrostatic, and Van Der Waals Forces on the Flow Structure of Water-Coal Fuel in Pipeline

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by projects “Integrated modeling for robust management of food-energy-water-social-environmental (FEWSE) nexus security and sustainable development” (IIASA-NASU, 22-501 (R-45-T)), “Comprehensive analysis of robust preventive and adaptive measures of food, energy, water and social management in the context of systemic risks and consequences of COVID-19” (0122U000552, 2022–2026), and “Development of the structure and ensuring the functioning of self-sufficient distributed generation” (0125U001572, 2025-2026), which are financed by the National Academy of Science of Ukraine.

detail.abstract: It has been shown for the first time that in the case of a pressure flow of a Newtonian fluid in a circular pipeline, the influence of forces of rheological origin, ion electrostatic and Van der Waals nature on the radius of the undeformed flow core is described by a third-degree polynomial with respect to the thickness of the layer, where the suspension structure is destroyed and its shear flow occurs. In this polynomial, the contributions of rheological forces and the influence of the hydraulic size of the solid-phase particles in the suspension enter as linear terms; ionic electrostatic and Van der Waals forces enter as quadratic and constant terms, respectively. For conditions typical of water-coal fuel, we demonstrate that the hydraulic (size) term is several orders of magnitude smaller than the leading terms and may be neglected, and that the quadratic term is negligible compared with the constant (free) term, so that the limiting value of the undeformed core radius is obtained as the real root of a cubic equation containing cubic, linear and constant terms. At DLVO equilibrium, the constant term vanishes, and the limiting relative core radius reduces to the rheological-hydraulic expression; away from equilibrium, the constant term becomes positive or negative, thereby altering the admissible interval of the relative core radius. Using Cardan's method, we show analytically that (i) when the cubic discriminant is positive, a single real root exists and physically admissible solutions occur only for a negative constant term; (ii) when the discriminant is negative, three real roots exist and the maximum relative radius at which the suspension structure is preserved shifts above or below the rheological-only radius depending on the sign of the constant term. Numerical evaluation of the proposed lyophobicity model for proportionality coefficients k 1 in the range 1-10 yields a lyophobicity function varying approximately from 0.67 to 1.06, confirming the modest but non-negligible role of interparticle interaction energy in modifying the undeformed core size under water-coal fuel conditions. These results quantify the competing roles of rheology and interparticle forces in determining the stability and extent of the undeformed core in pipeline transport of structured suspensions.

title: User-Generated Transformation: Intellectual Property, Social Justice, and Fanworks
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University School of Law

detail.title: User-Generated Transformation: Intellectual Property, Social Justice, and Fanworks

publicationDetails.detailsText: Handbook on Intellectual Property and Social Justice 339-261 (Mtima & Jamar, eds., Cambridge University, 2024)

detail.abstract: For as long as there have been works, there have been fanworks – works made by people who feel so passionately about something that they want to discuss it, make new things about it, and join with others who feel similarly about it. Fanworks are often described in the Internet age as kinds of “user-generated content.” Because anyone can make them, share them, and experience them, fanworks provide uncommonly powerful opportunities for expressive empowerment, access, and inclusion. In addition, fanworks are uniquely well suited to advancing social justice by using well known sources to highlight injustices; and the affinity groups that surround fanworks carry special potential to empower creators and act as sites of progress. At the same time, fanworks have a tense relationship with intellectual property (IP) doctrine and enforcement: fanwork creators areauthors in their own rights, but because fanworks build upon pre-existing material, they can also run afoul of actual, perceived, or threatened copyright and trademark risks. This chapter addresses those potentials and precarities. It explores the relationship between fanworks, social justice, and law to highlight how, by providing avenues for access, inclusion, and empowerment, IP doctrines that encourage fan endeavors also advance the goals of IP social justice (IP-SJ).

detail.abstract:
Background: India has the highest number of suicide deaths in the world. Suicide prevention requires policy attention and resource allocation. Evidence of economic losses due to disease burden can influence such allocations. We assessed the economic burden and its distribution across states and demographic groups in India.

Methods: We used the human capital approach in this retrospective cross-sectional analysis to assess the economic burden of suicide in India and its states and union territories for 2023. We calculated the monetary value of the years of life lost, disaggregated by state, age group, and sex. For sensitivity, we present a library of estimates using different discount rates, life expectancy thresholds, and population-specific estimates for the workforce-eligible population.

Findings: The national economic burden of suicide was US$ 8,844,483,363 (95% Uncertainty Interval: 4,590,654,583 – 14,501,572,102). The top three states, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu, contributed to 36.98% of the total burden in India. The age group 20-34 years had the largest suicide burden and contributed to 48.04% of the overall national economic burden (US$ 4,249,291,632 [2,262,795,401 – 6,844,801,475]). All states/UTs other than Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal had a greater economic burden for males than females.

Interpretation: The current analysis ascertains a high economic burden of suicide among the Indian youth and females, necessitating concerted multisectoral efforts and immediate investments.

title: Climate-Smart Agriculture in West Africa: A Quantitative Assessment of Crop-Specific Resilience and Environmental Thresholds in Sierra Leone (2000–2024)

detail.title: Climate-Smart Agriculture in West Africa: A Quantitative Assessment of Crop-Specific Resilience and Environmental Thresholds in Sierra Leone (2000–2024)
detail.abstract: Background: Sub-Saharan African agriculture is increasingly threatened by the acceleration of climate-driven volatility. In Sierra Leone, where over 60% of the population relies on rainfed subsistence farming, the lack of crop-specific climate risk data poses a critical barrier to food security planning. While national yields have grown due to post-conflict stabilization, the underlying biological thresholds of primary staples remain poorly understood, leaving the agricultural sector vulnerable to "tipping points" in thermal and hydrological stress. Objective: This research investigates the multi-decadal impact of climate variability on agricultural productivity in Sierra Leone. By integrating satellite-derived hydrological data with national production statistics, the study aims to identify crop-specific sensitivities to environmental stressors and establish biological temperature thresholds for staple crops. Methodology: The study utilizes a fused dataset combining FAOSTAT yield records, NASA soil moisture metrics, and localized atmospheric data from the Climate Initiative portal. A robust data science pipeline was employed, involving Z-score standardization, logtransformations for precipitation skewness, and the engineering of quadratic temperature terms. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models with interaction terms were utilized to evaluate the differential resilience of major staples, including Rice, Sorghum, Maize, and Cassava. Results: Findings reveal that while technological and infrastructural progress (Year) remains the primary driver of yield growth ($\beta=0.455, p<0.001$), agricultural output is increasingly constrained by non-linear temperature thresholds ($p=0.017$). Notably, the analysis identifies Sorghum as a highly resilient staple, demonstrating a unique ability to maintain yield stability during significant rainfall volatility ($p=0.009$), whereas Rice exhibits higher vulnerability to thermal anomalies. Furthermore, results suggest that excessive precipitation and drainage constraints currently present a higher statistical risk to productivity than drought. Conclusion: The study provides empirical evidence for the prioritization of drought-tolerant and flood-resilient cultivars in national food security policies. These findings offer actionable insights for climate adaptation strategies in West Africa, emphasizing the need for crop diversification and improved hydrological infrastructure to buffer against accelerating environmental volatility.

title: Sustainable Financing Mechanism for Energy System Development Toward a Decarbonized Economy: Conceptual Model and Management Framework

detail.abstract: The development of energy systems toward a decarbonized economy is increasingly constrained not only by technological challenges, but also by deficiencies in the organization, coordination, and governability of sustainable financing. This study aims to substantiate an integrated conceptual model and a multi-level governance framework for the sustainable financing mechanism of energy system development under decarbonization, ensuring the alignment of financial instruments with transition strategies, performance indicators, and feedback mechanisms. The methodology combines a bibliometric analysis of Scopusindexed journal publications with an examination of international statistical and analytical data produced by leading global organizations, complemented by systemic, institutional, and comparative analytical approaches. The bibliometric analysis was conducted in 2025 and covered peer-reviewed articles published during 2017-2025, while empirical financial indicators were synthesized for the most recent available period of 2022-2024 using comparable time-series data reported by international institutions. The results indicate that despite global energy investments reaching approximately $3 trillion in 2024-nearly $2 trillion of which was allocated to clean energy technologies-a persistent annual financing gap for climate change mitigation in the energy sector remains. Moreover, to remain consistent with the Net Zero trajectory, investments in clean energy must increase by approximately 1.7 times by 2030. The synthesis of contemporary research and empirical evidence reveals a predominance of studies focused on individual green and transition finance instruments, accompanied by persistent fragmentation between financial flows, governance structures, and measurable decarbonization outcomes. To address this gap, the paper proposes a conceptual model that interprets sustainable finance as a governed system rather than a collection of isolated instruments, together with a multi-level governance framework integrating strategic (policy), sectoral, and project-level decision-making with systems of key performance indicators, monitoring, and feedback. The findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of sustainable financing critically depends on the coherence between financial instruments, governance architectures, and decarbonization objectives, which ultimately determines the capacity to translate mobilized capital into tangible energy infrastructure modernization and measurable emissions reductions. The proposed approach provides a practical foundation for improving energy transition policies and investment strategies at both national and supranational levels.

title: Stock Markets and Terrorism Unrest in Africa
affiliations: Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, , ESIC University and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid

detail.title: Stock Markets and Terrorism Unrest in Africa
detail.abstract: This study documents the negative effects of terrorist attacks on African stock markets, including the initial market surprise and subsequent recovery. Higher levels of economic development mitigate these negative impacts. In contrast, a country's history of terrorism, the severity of attacks, and non-governmental objectives exacerbate adverse market reactions. The magnitude of market declines and recovery depends on foreign investment, whereas their economic significance is driven primarily by each country's level of economic development. By comparing pre-and post-attack periods, we find no evidence of transitory effects on the markets.

title: Populism as a Challenge to Legal-Rational Legitimacy: The Cases of Orbán and Trump
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title: Populism as a Challenge to Legal-Rational Legitimacy: The Cases of Orbán and Trump
detail.abstract: The global rise of xenophobia can hardly be detached from the global rise of populism. Understanding both, and the relationship between them, requires a comprehensive interpretation of populism that explains both its role vis-à-vis the constitutionalism of liberal democracy and what social psychological factors it answers to and generates. We have proposed such an understanding in our book, The Anatomy of Post-Communist Regimes (Magyar and Madlovics 2020). In this paper, we summarize that approach, which is a novel interpretation of populism as a challenge to legal-rational legitimacy and also as an ideological instrument for the political program of morally unconstrained collective egoism. We apply the theory to two examples: Viktor Orbán and Donald Trump. Similarities between the Hungarian prime minister and the former president of the United States have been noted not just by scholars but even by the actors themselves. During an official visit to the White House, Orbán was described by Trump as being “respected all over Europe,” although “like me, a little bit controversial,” referring to the criticisms Orbán has received for autocratic measures he has enacted since he first won a supermajority in elections in 2010 (Borger and Walker 2019). Orbán reportedly said at a private event that Trump, with whom he had a friendly relationship, was an “easygoing guy” because he always talked straight: “He at the other side of the ocean on a large scale and we here in the middle of Europe on a small scale do something similar” (G. Fodor 2021, 190). We conclude with a few thoughts about the problems and inefficiency of fighting populism from a dogmatic liberal point of view.

title: National Income Accounting And Circular Flow Of Income
affiliations: Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics and Nnamdi Azikiwe University - Department of Economics

detail.title: National Income Accounting And Circular Flow Of Income
detail.abstract: In the early 1930s, it was impossible for macroeconomics to exist in the form we know ittoday. This is because, many aggregate concepts had not yet been formulated, or they were lackingrigour. In the mid-1930s, two Keynesians - Simon Kuznets and Richard Stone began to developthis terminology. Consequently, they came up with “National Income Accounting”. The nationalincome accounting is a set of rules and definitions for measuring economic, activity in an aggregateeconomy. The Kuznets' national accounts brought tremendous breakthrough in economic analysisfor policy makers and economists alike. For the first time, governments had a framework forcollecting and organizing macroeconomic data mat allowed them to monitor the performance oftheir economics. Likewise, Kuznets' national accounting system enabled economists to put variousmacroeconomic theories to the test against actual data. It is important to point out here that thenational income accounting system is based on the logic of the circular flow model. As wedeveloped this model, attempt is made to point out a number of spending and income flows thatmust be measured if we are to gauge the extent of macroeconomic activity. In this chapter, weshow how these various spending and income flow relate to one another in the overall economy.We started by understanding what exactly we mean by national income and output; what peoplemean when they refer to GDP and how it differs from GNP. Also, we discussed the measurementof national output and how by summing the value added for each industry or sector we arrive at astandard measure of national product; and we also discussed how we can arrive at the samemeasure of national output both from the spending side of the economy and from adding up factor(inputs) incomes. In passing, an explicit result of these discussions is a demonstration of theequivalence of the concepts of national income and output, finally we discussed the circular flow of income.

title: Institutional Investment Horizons in Türkiye: The Role of Economic Factors
affiliations: Sabanci University - School of Management

detail.title: Institutional Investment Horizons in Türkiye: The Role of Economic Factors
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between institutional investment horizons, macroeconomic factors, and firm-specific factors in Türkiye. We hypothesize that greater macroeconomic stability encourages longer investment horizons, whereas greater economic uncertainty encourages shorter investment horizons. Consistent with our hypothesis, we find that the institutional investment horizon is negatively related to stock market volume, inflation, the foreign exchange rate, and gross domestic product (GDP) growth. The horizon increases with real interest rates, unemployment, stock market returns, and the quality of external governance mechanisms. At the firm level, the institutional investment horizon is higher for firms with higher institutional investment, higher revenue, higher risk, a larger board, higher executive diversity, smaller size, lower dividends, lower liquidity, lower profitability, younger age, and lower board independence. Further, long-and short-horizon investors have similar relationships with foreign exchange rates, real interest rates, and GDP growth. But they respond differently to increases in inflation and unemployment rates.

title: The Anatomy of Post-Communist Regimes
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: The Anatomy of Post-Communist Regimes
detail.abstract:
Offering a single, coherent framework of the political, economic, and social phenomena that characterize post-communist regimes, this is the most comprehensive work on the subject to date. Focusing on Central Europe, the post-Soviet countries and China, the study provides a systematic mapping of possible post-communist trajectories.

At exploring the structural foundations of post-communist regime development, the work discusses the types of state, with an emphasis on informality and patronalism; the variety of actors in the political, economic, and communal spheres; the ways autocrats neutralize media, elections, etc. The analysis embraces the color revolutions of civil resistance (as in Georgia and in Ukraine) and the defensive mechanisms of democracy and autocracy; the evolution of corruption and the workings of “relational economy”; an analysis of China as “market-exploiting dictatorship”; the sociology of “clientage society”; and the instrumental use of ideology, with an emphasis on populism. Beyond a cataloguing of phenomena—actors, institutions, and dynamics of post-communist democracies, autocracies, and dictatorships—Magyar and Madlovics also conceptualize everything as building blocks to a larger, coherent structure: a new language for post-communist regimes.

While being the most definitive book on the topic, the book is nevertheless written in an accessible style suitable for both beginners who wish to understand the logic of post-communism and scholars who are interested in original contributions to comparative regime theory. The book is equipped with QR codes that link to www.postcommunistregimes.com, which contains interactive, 3D supplementary material for teaching.

title: A Concise Field Guide to Post-Communist Regimes
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: A Concise Field Guide to Post-Communist Regimes
detail.abstract:
While the literature of hybrid regimes has given up the presumption that post-communist countries must democratize, its language and concepts still mostly relate to Western democracies. Magyar and Madlovics strongly argue for a vocabulary and grammar tailored to the specifics of the region. In 120 theses they unfold a conceptual framework with (1) a typology of post-communist regimes and (2) a detailed presentation of ideal-type actors and the political, economic, and social phenomena in these regimes. The book is a more digestible companion to the 800-page The Anatomy of Post-Communist Regimes (CEU Press, 2020), which was a detailed theoretical study with plenty of empirical illustrations.

Each of the 120 theses contains a statement and its concise discussion supported by illustrative tables, figures, and QR-codes that connect the interested reader to the more detailed analysis in the Anatomy. In a condensed variety, this book has kept the holistic approach of the Anatomy and treats the spheres of political, market, and communal action as parts of a single, coherent whole. The endeavor to synthesize a vast range of ideas does not, however, result in a too complicated text. On the contrary, freed from the implicit presumptions of democracy theory, the new terminology yields a readily usable toolkit of unambiguous means of expression to speak about post-communism.

title: The Response of Debtors to Rate Changes
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Nova School of Business and Economics, Goethe University Frankfurt, Goethe University Frankfurt and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: The Response of Debtors to Rate Changes

publicationDetails.journalName: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: How borrowers respond to future changes in the interest rate on their debt matters for the transmission of monetary policy and for household financial stability. Combining bank data, a letter RCT, and a survey, we study this question in the context of the German mortgage market, where since 2022 borrowers have faced high interest rates when their rate fixation period ends. We find that borrower actions substantially reduce the impact of higher rates on monthly payments. Survey responses corroborate high informedness and a strong propensity to prepare for rate changes. The letter intervention does not affect rate beliefs but increases awareness of available options and refinancing among borrowers close to expiration of their rate fixation.

detail.abstract: Once a famous tale of conquest, law and foreign bond markets, the saga of the Silesian Bonds of 1734-37 is missing from the literature on sovereign debt. The Silesian Bonds were among the earliest foreign currency sovereign bonds issued. They go into the market 84 years prior to the 1818 Prussian issue by the Rothschilds often described as the first Eurobond. The bonds were issued by Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor of the House of Habsburg, to investors in London and Amsterdam. They were tradable, denominated in foreign currency, and secured by a pledge of revenues from the estates of Silesia. Although bondholders seemed well-protected by a variety of covenants promising that the sovereign would refrain from raising defenses, there was reluctance to pay, delay, and ultimately partial repudiation. The story we tell centers around what happened to the debts after Frederick II of Prussia seized much of Silesia in 1740-42, agreed in the 1742 Peace of Berlin to take over from Austria the liability of the Silesian bonds, but then decided that he did not wish to pay. From the story, we draw clues about the state of international law, contracting practices, and the operation of the sovereign debt market in the mid 18th and early 19th centuries in Europe.

title: The Endogeneity of Wealth Differentiation: A Mathematical Proof Based on the Conservation of Financial Net Worth
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Endogeneity of Wealth Differentiation: A Mathematical Proof Based on the Conservation of Financial Net Worth
detail.abstract: This paper tests a fundamental hypothesis: whether wealth differentiation is endogenous to the mathematical structure of economic systems after excluding all exogenous factors. We elevate the micro-accounting fact—the conservation of financial net worth—to a macroeconomic axiom, and based on this, construct three types of stochastic process models: additive (baseline random), multiplicative (positive feedback from capital returns), and nonlinear (institutionally structured). Through numerical simulations that strictly satisfy mathematical constraints, we observe systematic evolution of wealth distribution. Theoretical derivations and numerical experiments consistently demonstrate that: the conservation of financial net worth necessarily leads to cash flow differentiation; variance grows linearly in additive processes and exponentially in multiplicative and nonlinear processes; multiplicative processes exhibit a structural inflection point of "rising then falling middle share"; in nonlinear processes, institutional parameters can only adjust the differentiation rate but cannot reverse the differentiation trend; all processes show bimodalization and thin long right tails. The conclusion indicates that wealth differentiation is not an exogenous product but an inevitable result of the mathematical structure of economic systems. Traditional policy tools face fundamental limits under the rigid constraint of financial net worth conservation. This study provides a new mathematical benchmark for understanding the universality and stubbornness of differentiation.

title: Post-Communist Mafia State: The Case of Hungary

detail.title: Post-Communist Mafia State: The Case of Hungary
detail.abstract: In an article in 2001 the author analyzed the way Fidesz, the party on government for the first time then, was eliminating the institutional system of the rule of law. At that time, many readers doubted the legitimacy of the new approach, whose key categories were the 'organized over-world', the 'state employing mafia methods' and the 'adopted political family'. Critics considered these categories metaphors rather than elements of a coherent conceptual framework. Ten years later Fidesz won a two-third majority in Parliament at the 2010 elections: the institutional obstacles of exerting power were thus largely removed. Just like the party, the state itself was placed under the control of a single individual, who since then has applied the techniques used within his party to enforce submission and obedience onto society as a whole. While in many post-communist systems a segment of the party and secret service became the elite in possession of not only political power but also of wealth, Fidesz, as a late-coming new political predator, was able to occupy this position through an aggressive change of elite. The actions of the post-communist mafia state model are led by the logic of power and wealth concentration in the hands of the clan. But while the classical mafia channeled wealth and economic players into its spheres of interest by means of direct coercion, the mafia state does the same by means of parliamentary legislation, legal prosecution, tax authority, police forces and secret service. The new conceptual framework is important and timely not only for Hungary, but also for other post-communist countries subjected to autocratic rules.

detail.abstract: We present the Resilient Economic Accounting Framework (REAF), a mathematical framework for analyzing financial system stability that treats survivability under stress as a first-class variable alongside traditional accounting metrics. Inspired by evolutionary biology, REAF introduces Resilience Potential (Φ) as a rigorously defined probability measure quantifying an entity's capacity to withstand extinction-level economic shocks. Unlike equilibrium-based regulatory frameworks, REAF models financial institutions, central banks, and sovereigns as nonlinear dynamical systems subject to confidence collapse, liquidity exhaustion, and irreversible phase transitions. We demonstrate the existence of a critical extinction threshold (Φ_crit ≈ 0.30) below which policy intervention loses effectiveness and systemic failure becomes inevitable. Empirical validation across 47 historical banking, currency, and sovereign crises between 1990 and 2023 shows that REAF anticipates 94 percent of failures with a median advance warning of 21 days, while traditional solvency and reserve metrics exhibit weak or no predictive power. The framework preserves classical accounting identities, introduces a shock-operator formalism for discontinuous events, and provides practical implementation protocols for financial institutions and regulators.

title: Predicting Employee Turnover Using Applied Machine Learning
affiliations: University of São Paulo (USP) - Institute of Physics

detail.title: Predicting Employee Turnover Using Applied Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Employee turnover is a fundamental process within organizations, reflecting the number of employees who leave a company within a specified timeframe. High turnover incurs substantial costs, so comprehending its causes and implementing corrective actions is crucial for maintaining acceptable levels of employee retention. This article uses predictive models to analyze employee turnover. The researcher developed and compared two machine learning algorithms (Binary Logistic Regression and Random Forest) and one deep learning algorithm (Artificial Neural Networks), utilizing the IBM dataset available on Kaggle. The article is structured in five parts: an introduction to the problem, methodological development, analysis of results, discussion, and conclusion. The findings indicate that neural networks are more efficient at prediction. Ultimately, the use of predictive models can help companies anticipate turnover, optimize selection processes, and promote more ethical and proactive human resource management.

title: Cocaine Goes Bananas: Global Spillovers from an Illicit Supply Shock
affiliations: University of Milan - Faculty of Law, Clemson University - John E. Walker Department of Economics and University of Turin

detail.title: Cocaine Goes Bananas: Global Spillovers from an Illicit Supply Shock
detail.abstract: We study how a sharp expansion in Colombian cocaine production propagated internationally through global trade networks, generating substantial social costs. In Colombia, the production surge increased homicide rates by 41% in port areas and by 26% in cocaine-producing municipalities. Violence then spilled across the border into Ecuador, a transit hub with negligible cocaine production but dense maritime trade links, contributing to a nearly five-fold increase in homicide rates. The shock traveled through criminal supply chains that exploit legitimate perishable export routes, notably bananas, concentrating activity at maritime chokepoints. In Europe, countries with stronger pre-shock trade ties to Colombia and Ecuador experienced sharp increases in cocaine seizures linked to these origins, lower retail prices, a 60% rise in cocaine consumption in port cities, and 5% higher violent crime in port provinces. Together, these results show that shocks in illicit markets propagate internationally through the same trade networks as legal trade shocks, concentrating violence at contested logistical bottlenecks and expanding downstream drug markets.

detail.abstract: This article challenges the notion of digital exceptionalism by demonstrating that platform capitalism replicates the structural dynamics of industrial capitalism, albeit intensified through digital technologies. Utilising a historical-comparative analysis spanning 1760 to 2023, alongside panel econometric methods applied to data from 38 OECD countries between 1995 and 2023, the study reveals the following: (1) wage-productivity elasticity varies by a factor of 2.3 according to institutional strength (0.89 vs 0.38), accounting for 87% of observed cross-country variation in distributive outcomes; (2) digital markups (2.7 times) and market concentration (3.3 times) surpass those observed during the industrial era; and (3) ten structural continuities endure. The distributive outcomes are contingent upon institutional frameworks rather than technological factors per se. Policy recommendations emphasise the reclassification of workers, enforcement of antitrust measures, implementation of progressive taxation, and promotion of platform cooperatives. These findings suggest that the distributive consequences of technological change are determined by political factors rather than being predetermined by technology, bearing significant implications for the democratic governance of digital capitalism.

title: Beyond the Short Run: The Term Structure of Implied Moment Risk Premia
affiliations: and Universidad de Zaragoza

detail.title: Beyond the Short Run: The Term Structure of Implied Moment Risk Premia
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the pricing of the term structure of risk-neutral moments. We construct slope factors by differencing six-month against one-month, and twelve-month against six-month implied moments to isolate incremental distributional risks. We document distinct pricing patterns across horizons: while variance commands a persistent negative premium, the pricing power for skewness and kurtosis is concentrated in the medium-term slope rather than the short-term level. Notably, the medium-term skewness slope carries a significant positive premium. Consistent with the ICAPM, these risk premia align with the factors' predictive power for future market returns. We also uncover a fundamental macrodichotomy: short-term variance tracks real economic activity, whereas the term structure of higher-order moments is linked to monetary conditions and credit stress. These findings are robust to alternative test assets, the exclusion of small-cap stocks, and controls for liquidity and momentum.

title: Sweat and Subjectivity Copyright Impulses
affiliations: Peking University School of Transnational Law

detail.title: Sweat and Subjectivity Copyright Impulses

publicationDetails.detailsText: 36 Fordham Intell. Prop. Media & Ent. L.J. 170 (2025) https://ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/iplj/vol36/iss1/3/

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (gAI) is generating vast vol- umes of content, including visual art with minimal human effort that competes directly with visual artists and threatens to dilute human culture in the process. In response, courts and copyright offices are quietly reintroducing two doctrines long considered incompatible with modern copyright: sweat of the brow, which rewards labor over originality, and aesthetic discrimination, which risks conditioning protection on perceived merit.

This article is the first to demonstrate how legal authorities are reintroducing these discredited doctrines under the guise of regulating AI-assisted outputs, thereby eroding the set of copyright doctrines accepted by most jurisdictions, which this author calls copy- right doctrinal acquis. This article bridges the philosophical foundations of copyright law, Lockean labor theory, Kantian autonomy, and Hegelian personality theory with questions raised by gAI and brain-computer interface convergence. It synthesizes case law from the U.S., China, and Europe to demonstrate a converging yet inco- herent response to AI-generated products that threatens to resurrect rejected doctrines under new terminology.

This Article reframes the copyright eligibility threshold in the age of gAI not around input quantity or output quality, but around demonstrable freedom of choice and human expressive originality.

It proposes four concrete, unprecedented policy reforms to re- calibrate copyright law in light of gAI: (1) a freedom of choice requirement, (2) evidentiary support, (3) streamlined formalities, and (4) tiered registration fees.

title: Affordable Housing Enables Productive Work: Evidence from Food Delivery Workers
affiliations: , Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU)

detail.title: Affordable Housing Enables Productive Work: Evidence from Food Delivery Workers
detail.abstract: Workers value non-wage job amenities, but less is known about how such benefits affect their job performance. Leveraging administrative delivery records, spatial variation in program availability, and a matched event study design, we estimate that an employer-assisted affordable housing program increases food delivery workers' working hours and output by 31-36 percent. The effects are comparable to a large wage rise and are primarily driven by peer effects, as the improvements are concentrated among previously less productive workers. We also find evidence of reciprocity but rule out alternative explanations, including changes in financial constraints, work stress, and commuting time.

title: A Methodology for Generative Narrative and Civilization-Modeling: The Speculative Ontological Engine (SOE) Framework

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Speculative Ontological Engine (SOE), a rigorous and extensible framework for civilization-modeling that treats narrative as an emergent, verifiable output of a complex system. We propose an alternative methodological framework for narrative construction, moving from traditional "world-building" to a disciplined form of civilization-modeling grounded in systems theory. While the reference implementation focuses on a school of design-fiction we term Speculative Procedural Ontopunk (SPO), the underlying architecture is genre-agnostic. The framework prioritizes the administrative, legal, and ontological protocols of a civilization as the primary drivers of conflict. The core of the SOE is a recursive causal algorithm, the Antivalent Cycle, which models historical progression as a series of codified systemic responses to emergent crises. This process is governed by the Antivalent Design Principle, grounded in theories of complex systems. We detail the MODEL Framework's four-component architecture-the Kernel, the Variable, the Cycle, and the CORE-and utilize the THREAD Axioms to constrain the logic of the reference simulation. The result is a transparent, repeatable engine for architecting "Societal Flight Simulators," reframing narrative creation as a disciplined form of speculative social modeling analogous to computational social science. The canonical instantiation of this framework is the Codex Totalis.

title: Government Agencies Exposure and Corporate Green Innovation
affiliations: University of Glasgow and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Government Agencies Exposure and Corporate Green Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper explores the relationship between government agencies exposure and green innovation. The results show that firms with high exposure to government agencies significantly increase green innovation outputs. To mitigate endogeneity concerns, we employ a quasi-natural experiment based on the EPA's 2009 Endangerment Finding and adopt entropy balancing and instrumental variable approaches. Moreover, our channel analysis indicates that the increase in green innovation outputs can be attributed to easing financing constraints, enhanced environmental disclosure, and posting more vacancies for Green-Tech jobs. Our cross-sectional heterogeneity results show that the positive effect of government agencies exposure on green innovation is more pronounced in firms with shorter horizons. The economic consequences indicate that green innovation can improve a firm's stock liquidity. In conclusion, these results demonstrate that government agencies exposure can indeed foster a positive impact on firm green innovation.

title: Monotone Optimality in Pooled Personalized Pricing: When Constraints Preserve Interval Partitions
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: Monotone Optimality in Pooled Personalized Pricing: When Constraints Preserve Interval Partitions
detail.abstract: Pricing with granular signals is often constrained by the need to pool: only a small number of distinct prices may be used for operational, regulatory, or fairness reasons. In one dimension, classical segmentation and quantization results imply that optimal pools are contiguous intervals when the objective is additive across segments. This paper studies a broader pooled personalized pricing problem motivated by insurance ratemaking, where the decision-maker chooses both tier boundaries and tier premiums while facing globally coupled requirements, including solvency/buffer constraints on portfolio averages and convex symmetric penalties that control premium dispersion across tiers. Our main result is a monotone optimality theorem: under increasing differences between the score and the charged premium, any collection of exchangeable global constraints preserves contiguity. Consequently, there exists an optimal solution implementable by thresholds, so that each tier corresponds to an interval of the score. This structural property reduces the design problem to a K-interval partition with computable interval costs, enabling exact dynamic programming; under additional Monge/quadrangle structure satisfied by common actuarial losses, the dynamic program admits standard speedups. We also characterize failure modes, such as individual-level Lipschitz fairness constraints that couple distant scores, and we outline a practical blueprint for implementing and validating tiered tariffs under heavy-tailed and regime-dependent losses.

title: Social Mobility in Western Countries: The Role of Families, Networks, and Institutions
affiliations: Uppsala University, University of Edinburgh and NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Economics

detail.title: Social Mobility in Western Countries: The Role of Families, Networks, and Institutions

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 01/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This chapter reviews recent advances on the drivers of intergenerational persistence in education and income, with a focus on causal mechanisms shaping social mobility across OECD countries. While the descriptive literature is vast, documenting substantial correlations between parents' and children's outcomes, recent research increasingly emphasizes the underlying factors driving these patterns. We begin with a brief illustration of global variation in intergenerational mobility using harmonized crosscountry data, before turning to the literature on mechanisms. We outline a general theoretical framework, which organizes the discussion around three domains: pre-market factors (e.g., early childhood investment, parenting, education systems), labor market dynamics (e.g., sorting, networks, firm heterogeneity), and post-market institutions. We review topics such as the timing and nature of parental investments, parenting styles, credit constraints, neighborhood effects, and the role of social networks in school and on the labor market. We highlight how new data and empirical designs have broadened our understanding of the drivers of intergenerational inequality and, ultimately, interventions with the potential to mitigate it.

title: Re-Evaluation of Japanese Eel Stock Assessment: Data, Assumptions, and Model Selection

detail.title: Re-Evaluation of Japanese Eel Stock Assessment: Data, Assumptions, and Model Selection
detail.abstract: Reliable stock assessment is fundamental to fisheries management, yet assessments for the Japanese eel have produced sharply contrasting conclusions. While official evaluations in Japan and most scientific studies consistently describe the stock as having undergone a long-term decline, two influential studies, Tanaka (2014) and Tanaka (2025), report a substantial increase in stock size since the 1990s, an interpretation that has already shaped national and international policy discussions. A detailed re-evaluation of these studies identifies four major sources of uncertainty affecting their conclusions: the calculation of CPUE, the use of indirectly inferred fishery statistics, the influence of stocked individuals, and model selection. CPUE indices used for parameter estimation incorporate fishing-effort metrics that include non-eel fisheries, such as bivalve fisheries, and several key input data, including glasseel catch and aquaculture production, are indirectly reconstructed and contain substantial uncertainty. Many eel catches originate from stocked rather than wild individuals, potentially biasing parameter estimates. Moreover, alternative scenarios in both Tanaka (2014, 2025) exhibit far lower AIC values than the base-case model (S1) yet appear to have received limited consideration in the author's conclusions. When these uncertainties are considered together, evidence for post-1990 stock recovery appears sensitive to data treatment and model assumptions.

title: Voluntary ESG Disclosure in Vertical Supply Chains with ESG-conscious Consumers
affiliations: University of Graz - Center for Accounting Research and University of Graz

detail.title: Voluntary ESG Disclosure in Vertical Supply Chains with ESG-conscious Consumers
detail.abstract: This study examines a monopoly firm’s strategic disclosure of externality-related information which also reveals information on marginal production costs, in a vertically competitive supply chain. By committing to a disclosure strategy, the firm influences ESG-conscious consumers’ willingness to pay, which incorporates a negative valuation of expected externalities and a positive valuation of a commitment transparency. Vertical competition introduces a trade-off between a negative cost effect, where upstream suppliers exploit the cost inferences drawn from disclosed externality information, and a positive demand effect, driven by ESG-conscious consumers, which feeds back into the firm’s pricing and quantity decisions. Both effects shape the firm’s optimal disclosure and production choices. We show that the firm prefers committing to disclosure only when the positive demand effect dominates, which requires a sufficiently high fraction of ESG-conscious consumers. In these cases, the firm chooses aggregated disclosure at intermediate fractions and disaggregated disclosure at high fractions. Without consumer valuation for transparency, vertical competition eliminates incentives for disaggregated disclosure, as aggregated disclosure softens the negative cost effect. Correlation between externalities does not affect disclosure incentives at low fractions of ESG-conscious consumers but can reverse the preference between aggregated and disaggregated reporting. Downstream competition preserves the core mechanism: disclosure occurs only when positive demand effects outweigh negative cost effects. Our findings highlight a key accounting and regulatory insight: voluntary ESG reporting may underprovide transparency related to ESG information, whereas disclosure mandates can improve expected total welfare. These results inform the design of ESG reporting mandates regarding the granularity and scope of disclosure.

title: Preferences and Misperceptions in Workplace Location Choice
affiliations: Seoul National University, Singapore Management University, Korea University and Seoul National University

detail.title: Preferences and Misperceptions in Workplace Location Choice
