detail.abstract: Standard discrete choice experiments (DCEs) assume that respondents evaluate attributes as presented, but location choices depend on perceptions about place-specific conditions that may diverge from reality. We combine DCEs with perception elicitation and randomized information provision to study how misperceptions relate to location preferences among Korean young adults. Respondents require wage premia of 18% for mid-range regional locations and 27% for distant locations relative to the Greater Seoul Area, with substantial misperceptions about regional conditions. Those with pessimistic misperceptions require 7-8 percentage points (pp) higher compensation and those without prior regional living experience require 22-26 pp higher compensation for regional employment. Providing statistical housing information increases regional employment intentions by 6.5 pp, while narrative information about regional quality of life does so by 9.0 pp despite producing smaller perception corrections on housing costs. These treatment effects concentrate among those with prior regional experience. Our findings demonstrate the importance of measuring respondent perceptions in DCEs when attributes are belief-dependent.

title: Wright's Law Extended: Experience Curves Across 150 Technologies Including Carbon Removal and AI
affiliations: Carbon Finance Labs

detail.title: Wright's Law Extended: Experience Curves Across 150 Technologies Including Carbon Removal and AI
detail.abstract:
Wright's Law -- the empirical regularity that unit costs decline as a power law of cumulative production -- has been validated across dozens of manufactured goods and energy technologies.
Building on the Performance Curve Database (PCDB) used by Nagy et al. (2013), we extend the analysis in three dimensions: (1) updating 29 existing technology curves to 2024, adding 15 years of new observations; (2) constructing 10 new experience curves for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies; and (3) constructing 5 new curves for artificial intelligence compute, inference, and capability metrics.
Our expanded dataset of 150 technologies (97 with Wright's Law fits) yields a median learning rate of 20.9% and mean of 20.1%, consistent with the original findings. We document that GPU compute cost exhibits the highest learning rate ever measured (89.1% cost reduction per doubling of cumulative production, R-squared = 0.995), while nuclear power exhibits persistent anti-learning (-88.1%).

CDR technologies, though data-limited, show early learning rates of 5-16% comparable to solar PV in the 1980s.
These results confirm that Wright's Law is a robust empirical regularity across technology domains and time periods, and provide the first systematic experience curve estimates for the CDR and AI sectors.

Finally, we introduce Phi-s (Symbolic Efficacy), a composite index inspired by Chaisson's free energy rate density (Phi-m) and Gogerty's (2013) symbolic evolution framework. Phi-s aggregates four multiplicative components -- compute efficiency (GFLOPS/$), energy efficiency (GFLOPS/W), algorithmic efficiency (capability/FLOP), and deployment reach -- to capture the total power of the AI symbolic layer. From 2012 to 2024, Phi-s grew by a factor of ~10^8, doubling approximately every 6 months, a rate that exceeds Moore's Law by two orders of magnitude and dwarfs the improvement
trajectories of solar PV, batteries, and all other technologies in the dataset.

title: Generating Alpha: A Hybrid AI-Driven Trading System Integrating Technical Analysis, Machine Learning and Financial Sentiment for Regime-Adaptive Equity Strategies
affiliations: ,  and Department of Computer and Engineering, Amrita School of Computing, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Amritapuri, India

detail.title: Generating Alpha: A Hybrid AI-Driven Trading System Integrating Technical Analysis, Machine Learning and Financial Sentiment for Regime-Adaptive Equity Strategies

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Conference on Computing Systems and Intelligent Applications (ComSIA 2026), to appear in Springer Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (LNNS).

detail.abstract: The intricate behavior patterns of financial markets are influenced by fundamental, technical, and psychological factors. During times of high volatility and regime shifts causes many traditional strategies like trend-following or mean-reversion to fail. This paper proposes a hybrid AI-based trading strategy that combines (1) trend-following and directional momentum capture via EMA and MACD, (2) detection of price normalization through mean-reversion using RSI and Bollinger Bands, (3) market psychological interpretation through sentiment analysis using FinBERT, (4) signal generation through machine learning using XGBoost and (5)dynamically adjusting exposure with market regime filtering based on volatility and return environments. The system achieved a final portfolio value of $235,492.83, yielding a return of 135.49% on initial investment over a period of 24 months. The hybrid model outperformed major benchmark indexes like S&P 500 ® and NASDAQ-100 over the same period showing strong flexibility and lower downside risk with superior profits validating the use of multi-modal AI in algorithmic trading.

title: Green is the New Black
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Green is the New Black

publicationDetails.journalName: Center for Financial Studies Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Donald Trump’s re-election and renewed exit from the Paris Agreement marked a deterioration in the US green bond market. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we estimate a 4.4-6.0 percentage point drop in issuance probability and a USD 20-28 million decline in monthly green-issuance volume per issuer. As a result, the share of green bonds in the US market dropped from 1.7 per cent in the pre-Trump period to just 0.6 per cent thereafter. At the same time, the greenium - the typically negative yield spread between green and traditional bonds with similar characteristics - turned from negative to positive. This change in the greenium, coupled with reduced issuance, signals weakened investors’ demand for green assets, likely driven by both reduced environmental concerns and less optimistic outlook for environmentally-conscious firms. The impact of Trump’s re-election and policies on green bonds was stronger in the US than in other markets, highlighting diverging trajectories in sustainable finance at the international level.

title: When Border Control Formalizes Labor: Evidence from Texas’s Operation Lone Star
affiliations: Texas A&M University - Department of Economics, International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and

detail.title: When Border Control Formalizes Labor: Evidence from Texas’s Operation Lone Star

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no relevant or material financial interests related to the research described in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Private Enterprise Research Center at Texas A&M University.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the complementarity between border control and legal migrant labor. Using administrative data on H-2A certifications from 2015 to 2025, we exploit the geographic concentration of Texas's Operation Lone Star (OLS) to study how intensified border enforcement affects employers' reliance on certified H-2A workers in agriculture. We find a large and persistent increase in H-2A certifications in border counties, which were more exposed to enforcement activity, following the policy's implementation, relative to interior counties. Complementary analyses show that the increase in certified workers was accompanied by a similar rise in employer applications, indicating greater reliance on the H-2A program rather than changes in certification or approval practices. At the same time, we find no evidence that intensified border enforcement coincided with contractions in agricultural production, land values, or total farm employment, or with broader changes in local economic conditions. Instead, the results are consistent with firms adjusting their hiring practices toward formal labor channels in response to heightened enforcement pressure. Overall, the findings imply that in high-enforcement contexts, border controls and guest worker programs function as policy complements, strengthening firms' incentives to utilize legal migration pathways and formalize labor use without displacing production.

title: Sex Bias in International Society of Biomechanics Conference Abstract Submissions: Patterns Across Cohorts, Countries, and Contexts
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Auckland and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sex Bias in International Society of Biomechanics Conference Abstract Submissions: Patterns Across Cohorts, Countries, and Contexts
detail.abstract: Sex bias in cohorts occurs when one sex is overrepresented. This study evaluated sex bias in study cohorts among abstracts accepted for the International Society of Biomechanics (ISB) Congress in 2025. Analyses focused on subject inclusion and abstract characteristics by lead author affiliated country, research topic, and cohort type. Using NotebookLM Gemini 1.5 Pro and a predefined prompt, data were extracted and analysed from 1,394 accepted abstracts. Overall, 43% of relevant abstracts did not report sex distribution, 13% had very small samples sizes (<6 subjects), 18% had an unbalanced cohort (<30% representation of one sex), and only 26% had a balanced cohort. Among unbalanced abstracts, 64% showed an overrepresentation of male subjects, for which a scientific justification was provided in only 1% of cases; in female‑biased abstracts, justification was provided in 18% of cases. Variation in sex representation and reporting was observed across countries, topics, and cohort types, with applied domains such as Military and Sport biomechanics and Animal studies demonstrating lower levels of balance or transparency. Taken together, these findings indicate that sex distribution is frequently insufficiently reported or unevenly represented at the conference abstract stage, a critical point in research dissemination at which study design and recruitment may still be modified prior to journal publication.

title: Divergent Shields: A Comparative Assessment of the "Iberian Mechanism" and Monetary Independence during the 2022 Energy Crisis

detail.title: Divergent Shields: A Comparative Assessment of the "Iberian Mechanism" and Monetary Independence during the 2022 Energy Crisis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study relies exclusively on publicly available aggregate macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The 2022 energy crisis constituted a symmetric terms-of-trade shock for Europe, yet triggered sharply divergent national policy responses. This paper contrasts the structural interventionism of Spain (Eurozone) with the orthodox stabilization mix of Poland (Inflation Targeter). We employ a dual identification strategy to quantify the trade-offs of these approaches. First, using an enhanced Synthetic Control Method (SCM) with multidimensional predictors, we construct a counterfactual “Spain without the Price Cap” and estimate that the Excepción Ibérica reduced headline inflation by 1.74 percentage points (year-over-year) relative to its synthetic peer group (p=0.20, permutation test), effectively decoupling domestic prices from the global marginal gas price. The model achieves excellent pre-intervention fit (R²=0.88, RMSPE=1.19). Second, employing Jordà’s Local Projections (LP) with full statistical inference on Polish data, we identify a “Pro-cyclical Exchange Rate Component,” finding that at the 12-month horizon, currency depreciation is associated with a 0.360 percentage point increase in headline inflation (p=0.073) and a 0.284 percentage point increase in core inflation (p=0.135). The exchange rate component can account for a substantial share of inflation deviation during the peak of the crisis. Our results suggest that for small open economies facing inelastic supply shocks, ad-hoc market decoupling mechanisms (Spain) proved superior to standard inflation targeting (Poland) in anchoring short-term expectations, albeit at a fiscal cost. The findings challenge the optimality of pure monetary responses to supply-side energy shocks in the presence of currency mismatches.

title: The Speculation Penalty: A State-Dependent Mortgage Rate to Curb Housing Bubbles

detail.title: The Speculation Penalty: A State-Dependent Mortgage Rate to Curb Housing Bubbles

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no conflicts of interest. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
In many developed economies, housing prices have persistently outpaced inflation despite aggressive interest-rate cycles. This paper proposes a state-dependent penalty rate, denoted as the p-rate (Penalty rate on Premium), as a housing-targeted second policy instrument that complements the benchmark interest rate. Empirical evidence suggests that modern housing bubbles are primarily driven by middle-class speculation using high leverage (4.5--8X), operating through the marginal buyer mechanism. The p-rate applies only to the above-inflation premium embedded in existing-home transactions, while fully exempting newly built housing, thereby curbing speculative demand without undermining supply incentives.

To address political feasibility and transition risks, the paper adopts a "cold start + progressive increase'' strategy (raising p from 0.005 to 0.5 over 10-15 years) together with a "wealth lock-in'' design. A game-theoretic analysis shows that the mechanism shifts the Nash equilibrium by making speculative resale chains increasingly fragile, inducing a rational wait-and-see strategy. Counterfactual simulations for Vancouver, Toronto, Shanghai, and Shenzhen indicate that if implemented a decade earlier, current housing prices would be 11%--31% lower, and household debt burdens reduced by 38%--55%. By decoupling housing stabilization from the benchmark rate, the p-rate allows central banks to cut rates during recessions without reigniting housing bubbles, consistent with Tinbergen’s Rule for dual-target stabilization.

title: Some Macroeconomic Evidence on Substitution Between Clean and Dirty Energy
affiliations: Williams College, University of California and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Some Macroeconomic Evidence on Substitution Between Clean and Dirty Energy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the aggregate substitution possibilities between fossil ("dirty") and non-fossil ("clean") sources of energy, a central building block of macroeconomic climate-economy models. These substitution possibilities are often captured by a single parameter: the aggregate elasticity of substitution between clean and dirty energy. Missing data on the price of clean energy makes it difficult to estimate this elasticity. We bound the elasticity using two objects: the real price of fossil fuels and the fossil fuel share of energy expenditure. Descriptive evidence and empirical impulse response functions suggest that the long-run elasticity of substitution between clean and dirty energy is close to one and the short-run elasticity is well below one. Together, these results imply that existing climate-economy models significantly overstate the ability of climate policies to reduce carbon emissions.

title: Can Digitalization Help Decarbonize? Evidence from Causal Forest Analysis

detail.title: Can Digitalization Help Decarbonize? Evidence from Causal Forest Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study utilizes publicly available secondary data.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation promises decarbonization, but global data centers now emit more CO2 than the aviation industry—raising a critical question: Does digitalization actually reduce emissions, or merely displace them? This paper provides causal evidence that the answer depends fundamentally on where you look. Using a Causal Forest framework (2,000 trees with rigorous overfitting controls: honest splitting, country-clustered cross-fitting) on a panel of 40 major economies (2000–2023, N=840), we demonstrate that domestic digital capacity reduces CO2 emissions by 1.73 metric tons per capita per standard deviation increase—but only in middle-income economies. We identify a distinct "Sweet Spot" where digital infrastructure delivers maximum climate benefits, while high-income countries show diminishing returns and low-income countries lack the complementary capacity to translate digitalization into emission reductions. Our Two-Dimensional Digitalization framework disentangles Domestic Digital Capacity (DCI) from External Digital Specialization (EDS), revealing that export-oriented digital specialization can dampen domestic efficiency gains. Instrumental variable estimates confirm these findings (−1.91 tons/capita, 95% CI: [−2.37, −1.46], with first-stage F-statistics of 12.34). Policy implication: Digital development assistance should prioritize middle-income countries with strong institutional capacity, where each dollar of digital investment yields the highest carbon returns.

title: Digitalization, Firm Resilience, and Inequality in Global Crises
affiliations: Keio University

detail.title: Digitalization, Firm Resilience, and Inequality in Global Crises
detail.abstract: Global crises underscore firm vulnerability and the fiscal burden of emergency support. This paper provides robust evidence on the association between digitalization and resilience during macroeconomic and political shocks, while exploring the catalytic role of fiscal institutions in technology diffusion. We construct a novel firm-level digitalization index for 1.9 million firms across 53 countries, enabling consistent cross-country comparisons. Our empirical strategy mitigates potential endogeneity by employing a state-dependent local projection framework with multi-way fixed effects and country- and industry-specific time trends, rigorously accounting for unobserved heterogeneity. We find substantial heterogeneity: digitalized firms sustain sales and profitability during shocks, whereas less-digitalized firms—particularly SMEs and service-sector firms —suffer persistent losses. While digitalization provides a buffer against contractionary shocks, it risks widening the digital divide. The analysis further points to a potential role of fiscal institutions, such as taxation and procurement rules, in fostering digital adoption. Promoting digitalization ex ante enables governments to enhance resilience while reducing reliance on costly, poorly targeted crisis interventions.

title: When Size Matters: Volatility-to-Liquidity Transmission in Cryptocurrency Networks
affiliations: Poznań University of Economics and Business and Wroclaw University of Economics and Business

detail.title: When Size Matters: Volatility-to-Liquidity Transmission in Cryptocurrency Networks
detail.abstract: The cryptocurrency market is evolving rapidly with dynamic changes in returns and volumes. This paper explores volatility and liquidity connectedness in the cryptocurrency market by examining spillovers across the 54 most capitalised cryptocurrencies continuously traded between January 2018 and December 2024. We construct spillover networks for both dimensions and identify the most systemically important cryptocurrencies—those that transmit and receive shocks most intensively. Our findings reveal several key patterns. First, volatility and liquidity networks share virtually identical architectures: the same large-cap cryptocurrencies (ETH, LTC, ADA) form the core as primary transmitters, while smaller assets remain peripheral receivers. Second, large-cap cryptocurrencies are structurally more interconnected, transmitting and receiving substantially more spillovers, whereas small-cap assets remain relatively isolated. Third, dynamic analysis shows that volatility spillovers consistently exceed liquidity spillovers, with total connectedness in both networks surging during market turbulence—notably after the 2018 crash, during COVID-19, and in early 2024. Fourth, using Granger causality and VAR models, we demonstrate that increases in volatility connectedness precede rises in liquidity connectedness and are sensitive to US equity market conditions. This evidence suggests that large-cap cryptocurrencies serve as transmission channels through which global risk shocks first amplify price interdependencies before subsequently affecting trading activity.

title: Is There a New High-Frequency Surprise Factor in the U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database?
affiliations: University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Helmut Schmidt Universität

detail.title: Is There a New High-Frequency Surprise Factor in the U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database?
detail.abstract: I revisit the factor decomposition methodology developed by Gürkaynak et al. (2005) and Swanson (2021) in light of the new U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD), provided by Acosta et al. (2025). I highlight evidence in favor of a new factor and suggest a decomposition which allows to structurally interpret this factor as an information surprise. The suggested procedure has the merit that it retains the well-known factor decomposition of Swanson (2021) for the first three factors. The new evidence underlines that central bank announcements are high-dimensional communication events.

title: Abnormally large insider trades and unscheduled firm disclosures

detail.title: Abnormally large insider trades and unscheduled firm disclosures

detail.abstract: We study whether abnormally large insider trades are correlated with forthcoming unscheduled press releases across GICS sectors, using press releases and insider transactions from 2019 to 2025. We use the Newcombe confidence interval to compare press-occurrence probabilities between days with abnormally large trades to days without such trades. For the Health Care sector, a daily dollar volume of insider purchases exceeding one and a half standard deviations compared to the firm historical norm is associated with a 11.4 percentage-point lift and 38.0% increase in probability of an unscheduled press release occurring within five trading days. Additionally, the Utilities, Energy, and Consumer Staples sectors observe a negative relationship regarding the effect. Specifically, a daily dollar volume of insider purchases within the Energy sector one standard deviation greater than the firm historical norm is associated with a -6.7 percentage-point lift and 36.0% decrease in probability of an unscheduled press release occurring within five trading days. We find significant heterogeneity between GICS sectors, suggesting this effect is consistent with sector-specific behaviors. Results from analysis of insider sales is not robust and evidence is not as apparent as for insider purchases. These results act as a foundation for creating predictive models for upcoming unscheduled press releases. Additionally, this study contributes to the literature on the predictive power of insider trades as well as sector differences in insider trading behaviors around corporate disclosures.

title: COVID-19 Lockdowns and Air Quality: Evidence from Brazil’s Largest Metropolitan Area
affiliations: FGV EAESP - Sao Paulo School of Business Administration, FGV-SP, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: COVID-19 Lockdowns and Air Quality: Evidence from Brazil’s Largest Metropolitan Area
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effects of COVID-19 lockdowns on air quality in the São Paulo Metropolitan Area, Brazil. Using a dynamic difference-in-differences approach, we analyze the impact of sharply reduced economic and transportation activity on key pollutants, including particulate matter, sulfur dioxide (SO2), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2). We find that PM2.5, PM10, and SO2 experienced temporary reductions during the strict lockdown period, but these effects dissipated within a few months as activities resumed. Other pollutants like NO2, O3 (ozone), and CO (carbon monoxide) showed little to no sustained change. Our results suggest that while short-term mobility restrictions led to modest improvements in air quality, these gains were not long-lasting without broader structural changes.

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Financial Stability: The Joint Responses of U.S. Firms and Banks
affiliations: Georgetown University

detail.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Financial Stability: The Joint Responses of U.S. Firms and Banks
detail.abstract: This dissertation examines how state-level economic policy uncertainty (EPU) shapes the decisions of non-financial firms and banking institutions in the United States. The analysis draws on Compustat data and Call Reports from 1994 to 2023, combined with state-level EPU indices, and employs an IV-GMM framework to address the endogeneity between policy uncertainty and economic outcomes. The results show that increases in uncertainty lead firms to scale back investment and reduce their reliance on external debt, while simultaneously accumulating larger buffers of liquid assets. Banks respond in a complementary manner by tightening credit supply, increasing holdings of liquid assets, and shifting toward more stable deposit funding. A mediation analysis indicates that part of the banking response operates through firms’ behavior, as weaker investment and higher cash holdings dampen credit demand and reshape deposit inflows. Additional evidence from event studies around the COVID-19 shock reinforces these findings. Overall, the dissertation highlights state-level policy uncertainty as a key driver of financial adjustments, with important implications for financial stability.

title: Hard Mandates, Soft Landings: Enhancing Systemic Stability through Compliance-by-Design Algorithmic Portfolios
affiliations: University of Greenwich and Huazhong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Hard Mandates, Soft Landings: Enhancing Systemic Stability through Compliance-by-Design Algorithmic Portfolios
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of strict regulatory enforcement on algorithmic portfolio performance under systemic stress. Unlike standard mean-variance frameworks that treat regulatory breaches as penalizable costs, we propose a Compliance-by-Design framework that internalizes Basel III prudential capital limits (SRISK) as hard constraints. By integrating a quadratic projection operator directly into a tri-objective evolutionary search, our approach ensures ex-ante compliance within the feasible region defined by regulatory mandates. Using a dataset of global systemically important assets (2008–2024), we provide empirical evidence that strictly constrained portfolios exhibit superior tail-risk characteristics. Contrary to the trade-off hypothesis, we find that the enforcement of solvency constraints generated a statistically significant survival premium during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 shock. The results suggest that embedding hard regulatory boundaries into algorithmic design mitigates endogenous instability without sacrificing risk-adjusted returns.

title: ESG ETFs: ARE THEY BETTER INVESMENT TOOLS?
affiliations: University of Louisiana at Lafayette - College of Business Administration and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ESG ETFs: ARE THEY BETTER INVESMENT TOOLS?
detail.abstract: ESGs have become well-known for their outperformance and risk resilience, however, little to know about the performance of ESG ETFs in the U.S. This paper provides an empirical analysis performance of ESG ETFs over an extensive course between 1996 and 2024, which includes various episodes of instability, such as Covid-19 pandemic and 2007 financial crisis by employing two types of benchmarks: (1) Fama-French factor adjusted-return and (2) benchmark adjusted-return. The results reveal that ESG ETFs outperform their benchmarks. Using Covid-19 and financial crisis as exogenous shocks, the results remain persistent, indicating that ETFs are better immune to investments during market crashes. This implies that investors and portfolio managers consider ETFs necessary investments rather than luxury goods or marketing tools, especially during the market crises. Once again, this paper confirms that ETFs have actual performance values rather than simply being marketing tools. Additionally, investors take into account of risk while making decisions, indicating that they are rewarded with greater return for bearing higher risk. Moreover, in response to economic downturns, a novel finding shows that ETFs are more risk resilient during the Covid-19 outbreak than 2007 financial crisis. This evidence suggests that investors adjust and adapt their investment strategies from previous market stress into the pandemic. Our findings and discussions carry important implications for investors and portfolio managers regarding their decision-making process.

detail.abstract: This study examined the impact of perceived longevity on individual wealth allocation in Singapore. A cross-sectional survey of 299 adults, recruited via convenience and snowball sampling, assessed the trade-offs between personal health investment, family support, and societal contribution. Descriptive statistics and multiple regression identified demographic patterns. Sixty-six percent reported incorporating life expectancy into financial planning, with consistent prioritization of health and family across age, income, and ethnicity. Strong public support was expressed for increased government investment in preventive care and cost containment. These findings suggest that longevity awareness substantially influences financial decision-making in aging, high-income societies.

title: Binding Feasibility Constraints and Economic Behavior

detail.title: Binding Feasibility Constraints and Economic Behavior
detail.abstract: Standard economic analysis typically assumes that actions are feasible and focuses on how prices, incentives, and preferences determine which actions are chosen. This paper instead emphasizes how the feasible choice set itself is shaped by the availability and reliability of lossabsorbing buffers that determine whether the consequences of failure can be absorbed without jeopardizing continuation. When buffers such as enforcement, recovery mechanisms, fallback options, or informal support reliably contain downside risk, a wide range of activities is economically admissible and behavior can be organized primarily around expected returns. When such buffers are weak, uneven, or unreliable, exposure to loss threatens future economic participation, rendering some otherwise profitable actions infeasible. The paper develops a conceptual framework centered on binding feasibility constraints and recoverability, distinguishing constraints that affect payoff ranking from those that determine whether actions can be safely attempted at all. It shows how variation in buffer conditions alters which constraints bind, why non-monetary mechanisms such as trust, access, and control acquire economic importance in some environments but not others, and how observed differences in behavior arise without invoking differences in preferences, culture, or rationality. By treating feasibility and recoverability as central economic objects, the framework clarifies patterns of delegation, experimentation, and investment across environments and provides a disciplined basis for interpreting behavior that appears cautious, relational, or risky when evaluated using assumptions drawn from settings with strong buffer conditions.

title: Liberal AI
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Liberal AI
detail.abstract: Can AI be liberal? In what sense? One answer points to the liberal insistence on freedom of choice, understood as a product of the commitment to personal autonomy and individual dignity. Mill and Hayek are of course defining figures here, emphasizing the epistemic foundations for freedom of choice. "Choice Engines," powered by AI and authorized or required by law, might promote liberal goals (and in the process, produce significant increases in human welfare). A key reason is that they can simultaneously (1) preserve autonomy, (2) respect dignity, and (3) help people to overcome inadequate information and behavioral biases, which can produce internalities, understood as costs that people impose on their future selves, and also externalities, understood as costs that people impose on others. Different consumers care about different things, of course, which is a reason to insist on a high degree of freedom of choice, even in the presence of internalities and externalities. AI-powered Choice Engines can respect that freedom, not least through personalization. Nonetheless, AI-powered Choice Engines might be enlisted by insufficiently informed or self-interested actors, who might exploit inadequate information or behavioral biases, and thus co5mpromise liberal goals. AI-powered Choice Engines might also be deceptive or manipulative, again compromising liberal goals, and legal safeguards are necessary to reduce the relevant risks. Illiberal or antiliberal AI is not merely imaginable; it is in place. Still, liberal AI is not an oxymoron. It could make life less nasty, less brutish, less short, and less hard - and more free.

title: Synergistic Effects of Environmental Pollution Liability Insurance and Environmental Regulation: A Perspective on Corporate Green Governance Strategy Selection
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Synergistic Effects of Environmental Pollution Liability Insurance and Environmental Regulation: A Perspective on Corporate Green Governance Strategy Selection
detail.abstract: Green insurance plays a pivotal and distinct role in fostering green and low-carbon socio-economic development. However, its advancement in developing nations faces numerous impediments. This paper utilizes China as a research setting to explore the synergistic effects between Environmental Pollution Liability Insurance (EPLI) and environmental regulatory policies. Based on the list of EPLI-insured enterprises released by China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment, and using A-share listed companies in heavy pollution industries as the research sample, this study examines the impact of EPLI and environmental regulation on corporate green governance strategy selection and their synergistic mechanisms. The findings indicate that EPLI and environmental regulation possess a synergistic effect in promoting corporate front-end green governance (including green investment and green innovation) while inhibiting end-of-pipe governance activities. These conclusions remain robust after updating the sample through pilot matching (extending the sample to 2023) and conducting other robustness tests. Mechanism analysis reveals that environmental regulation influences front-end green governance strategies by synergizing with EPLI to curb managerial myopia, while EPLI influences these strategies by synergizing with environmental regulation to alleviate corporate financing constraints and reduce environmental information asymmetry. Furthermore, considering heterogeneity in industries, regions, and drivers of willingness, the study finds that these synergistic effects are more pronounced in asset-intensive industries, regions with higher public environmental awareness, and among enterprises under mandatory insurance schemes. Theoretically, this paper extends the research on the linkage mechanisms between EPLI and other environmental policies; practically, it offers valuable insights for the development of green insurance in developing countries.

title: Beyond Incentives and Attitudes: The National EV Readiness Framework (NERF) A Multi-Dimensional Model for Understanding Electric Vehicle Adoption Variance

detail.title: Beyond Incentives and Attitudes: The National EV Readiness Framework (NERF) A Multi-Dimensional Model for Understanding Electric Vehicle Adoption Variance
detail.abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) adoption exhibits dramatic variance across nations with comparable levels of economic development, education, and climate commitments. Norway achieves approximately 90% battery electric vehicle (BEV) market share while Japan remains below 5%, despite both being wealthy, technologically advanced nations with strong environmental policies. This paper introduces the National EV Readiness Framework (NERF), a novel three-dimensional model that explains this variation through the interaction of National Energy Security Profile (NESP), Environmental Benefit Coefficient (EBC), and Infrastructure Substitutability Index (ISI). Drawing on comparative analysis of adoption patterns across twelve diverse contexts-from Norway's near-complete electrification to Nepal's remarkable 75% EV import share despite $1,300 GDP per capita-we demonstrate that conventional models emphasizing demographics, income, and environmental attitudes systematically fail to predict adoption outcomes. The framework reveals that sustainable EV transitions require alignment of energy security benefits, environmental improvements, and infrastructure readiness rather than relying on consumer subsidies alone. We develop eight distinct national archetypes ranging from 'Triple Winners' (high scores across all dimensions) to 'Wrong Bets' (misaligned policy and infrastructure), each requiring fundamentally different policy approaches. The model successfully predicts adoption patterns across cases as diverse as China's industrial-scale pathway (40.9% share), Germany's subsidy-driven volatility, Ethiopia's policy-induced import transformation, and the U.S. federal tax credit expiration (September 30, 2025). We demonstrate threshold effects: adoption accelerates rapidly once combined dimensional scores exceed a threshold band in the mid-60s to low-70s (approximately 65-70, with ±5-10 point variation depending on scoring normalization and market context), explaining Scurve patterns observed in high-performing markets. This framework challenges three critical disconnects in current policy discourse: between stated policy rationales and actual drivers, between environmental rhetoric and infrastructure reality, and between universal messaging and context-dependent readiness.

title: The Role of Central Agencies in the Field of Public Service Provision

detail.title: The Role of Central Agencies in the Field of Public Service Provision

publicationDetails.detailsText: Annales Universitatis Scientiarum Budapestinensis de Rolando Eötvös Nominatae. Sectio iuridica, volume 58, 2019[10.56749/annales.elteajk.2019.lviii.9.147]

detail.abstract: The paper reviews the role of central agencies in the field of public service provision in Hungary after 2010. The main hypotheses on public service providing role and independence of agencies are (1) service providing is a relatively new type of task among Hungarian central agencies, (2) agencies with service providing tasks are not independent or only relatively independent: In order to justify these hypotheses the paper examines the concept, historical background, function and powers of independent (regulatory) agencies. Then the paper presents agencies' role in public service providing: institution maintenance, funding and culturalideological tasks. The research confirms hypothesis no. 1 partly: the service providing task is relatively new in Hungary, however, funding and politicalideological tasks have some preludes. Hypothesis no. 2 is confirmed partly, too: agencies and service providers are under severe governmental/ministerial control.

title: From Trade Barriers to Economic Gains: Understanding the Contribution of U.S.-EU Relations to EU's Growth
affiliations: North-West University, Bucharest University of Economic Studies, Bucharest University of Economic Studies and Bucharest University of Economic Studies

detail.title: From Trade Barriers to Economic Gains: Understanding the Contribution of U.S.-EU Relations to EU's Growth
detail.abstract: In the context of globalisation, trade relations between the United States (U.S.) and the European Union (EU) serve as a platform for economic development, which influences the policies and economic cooperation of these two major powers. Our study investigates how the evolution of bilateral trade relations and foreign direct investment (FDI) impacts economic growth in the European Union. By examining the contemporary challenges posed by U.S.-EU trade policies, this paper confirms that regulatory frameworks, mutual agreements, and transnational collaborations can reduce trade barriers and foster a thriving economic development. The dataset used in our econometric model consists of data collected from 2013 to 2023 for all the 27 EU Member States and the U.S. In our model, economic growth is the dependent variable, while the main independent variables are the U.S.-EU trade balance and the foreign direct investment (FDI) from the U.S. to the EU. The results of our research show a strong positive correlation between EU’s economic growth and the U.S.-EU trade balance. This indicates that an increase in the trade balance with the U.S. will significantly contribute to the economic growth of EU’s Member States. Moreover, an increase in FDI from the U.S. would positively impact both the economic growth and the U.S.-EU trade balance in the EU Member States. Our research confirms that international trade is a catalyst for economic development, and that the benefits of U.S.-EU trade relations extend far beyond purely economic metrics. They can be showcased in a holistic approach to regional and global economic advancement. The conclusions of our study offer key insights to academics, researchers and policymakers, considering the current state of EU’s economic development and the United States’ influence on recent geopolitical dynamics.

title: Bitcoin’s Gold Price: History, Model, and Falsifiable Predictions Through 2035

detail.title: Bitcoin’s Gold Price: History, Model, and Falsifiable Predictions Through 2035
detail.abstract: We present a model that predicts Bitcoin's long-term value relative to Gold based on supply dynamics and adoption saturation. Gold's 2% annual supply growth dilutes existing holders; Bitcoin's supply is capped, with 95% already mined and the remainder released on a four-year halving cycle. This differential implies Bitcoin should outperform Gold by approximately 2% annually once adoption saturates. Our model captures the transition from exponential adoption to scarcity-driven growth using a saturating exponential with three free parameters. Fitted to 10 years of monthly data (2015-2024), the model achieves R 2 = 0.91 and correctly predicts 13 months of held-out test data (2025-2026). The leftover scatter after fitting reveals a shift in how widely prices swing after January 2023: standard deviation fell from σ = 0.478 to σ = 0.258 (p < 0.0001), coinciding with significant geopolitical shifts in reserve-asset markets. The model projects Bitcoin will reach 37 oz Gold by 2030 (95% CI: 22-62 oz) and 43 oz by 2035 (95% CI: 26-72 oz), with expected annual outperformance of 8.6% relative to Gold. These projections constitute falsifiable hypotheses about both trajectory and volatility.

title: Semantic Inflation: Coordination Failure and Navigational Drift in Economic Language

detail.title: Semantic Inflation: Coordination Failure and Navigational Drift in Economic Language
detail.abstract: This working paper develops a mid-range, conceptual account of when overload in economic coordination terms becomes an infrastructural failure rather than a benign semantic broadening. Drawing on frame semantics, coordination theory, and STS, it proposes a linking mechanismsymbolic overload → loss of cross-context comparability → navigation drag ("Orientation Disequilibrium"). Inflation serves as the focal case, but the mechanism is presented as potentially portable to other coordination terms such as affordability, cost of living, recession, and inequality. The contribution is non-empirical: rigor is pursued through construct definition, boundary conditions, contrasts with adjacent constructs (e.g., concept creep and neutral semantic broadening), and portability-oriented stress tests rather than statistical inference. Illustrative vignettes show how "inflation" can function as an overloaded symbolic container in everyday navigation, institutional messaging, and wage narratives-weakening alignment between public metrics and lived cost structures through semantic overload rather than factual error. The paper closes by sketching directions for experiential economic metrics and future operationalization, without proposing measurement instruments or policy claims.

title: Characteristic Function Neural Networks: A Unified Mathematical Framework for Distribution Learning
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Characteristic Function Neural Networks: A Unified Mathematical Framework for Distribution Learning
detail.abstract: We present a unified mathematical framework for Characteristic Function Neural Networks (CFNNs), a class of architectures that learn probability distributions through their characteristic functions. The characteristic function φ µ (ξ) = E[e i⟨ξ,X⟩ ] uniquely determines any probability measure via Bochner's theorem, providing a principled foundation for distribution learning. We develop five complementary architectures spanning increasing levels of structure: (I) foundational CFNNs with three Bochner-valid constructions-constraint-based, pushforward, and Gaussian mixture; (II) Transformer-CFNNs (TR-CFNN) where multi-head attention implements learned mixtures of Hilbert-Schmidt operators on frequency space; (III) LSTM-CFNNs with provably contractive dynamics, exponential forgetting, and Volterra series interpretations; (IV) VAE-CFNNs combining variational inference with CF decoders, equipped with Fisher information geometry on latent manifolds; and (V) Signature-CFNNs (Sig-CFNN) unifying path signatures from rough path theory with characteristic functions for path-dependent distributions. We establish fundamental theoretical results including: (a) the weighted CF loss equals Maximum Mean Discrepancy under explicit kernel correspondence; (b) universal approximation within the positive definite cone with quantified obstruction for bounded frequency domains; (c) Sobolev convergence rates O(N-2s/d) + O(n-2s/(2s+d)) decomposing approximation and estimation error; (d) expressivity separation showing TR-CFNN strictly dominates MLP-CFNN for cross-frequency interactions; (e) expected signatures determine process laws-the path-space analogue of Bochner's theorem. A unifying meta-theorem shows that CFNNs act as nonlinear operators on the Bochner cone of characteristic functions, and that a Lévy-Khintchine-constrained subclass acts on the cone of infinitely divisible laws; architectural differences correspond to distinct parameterizations of drift, diffusion, and jump components. Applications to financial derivative pricing via Fourier methods, density estimation, and sequential prediction demonstrate the framework's practical utility.

title: Integration Challenges of Azerbaijani Migrants in the United States

detail.title: Integration Challenges of Azerbaijani Migrants in the United States
detail.abstract: Migrants who migrated from Azerbaijan to the USA in different waves over the last 30 years tried to take a place in the new social environment due to economic provisions, education, and forced reasons arising from the war. However, studies show that the integration of this community remains weak in institutional, social, and cultural aspects. Weakness of language skills in the first years, delay of economic integration, difficulty of coordination in diaspora organizations, fading of ties with Azerbaijan over time, and psychosocial difficulties complicate the integration process. Indepth interviews conducted by Efendiyev (2021) show that integration among Azerbaijani migrants is heterogeneous, and even long-term residents experience weakening diaspora and homeland ties. This policy brief analyzes the structural functioning of integration weaknesses, reveals how U.S. policies fail migrants, reveals the functional gaps in diaspora organizations, and explains how the culture-centric model of the Azerbaijan Republic Agency for Diaspora Affairs fails to meet integration needs. The result is a practical, independent, and realistic policy proposal for the U.S. government, diaspora associations, and Azerbaijani state.

title: MediQuills' Feedback on the EU’s Legislation on Medicines for Children and Rare Diseases
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Academies of Loudoun, Academies of Loudoun

detail.title: MediQuills' Feedback on the EU’s Legislation on Medicines for Children and Rare Diseases
detail.abstract: Biotechnology for rare diseases and paediatric conditions has seen significant advances over the course of the twenty-first century, especially throughout Europe, and there are specific aspects of vaccines and medications that have been developed to alleviate such health issues. Some of them include recombinant technology and biomarker integration, which targets the molecular processes occurring inside disease-affected cells and other microscopic material found throughout the human body. mRNA technology advancements are central to this biotechnological revolution in specialised patient care, and over the past two decades, research investigators have formulated evidence-based ideas that have connected discoveries within the biomedical realm to those in need of individualised treatment. Despite such promise within the scientific realm, biotechnology manufacturers and pharmaceutical companies throughout Europe have failed to create and market the most effective specialised therapy for patients suffering from less prevalent diseases – specifically children. Despite these advances, and nearly two decades of EU legislation designed to stimulate innovation, the majority of rare diseases, particularly paediatric rare diseases, still lack authorised and effective treatments. Although the European Union (EU) has passed legislation promoting the manufacturing of such treatments for nearly twenty years, there has been little improvement in ensuring that rare diseases have unique treatments that could better target their effects on patients. Hence, the EU has issued potential revisions to the regulations it has previously passed, including modulating incentives to manufacturers and pharmaceutical companies that improve the availability and accessibility of rare disease medicine, thus ensuring that these corporations are motivated to continue performing this task, which we at Mediquills support subject to targeted modifications to improve translational effectiveness.This paper summarises the persistent translational gap between biotechnology innovation and pharmaceutical manufacturing, reviews the historical performance of EU orphan and paediatric legislation, and identifies structural weaknesses limiting the development of genuinely novel therapies. Many areas that need to be emphasised to assure success include stronger support for biotechnology–pharmaceutical integration, explicit incentives for platform-based innovation (e.g., recombinant and biomarker-driven therapies), and regulatory flexibility proportionate to scientific risk. When executed with these considerations, EU revisions on medicines for children and rare diseases will more likely guarantee durable, innovation-driven improvements in specialised treatment access for paediatric and rare disease populations for decades to come.

title: Constructed Environment for Tourism: A Case Study Using a Conceptual Framework and Guidelines
affiliations: Assam University - Department of Business Administration, Assam University - Department of Business Administration and Jawaharlal Nehru University

detail.title: Constructed Environment for Tourism: A Case Study Using a Conceptual Framework and Guidelines
detail.abstract: This book emerges from my enduring passion for research, driven by a desire to explore uncharted dimensions and push the boundaries of knowledge. Among the many themes that shape the discourse on tourism development, the concept of the Constructed Environment—though long present in practice—had remained unnamed and underexplored. Through this study, I have sought to define and contextualise this concept, bringing it into the academic and practical forefront. The Constructed Environment refers to a thoughtfully designed and systematically executed space created to enhance tourist satisfaction, ensure sustainability, and promote the optimal use of available resources. Its success depends on the active collaboration and competence of various stakeholders. To advance the tourism industry, it is crucial to comprehend both the tangible and intangible characteristics that influence its development. This work is presented through a structured series of chapters covering key dimensions such as an overview of the tourism industry, the theoretical foundation of the Constructed Environment, an extensive literature review, research methodology and objectives, data analysis and interpretation, findings, and strategic recommendations. The findings herein are the result of extensive fieldwork and in-depth analysis, culminating in the title: Constructed Environment for Tourism Industries – A Case Study Based on the Conceptual Framework and Guidelines for Best Practices. I am confident that this study will serve as a valuable resource for scholars, practitioners, students, and policy-makers who are seeking insights into the emerging relevance of the Constructed Environment in tourism. It is my hope that this work contributes meaningfully to the body of knowledge by bridging the existing gap between tourist perceptions and the vision of policy-makers— an alignment that, until now, had not been clearly articulated. Moreover, this book aspires to raise awareness among stakeholders across North-East India and beyond, encouraging a more conscious, inclusive, and strategic approach to tourism development.

title: Feedback on the Advanced Materials Act
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Academies of Loudoun, Academies of Loudoun

detail.title: Feedback on the Advanced Materials Act
detail.abstract:
The Advanced Materials Act aims to advance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth by shortening the timeline from discovery to application of a new material. Specifically, the act would focus on boosting Research and Innovation (R&I) capacity, increasing availability and sustainability, and reducing regulatory barriers. The act aims to address all sectors rather than introducing sector-specific regulations while also tying into existing EU regulations.

This paper argues that in order to achieve the Advanced Materials Act’s intended impacts, it is essential to bridge the gap between regulation and innovation literacy. Many sustainable or novel technologies, like those included in the Advanced Materials Act, can be involved in stigma where they are believed to be inferior to more historically well-established materials. As such, MediQuills recommends measures to improve educational engagement and youth science and innovation literacy.

title: Social Media as an Investment Information Channel: Evidence from U.S. Households
affiliations: , Texas Tech University and Missouri Southern State University - Plaster School of Business

detail.title: Social Media as an Investment Information Channel: Evidence from U.S. Households
detail.abstract: This paper examines how social media operates as an investment-information channel and whether platform-specific usage is associated with speculative retail trading. Using nationally representative household data from the 2024 U.S. National Financial Capability Study, we link investor-reported use of individual social media platforms for investment information to self-reported participation in meme stocks. We estimate platform-by-platform logit models and report average marginal effects to measure the economic impact of social media-based information acquisition. The results reveal a pronounced platform gradient in speculative participation. Engagement with community-driven, discussion-oriented platforms-most notably Reddit, Discord, and Telegram-is consistently associated with a higher probability of memestock purchasing. In contrast, broadcast-style or professionally oriented platforms such as YouTube and LinkedIn exhibit economically small and statistically insignificant effects, while several mainstream platforms show weaker and imprecise associations. Reliance on financial influencers does not predict speculative participation once platform exposure is accounted for. These findings highlight the central role of peer interaction and collective narratives, rather than one-to-many persuasion, in driving speculative retail trading and inform debates on investor protection and platform design.

title: FIDIC Contracts: Indian Judicial Engagement in 2025
affiliations: Dhirubhai Ambani University’s School of Law

detail.title: FIDIC Contracts: Indian Judicial Engagement in 2025

publicationDetails.detailsText: Dhirubhai Ambani University, School of Law's blog.

detail.abstract: This article examines how Indian courts interpreted FIDIC forms of contract in 2025. In India, FIDIC forms are used mainly for internationally funded projects. Every year, Indian courts interpret only a few FIDIC contracts. Indian courts’ experience with standard form contracts contributes to the broader jurisprudence on their interpretation.

title: Learning Market Beliefs from Credit Ratings: Evidence from the Timing of Corporate Bond Issuances
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Fordham University and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Learning Market Beliefs from Credit Ratings: Evidence from the Timing of Corporate Bond Issuances
detail.abstract: Bond issuers face a higher-order belief problem: to avoid the financial and reputational costs of issuance failures, they have incentives to infer investor beliefs. We show that firms strategically time bond offerings around rating changes. Specifically, issuers are more likely to initiate offerings shortly after rating upgrades of their outstanding bonds; conditional on initiation, such issuances are more likely to succeed. These patterns are not explained by shifts in issuer fundamentals or changes in macroeconomic conditions. Our findings identify bond rating changes as a critical information channel through which issuers learn about market perceptions and mitigate the higher-order belief problem.

title: State Regulatory Accumulation and Municipal Bond Yields at Issuance
affiliations: and Seton Hall University

detail.title: State Regulatory Accumulation and Municipal Bond Yields at Issuance
detail.abstract: Using data on state-level regulatory growth from RegData and primary-market municipal bond issuances from Bloomberg, we test whether growth in regulatory restrictions is associated with higher yields to maturity. Regulatory accumulation may raise yields by increasing transaction-level compliance burdens that affect primary market pricing, or by constraining long-run fiscal capacity in ways that would be reflected in aggregate state borrowing conditions. We find consistent evidence that regulatory growth is positively associated with higher yields at issuance at the transaction level, indicating that regulatory conditions are priced in primary-market municipal debt, with larger effects for longer-maturity bonds. In contrast, the aggregate state-year estimates are imprecise and do not provide robust evidence of a relationship in our sample. However, fiscal balance-sheet fundamentals, especially net pension liabilities per capita, are consistently associated with higher yields for longermaturity debt, highlighting the importance of long-run fiscal obligations in the pricing of municipal debt.

title: Interest Rate Risk around Monetary Policy Announcements and Asset Duration
affiliations: Bank of Japan

detail.title: Interest Rate Risk around Monetary Policy Announcements and Asset Duration
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines the monetary policy announcement premium by focusing on interest rate risk and asset duration. First, the average returns of long-duration Treasury bonds are higher than those of short-duration bonds on monetary policy announcement days. Second, the average returns of long-duration equities are statistically indistinguishable from those of short-duration equities on announcement days, whereas on non-announcement days, long-duration equities yield lower returns. This term structure on announcement days is attributed to the resolution of interest rate risk. Third, the elasticity of returns with respect to changes in interest rate risk is greater for long-duration assets than for short-duration assets, a result that holds for both bonds and equities.

title: Analysis of the Mitigating Effect of Financial Regulatory Penalties On Bank Systemic Risk
affiliations: Shaanxi Normal University, Shaanxi Normal University and Shaanxi Normal University

detail.title: Analysis of the Mitigating Effect of Financial Regulatory Penalties On Bank Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: This study developed a theoretical analytical framework grounded in the alignment between microprudential regulation and macroprudential supervision objectives, and analyzed the actual impact of financial regulatory penalties on bank systemic risk based on penalty data from the PBC and the NFRA from 2014 to 2023. The study found that financial regulatory penalties exhibits a distinct mitigating effect on bank systemic risk. The main control channels are two: first, by reducing the idiosyncratic risk of individual bank; and second, by weakening the intensity of risk transmission across institutions. The impact is significantly strengthened by the regulatory environment pressure effect and the creditor monitoring effect, and is predominantly observed in banks by regulatory fine, provincial and municipal-level branches, and conducted by the NFRA. It is worth noting that when banking institutions and the banking system are in extreme risk situation, penalties may not be an effective way to control bank systemic risk.

title: Bagehot’s Rule, Collateral, and Solvency
affiliations: Swiss National Bank

detail.title: Bagehot’s Rule, Collateral, and Solvency
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a theory of emergency liquidity assistance (ELA) to troubled banks that is based on the notion that the central bank has a greater capacity than private lenders to monitor a distressed bank's conduct. The model shows how collateralized emergency loans can play a stabilizing role even if banks have access to private secured funding at all times. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the conditions under which the two standard requirements for a bank to be eligible for ELA - solvency and enough collateral - are equivalent. In such cases, valuing a bank's available collateral is sufficient to implement ``Bagehot's rule'' that only solvent banks should receive support.

title: A Time-Dependent Quantification of Quantitative Easing, Quantitative Tightening and Forward Guidance: The Role of High-Frequency Functional versus Factor Surprises
affiliations: University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Helmut Schmidt Universität

detail.title: A Time-Dependent Quantification of Quantitative Easing, Quantitative Tightening and Forward Guidance: The Role of High-Frequency Functional versus Factor Surprises
detail.abstract: In the light of the new U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD), provided by Acosta et al. (2025), and available since December 2025, this paper revisits the empirical literature on the macroeconomic effects of unconventional monetary policy. The literature on the quantification of the macroeconomic effects of monetary policy has mushroomed and lacks a consensus on how to model unconventional monetary policy. The identification of policies like quantitative easing poses many challenges to the econometrician, because such policies are anticipated ahead of their implementation and short-term interest rate measures lack sufficient variation due to the zero lower bound. Early generations of empirical studies relied on zero restrictions or sign restrictions in combination with stock variables derived from the respective central bank's balance sheet or simply accumulated asset purchase announcements. Alternatively, different interest rate measures have been suggested like interest rate spreads or shadow rates to study macroeconomic effects of quantitative easing and forward guidance. Instead, more recent studies rely on methods from the event study literature and structural vector autoregressive models with external and internal instruments have become a leading tool. Promising identification strategies rely on instruments extracted from high-frequency asset price changes around monetary policy events. However, identification strategies differ in terms of how these high-frequency asset price changes are processed to identify the effects of the policies of interest. The suggested approaches range from the extraction of specific surprise factors to more holistic approaches accounting for functional shocks along the yield curve or using high-frequency changes throughout the yield curve directly. I revisit the use of both factor and (multivariate) functional surprises which can be accommodated in a VAR-X model with both time-varying parameters and volatility.

title: Trump, Hitler, and Weimar: An Institutional Analysis

detail.title: Trump, Hitler, and Weimar: An Institutional Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent truth seeker

detail.abstract:
Public debate increasingly invokes analogies between contemporary American politics and interwar Germany, often framed as personality‑based comparisons between Donald Trump and Adolf Hitler. These analogies are either embraced as moral warnings or rejected as historically irresponsible, but in both cases they are treated as verdicts rather than as objects of analysis. This paper departs from that pattern by treating the “Trump–Hitler–Weimar” comparison itself as evidence of institutional anxiety and as an occasion for systematic, mechanism‑focused inquiry.

Through a comparative examination of Weimar Germany’s pre‑catastrophic phase and contemporary American governance, the paper identifies two recurring structural failure modes. The Advanced Society Illusion is elite confidence that mature institutions can safely normalize emergency powers, tolerate anti‑pluralist forces, and absorb hostile influences without risking democratic capture. Asymmetric Openness is a condition in which internal political dissent is policed more aggressively than external exploitation or ideologically aligned actors who benefit from the system’s openness. Together, these dynamics erode democratic guardrails while leaving democratic self‑understanding intact.

The analysis foregrounds legal normalization, habit‑formation, and elite decision‑making under crisis framing rather than mass psychology, personality, or ideological content. Weimar Germany’s reliance on Article 48, selective repression and tolerated violence, and elite instrumentalization of anti‑pluralist movements are treated as a case study in how advanced societies gradually weaken their own restraints while maintaining constitutional form. Justice Antonin Scalia’s 1997 Holocaust Remembrance Day remarks are used as a diagnostic lens, highlighting the dangers of law detached from moral restraint, institutional self‑exemption, and civilizational hubris.

Applied to contemporary U.S. institutions, the framework emphasizes the normalization of emergency logic and norm flexibility, asymmetries in the treatment of internal dissent versus foreign influence, and media narratives—particularly “Trump‑as‑fascism”—that misidentify structural risk by centering personality rather than institutional behavior. The paper argues that Trump functions less as an elite‑indulged analogue to historical dictators than as a stress test of institutional resistance within a system already characterized by emergency normalization and asymmetric openness.

The argument is deliberately bounded. It does not claim outcome equivalence, inevitability, or deterministic repetition. Instead, it identifies the present moment as a pre‑catastrophic risk phase in which democratic guardrails remain formally in place but are weakened by elite hubris, normalized exception, and misdirected threat perception—conditions historically associated with democratic vulnerability rather than democratic collapse itself.

title: Revenue Dynamics in India :Direct vs Indirect Taxes (2014-2024)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Revenue Dynamics in India :Direct vs Indirect Taxes (2014-2024)

contentType.other: not yet published in any article

detail.abstract: This study undertakes a comparative analysis of revenue generation through direct and indirect taxes in India during the period 2014-2024, a decade marked by significant fiscal reforms and economic challenges. The research examines structural shifts in the tax system, with particular emphasis on the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax, (GST), corporate tax rationalization, and the new income tax regime. Using secondary data from government sources and applying statistical tools such as percentage analysis, year on year growth, CAGR and paired t test, the study evaluates trends, growth, patterns and relative  contribution of direct and indirect taxes to the Union Budget. The findings reveal a growing reliance on direct taxes, improved compliance, and simplification of indirect tax structures post-GST. Major events such as demonetization and the COVID -19 pandemic are shown to have reshaped tax collection dynamics. The study concludes that India's taxation system is evolving toward greater efficiency and equity, offering valuable insights for future fiscal policy and tax administration strategies.

title: Understanding Debanking: Evaluating Governmental, Operational, Political, and Religious Financial Account Closures
affiliations: Cato Institute

detail.title: Understanding Debanking: Evaluating Governmental, Operational, Political, and Religious Financial Account Closures
detail.abstract: This study examines the growing phenomenon of debanking—the sudden and often unexplained closure of individuals’ or organizations’ financial accounts. While media and political narratives often attribute these closures to political or religious discrimination, this study finds that the majority of debanking cases stem from governmental pressure. To identify this cause more accurately, the study distinguishes between four forms of debanking—governmental, operational, political, and religious—evaluating each form in turn. Based on public evidence, governmental debanking appears to be the most significant issue. Congress can correct this issue by reforming the Bank Secrecy Act, repealing confidentiality laws, and permanently ending reputational risk regulation. Doing so would reduce the incentives to debank, expose how widespread debanking has become, and cut out the tools that the government has used to pressure banks and other financial institutions.

title: The Inflationary Effects of Tax Increases: Evidence from the Final Consumer Burden
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Inflationary Effects of Tax Increases: Evidence from the Final Consumer Burden
detail.abstract: Conventional economic theory often posits taxation as a tool for fiscal consolidation and demand management, with ambiguous short-term effects on the price level. This paper challenges the view that tax increases are inherently disinflationary. It argues that, particularly in markets characterized by inelastic demand and concentrated supply, a significant portion of the tax burden is shifted forward to the final consumer. This forward shifting manifests as higher final prices, contributing directly to consumer price inflation. The paper employs a comparative analysis of recent fiscal policy shifts in several economies, correlating the implementation or increase of broad-based consumption taxes (e.g., Value-Added Tax or VAT) and specific excise duties with short-to-medium-term movements in headline and core inflation metrics. Empirical evidence from the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and Egypt supports the hypothesis that tax hikes, especially when enacted in a non-competitive economic environment or during supply-constrained periods, can exert significant upward pressure on prices, thereby fueling inflation.

title: Education, Algorithmic Governance and Human Ecosystems: Public Policies, Ethnic Plurality and Mental Health in Contexts of Social Reorganization

detail.title: Education, Algorithmic Governance and Human Ecosystems: Public Policies, Ethnic Plurality and Mental Health in Contexts of Social Reorganization

detail.abstract: The first decades of the XXI century have been marked by profound institutional transformations resulting from intensified migration flows, the crisis of classical models of the State, the reconfiguration of labor relations, and the massive incorporation of algorithmic systems into decision-making processes. In this context, education, health, law, and technology no longer operate as relatively autonomous fields, but rather as interdependent dimensions of a single process of social reorganization. This article proposes an ecosystem-based reading of educational public policies, articulating algorithmic governance, ethnic plurality, and mental health as inseparable axes in the contemporary production of subjectivities and social trajectories. It argues that the educational crisis should not be understood as a sectoral dysfunction, but as the manifestation of an ecosystemic failure, in which fragile institutional architectures generate youth frustration, the judicialization of school life, medicalization, and the precarization of future horizons. The STREAM model is introduced as a horizon for educational reorganization oriented toward the reconstruction of human ecosystems capable of integrating science, technology, culture, language, ethics, and care. Finally, it is argued that emancipatory educational public policies should be assessed less by performance indicators and more by their capacity to produce institutional conditions of existence, belonging, and social agency in contexts of algorithmic mediation.

title: Currency Pegs, Trade Imbalances and Unemployment: A Reevaluation of the China Shock
affiliations: Williams College, University of Navarra and Boston University

detail.title: Currency Pegs, Trade Imbalances and Unemployment: A Reevaluation of the China Shock

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We develop a dynamic quantitative model of trade and labor adjustment, incorporating nominal wage rigidity and consumption–saving decisions, to study how China’s currency peg interacted with its rapid growth in shaping the US economy. We show that the peg temporarily boosts China’s export growth by preventing an appreciation of the Chinese currency, thereby amplifying the US labor-market consequences of the China shock. At the same time, the temporary export boom increases China’s savings and leads to a larger US trade deficit. Calibrating the model to match trade and labor-market flow data, we find that China’s currency peg played a quantitatively important role in the US manufacturing decline, the widening US trade deficit, and unemployment dynamics. These results underscore the importance of exchange-rate adjustment (or the lack thereof) for understanding trade shocks. We also find that the overall welfare impact of the China shock remains significant and positive.

title: Hierarchy and Performance Pay: Experimental Evidence from the Public Sector
affiliations: Georgetown University - Department of Economics, University of Bristol and The World Bank

detail.title: Hierarchy and Performance Pay: Experimental Evidence from the Public Sector

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Frontline workers in public bureaucracies perform multidimensional tasks and rely on supervisors who both monitor performance and supply essential managerial inputs. We study how incentive design should account for these interactions using a conceptual framework and a province-wide randomized experiment with the Punjab Agriculture Extension Department in Pakistan. Across 131 tehsils, we compare: (i) an Objective pay-for-performance scheme tied to digital activity metrics; (ii) a Subjective scheme in which supervisors allocate bonuses; and (iii) a Subjective Plus scheme that preserves discretion but introduces light-touch oversight of supervisors. All three schemes increase outreach, but through distinct channels. Objective incentives primarily raise intensive effort—repeat visits to the same farmers—while Subjective Plus expands the extensive margin by inducing supervisors to schedule more farmer trainings and broaden geographic coverage. Contrary to standard multitasking concerns, meeting length—a proxy for engagement quality—increases across all arms. Oversight of supervisors also reduces favoritism in bonus allocation and improves merit-based evaluation, leading to greater access and yield gains among marginalized farmers. The results show that light-touch monitoring of middle management can substantially amplify the effectiveness and equity of performance pay in multi-layered bureaucracies.

title: Bank Income Smoothing and Loan Loss Provisioning Practices in Africa
