detail.title: Bank Income Smoothing and Loan Loss Provisioning Practices in Africa
detail.abstract: The primary objective of the thesis is to investigate whether African banks use loans loss provisions estimates to smooth reported earnings, and to determine the factors that influence the extent of earnings smoothing among African banks. Earnings smoothing via loan loss provision has been examined in several regions, but the case of Africa remain unexplored in the literature. In the thesis, earnings smoothing is viewed as an earnings management practice while loan loss provisions estimate is considered to be the tool used by African banks to smooth reported earnings. Using African bank data obtained from Bankscope database, I test the earnings smoothing hypothesis for 370 African banks during the 2002 to 2014 period using the specific-accrual approach. The specificaccrual approach estimates a specific discretionary accrual as a function of its non-discretionary determinants and other factors that influence the manipulation of the specific accrual. The model specification expresses discretionary loan loss provisions as a function of earnings before provisions and tax, its non-discretionary determinants and other factors that influence the decision regarding the level of bank provisions for each period. The findings indicate that African banks manipulate loan loss provisions estimates to smooth reported earnings and this behaviour is influenced by bank differences, accounting disclosure differences and institutional differences across African countries. The primary contribution to knowledge of the thesis is its extension of our understanding of the role of discretionary accruals in the bank financial reporting, focusing on African banks - a context that has not been extensively examined in the literature. Also, the thesis extends the bank earnings smoothing debate to the African context and the findings of this study are useful to bank regulators in Africa in their evaluation of whether bank loan loss provisions solely reflect credit risk considerations or whether bank loan loss provisions estimates reflect opportunistic considerations of African bank managers. Finally, the findings are useful to local accounting standard setters in the region in their evaluation of several accounting numbers that bank managers might use to manipulate reported earnings.

title: Marriage and the Intergenerational Mobility of Women: Evidence from Marriage Certificates 1850-1920

detail.title: Marriage and the Intergenerational Mobility of Women: Evidence from Marriage Certificates 1850-1920

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We document that women’s economic mobility improved nearly a century before married women gained broad labor market opportunities. Using Massachusetts marriage registers linked to U.S. censuses (1850–1920), we create new father–child links for women to estimate intergenerational mobility and assortative mating, overcoming a key historical linkage barrier. Estimates from a structural marriage market model suggest assortative mating fell 61% from 1850–1870 to 1900–1920. Counterfactuals imply women’s mobility would have been far lower absent the decline in assortative mating. Had late cohorts faced early cohort sorting, the rank–rank slope between a woman’s father and husband would have been 2.5 times higher.

title: Incentives and Prosocial Discomfort: A Laboratory Experiment
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, , University of Bologna, Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Incentives and Prosocial Discomfort: A Laboratory Experiment

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We conducted a within-subject laboratory experiment in which participants decided whether to experience physical discomfort for charity, with or without additional personal compensation. Acceptance decreased with greater discomfort and increased with both larger charitable donations and personal payments. We show that private monetary incentives and prosocial benefits interact in a less-than-additive way: personal compensation raises participation but attenuates the marginal impact of charitable donations, making the combined impact of private and social rewards smaller than the sum of their separate effects. We also find suggestive evidence that the sequencing of compensated and uncompensated choices may change the responsiveness to charitable benefits. Overall, our results indicate that context, especially the presence (and timing) of private rewards, can affect the relationship between incentives and prosocial behavior.

title: Threshold Disclosure in Collective Decisions
affiliations: Bocconi University, University of Chicago - Department of Economics and University of Chicago

detail.title: Threshold Disclosure in Collective Decisions

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Voting-based collective decisions are typically made either anonymously or publicly. Anonymous voting protects truthful expression but conceals individual behavior; public voting provides information about individual votes, but, when one option is socially stigmatized, it can distort participation and choices. We introduce threshold majority voting, in which voters choose a disclosure threshold determining whether and when their votes are revealed. In an experiment at UC Berkeley on the participation of transgender women in women’s sports, public voting nearly doubles abstention and reduces support for the stigmatized option. Threshold voting eliminates these distortions while revealing one-third of individual votes.

title: Interest Rate Pass-Through With Adjustable Rate Mortgages
affiliations: Duke University, Nova School of Business and Economics and

detail.title: Interest Rate Pass-Through With Adjustable Rate Mortgages

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) transmit monetary policy less directly than often assumed. We exploit quasi-experimental variation in ARM rate reset timing in Portugal—where over 92% of mortgages are indexed to Euribor—around the ECB’s 2022–2023 tightening cycle to estimate responses to mortgage payment shocks. After reset dates, mortgage renegotiations increase by 10 percentage points, lender switching by 4, partial prepayments by 5, and full prepayments by 3, offsetting about 17% of the payment increase implied by policy rates. Responses occur only immediately after resets, consistent with selective inattention, and are largest among younger, more educated, and higher-balance borrowers. Supply-side factors amplify these effects: as rates rise and bank competition intensifies, households at more flexible banks renegotiate, switch lenders, and prepay more, while greater broker presence further increases lender switching. Our findings suggest that monetary policy pass-through in ARM-dominated markets depends on borrower behavior, market frictions, and sticky deposit rates.

title: Seeing Green: The Effects of Financial Exposures on Support for Climate Action
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Stanford Graduate School of Business, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and University of Toronto

detail.title: Seeing Green: The Effects of Financial Exposures on Support for Climate Action

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Despite the large common net benefits of climate mitigation, broad-based political consensus for large-scale policy action remains elusive. We hypothesize that financial exposure to energy stocks central to the green transition can induce learning and greater support for climate mitigation policies. We conduct a RCT which randomizes both the presence of financial market exposure to the energy sector, as well as which type of portfolio—fossil-fuel (brown) or renewable energy (green)—is given to an individual. Treatment increases support for mitigation action and intent to undertake adaptation, with positive support caused by ownership of both green and brown assets. The effects are particularly pronounced among individuals who are initially more climate-skeptic, and persist eight months after treatment. We present evidence consistent with learning as the primary mechanism: treated respondents are more likely to consume financial news and become more financially knowledgeable, less likely to obtain news from polarized sources, and better able to accurately predict the environmental impacts of green and brown firms.

title: Post-GDPR Regulatory Enforcement of UK Data Protection: Reality, Scrutiny, Oversight and Future
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Faculty of  Law

detail.title: Post-GDPR Regulatory Enforcement of UK Data Protection: Reality, Scrutiny, Oversight and Future

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No. 1/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The General Data Protection Regulation and associated legal reforms in 2018 promised strong regulatory enforcement secured primarily through comprehensive and dissuasive fines. Although this law has largely continued post-Brexit, UK regulatory realities are starkly - and generally increasingly – different.  Despite receiving a yearly average of nearly 40,000 complaints alleging data protection infringement, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) issued an average of just 6.6 fines each year from 2018/19 to 2024/25.  In 2024/25 itself this figure was just 2 and totalled a mere £3.8m.  There were also zero enforcement notice actions in 2024/25 and, on average, only 1.7 such actions since 2018/19 which highlights a lack of robust appropriate measures compensating for limited fines.  Effective scrutiny of individual ICO decisions has not been secured through the Tribunal, the Ombudsman or the High Court. The ICO’s parliamentary oversight committee has, in general, also failed to ensure systematic holistic accountability and the Equality and Human Rights Commission has entirely avoided addressing enforcement issues.  Notably by placing the ICO under a range of new duties which sit in tension with data protection, the Data (Use and Access) Act may exacerbate current realities.  Nevertheless, following revelation of the 2022 Afghan data breach and the absence of ICO investigation, the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee has committed to securing enhanced accountability.  The Ombudsman has also indicated that the ICO must respond to complaints with, at least, a probabilistic assessment of compliance.  Finally, UK case law has affirmed that the Tribunal must objectively and independently ensure the appropriateness of ICO investigations of complaints and, in relation to judicial review, persuasive Court of Justice case law has enunciated a far-reaching lawfulness obligation of supervisory authorities to respond to infringements through use of formal corrective powers other than in truly exceptional and enumerated situations.

title: Bank Failures: The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Bank Failures: The Roles of Solvency and Liquidity

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1181
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Bank failures can stem from runs on otherwise solvent banks or from losses that render banks insolvent, regardless of withdrawals. Disentangling the relative importance of liquidity and solvency in explaining bank failures is central to understanding financial crises and designing effective financial stability policies. This paper reviews evidence on the causes of bank failures. Bank failures-both with and without runs-are almost always related to poor fundamentals. Low recovery rates in failure suggest that most failed banks that experienced runs were likely fundamentally insolvent. Examiners' postmortem assessments also emphasize the primacy of poor asset quality and solvency problems. Before deposit insurance, runs commonly triggered the failure of insolvent banks. However, runs rarely caused the failure of strong banks, as such runs were typically resolved through other mechanisms, including interbank cooperation, equity injections, public signals of strength, or suspension of convertibility. We discuss the policy implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

title: Risk-informed Credibility Assessment for Clinical AI/ML Models: A Practical Stage-based Pathway with ISCT-oriented Case Walkthroughs
affiliations: Biomedical Engineering Research Center, Asan Institute for Life Sciences, Asan Medical Center

detail.title: Risk-informed Credibility Assessment for Clinical AI/ML Models: A Practical Stage-based Pathway with ISCT-oriented Case Walkthroughs
detail.abstract:
Background and Objectives 
Clinical AI/ML models increasingly inform healthcare and decision support, yet credibility appraisal is often ad hoc—especially for non-deterministic, lifecycle-dependent models. A risk-informed, stage-based diagnostic pathway is proposed to plan and audit credibility evidence in in silico clinical trial (ISCT) settings and related evaluation pipelines, without introducing scores or maturity levels.
Methods
Question of interest (QOI), context of use (COU), and model risk assessment are operationalized by adapting credibility principles from computational modeling guidance (e.g., ASME V&V 40; FDA credibility guidance). Evidence is organized into five stages: data quality assessment, internal validation, external validation, scenario-based evaluation of decision relevance and robustness, and post-deployment monitoring and change control. Explainability, dataset shift/drift susceptibility, and update intent are treated as cross-cutting evidence targets, supported by a minimal documentation set.
Results
Two retrospective, publication-based walkthroughs were conducted. For an acute ischemic stroke outcome prediction study, gaps were identified in external validation of newly developed models, subgroup calibration evidence, and lifecycle monitoring intent. For a dynamic kidney failure prediction model with prospective external validation, residual implementation-facing gaps persisted despite decision-curve analysis, particularly COU-linked operating thresholds, quantitative calibration/uncertainty at clinically relevant horizons, and monitoring/update planning.
Conclusions
The pathway offers a practical, risk-tiered approach to plan and audit credibility evidence, shifting attention beyond discrimination toward COU-linked reliability, clinical utility, and lifecycle readiness.

title: Existential Risk and Axiomatic Rationality: Lexical Convergence within Expected Utility Theory
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Existential Risk and Axiomatic Rationality: Lexical Convergence within Expected Utility Theory
detail.abstract: Standard Expected Utility Theory (EUT) is widely believed to fail or yield paradoxical results when outcomes include ``infinite value'' or existential risk. This paper demonstrates that when such outcomes are modeled as \emph{structurally non-compensable}---absorbing states that permanently foreclose future value---standard vNM representations exhibit determinate limiting behavior without ad hoc axiom modifications. We prove that under axiom-preserving affine normalization, the presence of a structurally non-compensable outcome forces all finite utilities to compress into a vanishing band. In the limit, this compression induces a lexicographic ordering: policies are ranked first by their probability of avoiding extinction, and secondarily, in the case of a tie, by expected utility over finite outcomes. Crucially, this lexicographic structure is not primitively postulated (as in classical lexicographic preference theory) but emerges as the unique limit of Archimedean expected-utility representations. For any finite menu of policies, the standard EUT ordering stabilizes to exact lexicographic comparison for sufficiently severe modeling of non-compensability. We further prove that major alternative decision theories (Rank-Dependent Utility, Cumulative Prospect Theory) converge to this same rule in existential domains, suggesting structural robustness rather than a theory-specific artifact. These results resolve the apparent conflict between standard rationality axioms and strong intuitive priority for extinction avoidance, providing axiomatic foundations and normative authority for economic policy analysis of modern existential risks such as those of AI safety and climate tipping points.

title: Energy Five Imperatives Framework (E-5IF): A Utilitarian -Bargaining and Human-Rights Proportionality Framework for Energy Regulation
affiliations: King’s College London, Dickson Poon School of Law

detail.title: Energy Five Imperatives Framework (E-5IF): A Utilitarian -Bargaining and Human-Rights Proportionality Framework for Energy Regulation
detail.abstract:
Energy regulators and governments increasingly face decisions that must reconcile fast-changing electricity demand (including from digitalisation, AI and data centre growth) with security of supply, affordability, sustainability, distributional equity and the speed of delivery. Existing “energy trilemma” framings are helpful but often too static for time-dependent choices that are also legally contestable. This paper proposes the Energy Five Imperatives Framework (E-5IF) as a practical decision aid that couples (i) a utilitarian compromise-selection mechanism based on Nash bargaining with (ii) a court-aware proportionality/necessity audit to strengthen legitimacy, transparency and defensibility of regulatory choices. E-5IF makes explicit five imperatives: security; affordability and access; sustainability (life-cycle impacts, not only greenhouse-gas emissions); equity (distribution of burdens and benefits); and timing (consistent with intergenerational fairness). Decision-makers set minimum acceptable levels for each imperative, screen out unacceptable options, and then select a defensible compromise. In Step 1, policy alternatives are scored by defining imperative-specific “gains” relative to a baseline and computing a Nash bargaining score (Nash product or equivalent monotone aggregation) that rewards balanced improvements and penalises options that advance one objective by collapsing another. In Step 2, the preferred option is documented through a four-stage proportionality analysis, legitimate aim, suitability, necessity and proportionality stricto sensu, linking technical trade-offs to the structured reasoning used in judicial and oversight review. A stylised UK example compares three packages for rapid demand growth, selects an option that improves security without compromising sustainability, and articulates that choice through the audit for accountability in review or litigation. The framework is further positioned to address Brazil-oriented regulatory design questions (e.g., battery storage and smart metering operators) and, more broadly, contexts where infrastructure constraints and emerging technologies intensify conflicts among public aims.

The E-5IF is available at www.e-5if.com to help the decision making on public policies or project selection.

title:
Gaining Leverage Over the U.S. Housing Shortage:
How the Private Capital Markets are Enhancing U.S. Fiscal Policy to Expand Affordable Housing

detail.title:
Gaining Leverage Over the U.S. Housing Shortage:
How the Private Capital Markets are Enhancing U.S. Fiscal Policy to Expand Affordable Housing
detail.abstract: With $1.1 billion in national allocation capacity of so-called “9% tax credits” annually, enhanced by $48.3 billion in annual private activity bond issuance in connection with projects qualifying for so-called “4% tax credits,” as of 2025, the U.S. federal government’s Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program – pursuant to Section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) of 1986 – accounts for the production of approximately 25% of the multifamily housing unit construction in the U.S. each year. This production, averaging roughly 86,000 units per annum since 1990, pales in comparison to the estimated housing unit supply shortage of 4.7 million to 4.9 million total units, and is even more daunting when contrasted with the estimated 7.1 million unit shortage in the case of households earning 30% or less of the Area Median Income. After considering the pace of obsolescence of existing housing units, it would take current levels of affordable housing production well over a century to eliminate the shortfall in supply. Resistance to increased federal spending – even after a substantial increase in LIHTC allocations and other assistance to the industry under the first and second Trump administrations (most recently in the One Big Beautiful Act of 2025, “OBBA”) – makes it unlikely that the housing gap can be closed via fiscal outlays alone, however efficient the program has proven itself to be in terms of both economic (fiscal) multipliers and social benefits. Yet there has been substantial promise emerging from private efforts to leverage fiscal inputs through a novel debt capital markets solution that pulls forward long-dated economic returns to owner/developers of affordable multifamily housing portfolios using a customized, investment-grade-rated asset-backed securities (ABS) structure, thus enabling the development of nearly 28% new (as well as preservation of existing) LIHTC-eligible housing units pursuant to the assumptions set forth herein. This relatively new financial tool produces demonstrable increases the macroeconomic benefits to the economy (thus increasing the fiscal multipliers) derived from the original tax credit outlays by a demonstrable factor of over 17%. Further, this form of financing is a timely compliment to provisions of the OBBA providing for both (i) the permanent increase in 9% tax credits; and (ii) the reduction in required amounts of tax-exempt mortgage debt required to secure as-of-right 4% tax credits under the LIHTC program. Several versions of this financing vehicle have raised over $4 billion in proceeds for the affordable housing industry since 2019. This paper covers the challenges impacting the provision of adequate quantities of housing in the United States; specific problems posed in the development of affordable housing, particularly in areas with high land cost; an outline of the Affordable Housing Future Flow Contributive ABS transaction (AHFFC-ABS) that has been the dominant form of the type of issuance referenced above; and the implications of such a private sector tool in acting as a force and fiscal multiplier of the policy goals of Congress related to the production of affordable housing.

title: Promoting Collaborative Care: Relative Performance-based Payment Models for Hospitals and Post-acute Care Providers
affiliations: UCL School of Management, University College London, Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University and Rice University

detail.title: Promoting Collaborative Care: Relative Performance-based Payment Models for Hospitals and Post-acute Care Providers
detail.abstract: Bundled payment models are widely used in healthcare reimbursement but they were primarily designed for conditions managed by a single provider in a centralized manner. Therefore, these models do not account for the complexities of conditions requiring post-acute care (PAC) after hospitalization, resulting in weak incentives for care coordination between hospitals and PAC providers, particularly in decentralized settings. Motivated by the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) payment model introduced by CMS—which holds hospitals accountable for the cost and quality of the entire episode, including PAC—we examine the eﬀectiveness of existing payment models in decentralized care. Our analysis shows that bundled payment models and the CJR framework, especially without gainsharing agreements, do not fully align provider incentives. To address these shortcomings, we propose a payment model that explicitly links hospital and PAC provider reimbursements. Using a game-theoretical framework, we show that this model results in socially optimal provider actions. Moreover, we establish that similar eﬃciency gains can be achieved within the CJR framework if hospitals and PAC providers adopt structured gainsharing agreements. Numerical simulations show that implementing this approach could reduce readmission costs by 12%, generating over $150 million in annual savings for Medicare joint replacement procedures alone.

title: Asymmetric Cost Behavior and Non-Financial Firms' Risky Financial Investments
affiliations: University of Mississippi - Department of Finance

detail.title: Asymmetric Cost Behavior and Non-Financial Firms' Risky Financial Investments
detail.abstract: Using hand-collected data on non-financial firms' financial portfolios, I examine how asymmetric cost behavior (or cost stickiness) affects risky financial investments. Sticky costs amplify the downward effect of sales decrease on profits because costs do not fall when sales decrease by as much as they rise when sales increase. Firms with sticky selling, general, and administrative costs (SG&A) avoid risky securities because of expected liquidity needs and the trade-off between operating and financial risk. For firms with sticky costs, investing in risky securities increases total and idiosyncratic stock volatility without creating shareholder value.

title: From Developmental Success to Constitutional Trap: Why Human Dignity must Guide Constitutional Design after Catch-Up Development

detail.title: From Developmental Success to Constitutional Trap: Why Human Dignity must Guide Constitutional Design after Catch-Up Development
detail.abstract:
Under what conditions do institutions that enable catch-up development become binding constraints once economies reach the technological frontier? This paper argues that post-catch-up development is governed less by policy choice than by constitutional time-horizon architecture, and that human dignity must operate as the constitutional meta-principle guiding constitutional design and evolution. Here, dignity is understood institutionally: as the constitutional duty of the state to protect individuals’ and communities’ capacity for long-horizon self-directed life planning, rather than managing them instrumentally through short-term political intervention.

The paper introduces a constitutional time horizons framework distinguishing political, administrative, and constitutional horizons, and shows how Korea’s 1987 democratization dismantled personalized long-horizon mechanisms without constitutional replacement. Developmental-state provisions (Articles 117, 119[2]) were preserved while political time was compressed to five-year electoral cycles (Article 70), producing a structural temporal mismatch: institutions designed for long horizons now operating under short democratic cycles.

Post-catch-up innovation requires distributed experimentation and learning cycles that exceed electoral terms, but constitutional centralization and compressed horizons systematically suppress both. This credibility deficit manifests most starkly in demographic collapse. Korea exhibits a distinctive reversal in the fertility–growth correlation (from −0.073 to +0.533), a pattern rarely observed among advanced economies. No actor intends fertility collapse; it emerges endogenously as households rationally avoid irreversible life commitments under a constitutional order that cannot credibly protect long-horizon expectations—a dignity failure at constitutional scale.

Comparative analysis with Mexico demonstrates that constitutional entrenchment of long-horizon commitments becomes outcome-determining under post-catch-up conditions characterized by radical uncertainty, capital mobility, compressed political horizons, and centralized authority.

title: Economic Diversity and the Resilience of Cities
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis and

detail.title: Economic Diversity and the Resilience of Cities

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: We develop a framework to assess how economic shocks affect local labor markets and worker welfare, with a focus on city-level economic diversity. Using detailed worker flow data across cities, sectors, and occupations, we construct theory-consistent welfare measures. Our approach combines a dynamic discrete choice model with a dual representation that captures both direct effects and the insurance value of local economic diversity. Applied to French labor markets, we find that diversification dampens the effect of negative shocks: both job-to-job moves and net inflows decline less in diverse cities than in concentrated ones. Overall, we document sizable welfare insurance gains from local economic diversity.

title: What Do LLMs Want?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, , Federal Reserve Board of Governors and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: What Do LLMs Want?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-006, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.006]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now used for economic reasoning, but their implicit "preferences" are poorly understood. We study these preferences by analyzing revealed choices in canonical allocation games and a sequential job-search environment. In dictator-style allocation games, most models favor equal splits, consistent with inequality aversion. Structural estimation of Fehr-Schmidt parameters suggests this aversion exceeds levels typically observed in human experiments. However, LLM preferences prove malleable. Interventions such as prompt framing (e.g., masking social context) and control vectors reliably shift models toward more payoff-maximizing behavior, while persona-based prompting has more limited impact. We then extend our analysis to a sequential decision-making environment based on the McCall job search model. Here, we recover implied discount factors from accept/reject behavior, but find that responses are less consistently rationalizable and preferences more fragile. Our findings highlight two core insights: (i) LLMs exhibit structured, latent preferences that often align with human behavioral norms, and (ii) these preferences can be steered, albeit more effectively in simple settings than in complex, dynamic ones.

title: Impact Assessment of Agricultural Technologies: Econometric Approach
affiliations: ICAR Sugarcane Breeding Institute,  and Rani Lakshmi Bai Central Agricultural University

detail.title: Impact Assessment of Agricultural Technologies: Econometric Approach

publicationDetails.detailsText: P. Murali, P. Jagadeshwaran and V. David Chella Baskar. 2025. Impact Assessment of Agricultural Technologies: Econometric Approach. In P. Murali, Lakshmi Pathy, T, Vinayaka and Jagadeshwaran, P (Eds.). Basic and Applied R programming for Agricultural Research (pp. 193-204). ISBN 978-81-998370-8-9

detail.abstract:
This chapter presents a comprehensive econometric framework for assessing the causal impact of agricultural technologies on key outcomes such as crop yield, farm income, and technology adoption. Impact evaluation in agriculture is often challenged by selection bias, non-random program placement, and endogeneity arising from observational data. To address these issues, the chapter systematically discusses major quasi-experimental econometric methods that enable credible counterfactual construction in non-experimental settings. The core approaches covered include Propensity Score Matching (PSM), Difference-in-Differences (DID), and Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), with emphasis on their assumptions, identification strategies, estimation procedures, and practical implementation.

The chapter explains how PSM reduces observable selection bias through statistical matching, how DID controls for time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity using before-and-after comparisons between treatment and control groups, and how RDD exploits eligibility thresholds to identify local causal effects. Conceptual foundations are supported with mathematical formulations and graphical illustrations of common support, double-difference estimation, and discontinuity-based identification. In addition, the chapter provides applied R programming examples for each method, enabling researchers to implement matching, treatment effect estimation, diagnostic checks, and visualization of results.

 By integrating econometric theory with reproducible R-based workflows, this chapter serves as a practical guide for researchers, students, and practitioners engaged in agricultural impact assessment. It facilitates rigorous evaluation of technology interventions and supports evidence-based decision-making in agricultural research and policy design.

title: Building Trust and Emotional Safety in Public Sector Change Initiatives
affiliations: Cape Breton University and Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University (TSU)

detail.abstract: Purpose: Public sector reforms frequently fail not due to technical design flaws, but because they neglect the emotional experiences of civil servants during change. This article examines emotion-centred change management within Georgia's public administration reform and proposes an integrated framework that synthesises behavioral and strategic perspectives to enhance reform implementation in transitional governance systems. Originality/significance/value: This is one of the first studies to operationalise emotion-centred change management for public-sector reform in a post-Soviet transitional setting. It presents an empirically grounded framework that treats emotional readiness as a strategic variable and shows how synchronising emotional, behavioural and structural dimensions can stabilise reform outcomes.

title: Deploying The "Trade Bazooka": How The Anti-Coercion Instrument Reshapes EU Public Procurement
affiliations: and George Washington University - Law School

detail.title: Deploying The "Trade Bazooka": How The Anti-Coercion Instrument Reshapes EU Public Procurement

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-14
publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: As trade disputes continue to batter the relationship between the U.S. and its partners in the European Union, a new countermeasure by the EU—the Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI)—has emerged as a serious threat to trade flows, including in public procurement. Although formally framed as a trade-defense mechanism, the ACI is a legal instrument capable of addressing a broad range of economic coercion. Notably, although the ACI is presented as a means of deterrence and de-escalation, the ACI authorizes countermeasures that extend well beyond tariffs, and can severely restrict foreign firms’ access to EU public procurement markets. This article provides an historical overview of the ACI, explains how it operates, and postulates what its implementation could mean for public procurement. With special attention to the geopolitical shifts which shaped the ACI, the article reviews a new operational landscape for transatlantic procurement markets that may prove vulnerable to clashes among allies.

title: Feedback on Blood, Tissues, and Cells for Medical Treatments - Revised EU Rules (2022)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Academies of Loudoun, Academies of Loudoun

detail.title: Feedback on Blood, Tissues, and Cells for Medical Treatments - Revised EU Rules (2022)
detail.abstract: Biotechnology for rare diseases and paediatric conditions has advanced substantially over the past two decades, particularly through the development of recombinant technologies, biomarker-guided therapeutics, and nucleic-acid–based platforms such as mRNA. These innovations have transformed the scientific feasibility of designing highly targeted therapies for small and heterogeneous patient populations, including children. In principle, these advances should have enabled a new generation of individualised treatments for rare and paediatric diseases. A similar translational challenge exists in the governance and use of substances of human origin (SoHOs), including blood, tissues, and cells, where scientific capability has advanced more rapidly than regulatory harmonisation and public trust mechanisms.In practice, however, scientific progress has not translated into commensurate therapeutic availability. Despite nearly twenty years of EU legislation intended to stimulate innovation in this space, the majority of rare diseases, especially paediatric rare diseases, still lack authorised and effective treatment options. Evaluations of the Orphan Regulation (EC No 141/2000) and the Paediatric Regulation (EC No 1901/2006) demonstrate that while incentives have increased the number of authorised medicines, they have disproportionately benefited conditions with existing development pathways, leaving many high-unmet-need diseases without viable therapies.The European Commission’s proposed revisions to the pharmaceutical framework, including the recalibration of incentives for orphan and paediatric medicines, represent a necessary and timely intervention. MediQuills supports the Commission’s objective of improving the availability, accessibility, and affordability of medicines for children and patients with rare diseases. However, the effectiveness of these reforms will depend on whether they explicitly address structural weaknesses in the biotechnology–pharmaceutical pipeline, introduce regulatory flexibility proportionate to scientific and clinical risk, and align incentives with genuinely unmet medical need rather than incremental innovation.This paper analyses the disconnect between biotechnology innovation and pharmaceutical manufacturing for specialised therapies, evaluates limitations in the current legislative framework, and proposes targeted policy refinements. MediQuills recommends strengthening support for recombinant and biomarker-driven platforms, streamlining regulatory pathways, enabling flexible clinical trial designs for small populations, and improving transparency in incentive monitoring. With these modifications, EU reforms are more likely to translate scientific innovation into durable, equitable therapeutic access for paediatric and rare-disease populations across Europe.

title: Pollution Accumulation and the Role of Developing Countries in International Environmental Agreements
affiliations: Kyushu University and Kyushu University

detail.title: Pollution Accumulation and the Role of Developing Countries in International Environmental Agreements
detail.abstract: This study develops a long-term strategic framework for international environmental agreements (IEAs), incorporating countries’ concerns about the cumulative nature of pollution over time. It compares the stability and social welfare of agreements limited to developed countries with those that also include developing countries. The results show that coalition stability depends on the ratio of abatement costs to benefits as well as on countries’ environmental awareness. Importantly, the participation of developing countries does not weaken long-term cooperation among developed countries. With respect to overall welfare, participation by developing countries is efficient if their abatement costs are lower than the global benefits they generate; otherwise, it is inefficient. This highlights the importance of reducing the cost burden on developing countries to ensure their effective involvement. Without such measures, an IEA limited to developed countries may yield greater overall benefits. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that when developing countries are involved, harmonizing abatement costs is more effective than harmonizing abatement quantities.

title: High Equity Risk Premia with Near-Unit Risk Aversion
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: High Equity Risk Premia with Near-Unit Risk Aversion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The Equity Risk Premium (ERP) puzzle persists because standard consumption-based models cannot justify observed premia without imputing implausibly high risk aversion (CRRA>4 ). This paper resolves the anomaly by decoupling equity valuation from aggregate consumption and focusing on the long-term variance of the dividend stream itself. Applying Green-Kubo relations to a model of stochastic drift resets, we demonstrate that standard estimation techniques systematically understate long-term risk by assuming constant drift. When accounted for, the variance of the dividend stream is not the placid 55 basis points (bps) observed in quarterly samples but exceeds 190 bps-an annualized volatility of at least 14%. Empirical estimation associates an average risk premium of 400 bps with CRRA ~1,3, consistent with the "robust control" preferences of wealth-maximizing investors. The finding that long-term dividend volatility rivals market volatility challenges the "irrational exuberance" hypothesis, suggesting instead that markets identified risks better than their main critics.

title: Politics in Aisle 3: Whether and How Brand Sociopolitical Involvement Shapes Customer Store Visits
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business, Marketing Department, Students and University of Southern California

detail.title: Politics in Aisle 3: Whether and How Brand Sociopolitical Involvement Shapes Customer Store Visits
detail.abstract: We examine how brands' sociopolitical involvement affects customer store visits. We assemble a unique, large-scale dataset that combines granular weekly foot traffic for approximately 150,000 U.S. stores operated by 47 major brands from 2018-2022 with detailed local demographic and presidential election data to characterize store neighborhoods and visitors. We then use Google News to identify instances of sociopolitical involvement associated with these brands, spanning issues such as firearm regulation, race, and sexual orientation, and arising from either corporate actions or employee behavior. To estimate the impact of each event, we apply a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences model combined with Coarsened Exact Matching, comparing foot traffic at affected versus unaffected brands' stores. On average, sociopolitical involvement leads to a 0.8% decline in store visits, with substantial heterogeneity across events. Corporate-initiated actions tend to generate more variable and less negative responses than employee-triggered incidents. Moreover, brands' subsequent responses—such as public apologies or employee training initiatives—appear to attenuate negative consumer reactions. Three case studies further show that these effects vary systematically with store neighborhood characteristics, including political preferences and racial composition. To our knowledge, this study is among the first large-scale empirical research to examine the effects of brands' sociopolitical involvement on consumer store visits.

title: Conversational AI and Transparency Statements: Design Options and Impact on User Perceptions
affiliations: SINTEF Digital, SINTEF Digital, Telenor, SINTEF Digital and boost.ai

detail.title: Conversational AI and Transparency Statements: Design Options and Impact on User Perceptions
detail.abstract: Conversational AI powered by large language models is increasingly seen as an attractive technology for customer service due to its ability to provide fluent, efficient support. However, the technology's humanlike qualities can make it hard for users to realize they're interacting with an AI rather than a human employee, and the unpredictability of LLMs increases the risk of misleading or inaccurate outputs. This creates a conversational AI transparency design challenge: How can we disclose conversational AI use and communicate its limitations in ways that users notice and understand? To address this, we conducted two complementary studies examining user perceptions and the effects of transparency statements (disclosures and disclaimers) in customer service contexts. In Study 1 (N = 300), participants evaluated multiple transparency design options presented as chat screenshots, varying statement wording and placement (e.g., top/bottom of the interface vs. message-level labels with and without tooltips). The results indicate that participants' preferences were driven primarily by visual prominence and low interaction cost; clear wording at the top or bottom of the interface was often seen as beneficial, tooltipbased designs were seen as easy to miss, and selective message-level labeling risked confusing users about which messages were AI-generated. In Study 2 (N = 208), participants interacted with a GPT4o-powered conversational AI prototype under three conditions (no disclosure, disclosure only, disclosure and disclaimer). The results show that many participants did not notice or retain the transparency statements, and we found no significant differences across conditions in regard to trust, willingness to use, or likelihood of following advice. Together, the results suggest that while transparency statements are necessary to comply with transparency requirements and have been thought to be beneficial for trust calibration, designing transparency statements that users notice and remember remains an important design challenge.

title: Border Adjustment Taxes, Carbon Pricing, and the Stability of Trade Agreements
affiliations: Western University and Ryerson University

detail.title: Border Adjustment Taxes, Carbon Pricing, and the Stability of Trade Agreements
detail.abstract: Border adjustment taxes (BATs) are intended to equalize the cost of carbon between domestic and foreign producers, yet their broader effects on trade and cooperation remain uncertain. We show that when countries differ in production carbon intensity, BATs can have unintended strategic consequences. In equilibrium, BATs undermine free market access and cleaner importers that impose BATs become isolated, while countries with weaker or intermediate environmental standards form stable trade alliances. These “dirty coalitions” expand trade among less regulated exporters but reduce the prospects for inclusive global cooperation. The analysis highlights how policies intended to support climate goals can also reshape the geography of trade and limit the scope for collective action.

title: On Conditional and Unconditional Quantile DiD: Identification, Weighting, and Estimation

detail.title: On Conditional and Unconditional Quantile DiD: Identification, Weighting, and Estimation
detail.abstract: We study quantile difference-indifferences (DiD) in panel settings and clarify the relationship between conditional and unconditional quantile DiD estimands. We formalize Conditional Quantile DiD (CQDD) and Unconditional Quantile DiD (UCQDD), show that they coincide without covariates but generally diverge with covariates, and provide intuition for why empirical "conditional" and "unconditional" procedures can differ even in simple designs. We then analyze two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) implementations based on quantile regression and recentered influence functions. While TWFE identifies the intended quantile DiD contrast in the canonical 2 × 2 design, it delivers density-weighted mixtures with multiple post-treatment periods and, under staggered adoption, combines cohort-time effects with potentially negative weights, undermining causal interpretation. Motivated by these results, we propose clean quantile DiD estimators for staggered adoption based on valid cohort-time comparisons and transparent convex aggregation. Simulations show that the proposed estimators eliminate the large distortions that can arise from TWFE quantile regressions under heterogeneous effects and staggered timing.

title: The Broken Home Effect: Relationship Disruptions Trigger Loss of Meaning and Increase Spending on Eudaimonic Product Categories
affiliations: Department of Marketing, Monash Business School, Monash University - Department of Marketing, INCAE - INCAE Business School, University of Alberta - Department of Marketing, Business Economics & Law and Babson College - Marketing Division

detail.title: The Broken Home Effect: Relationship Disruptions Trigger Loss of Meaning and Increase Spending on Eudaimonic Product Categories

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: Relationship disruptions such as death of a spouse and divorce are among the most impactful events in someone's life, yet current retailing literature does not document their influence on shopping behavior. In this research, we study the effect of relational disruptions on the shift in basket-level purchases towards specific value orientations (utilitarian vs. hedonic vs. eudaimonic). Since people derive meaning from their social connections, we expect that relational disruptions shift basket-level purchases towards product categories that offer more eudaimonic value, reflecting a search for deeper meaning. We apply difference-indifference models and propensity score matching to a longitudinal datasets of U.S. households' purchase data of 998 product sub-categories, finding that households experiencing such negative life events spend more on products high in eudaimonic value-a finding we term the broken home effect. The effect attenuates when other family members are present in the household. A follow-up experiment addresses endogeneity concerns by providing a causal replication of this effect, and reveals search for meaning as the most likely underlying mechanism. These findings contribute to literature on life events and retailing, and offer key managerial implications for category management and retail strategy.

title: Tax Department Design, Tax Planning, and Tax Risk
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business, ,  and

detail.title: Tax Department Design, Tax Planning, and Tax Risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series No. 2026-02
publicationDetails.journalName: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite the central role of corporate tax departments in managing multinational enterprises' (MNEs) global tax positions, little is known about how their internal design shapes corporate tax behavior. Drawing on hand-collected data on more than 8,000 tax employees across 309 publicly listed European MNEs, we examine the association between tax department centralization and firm-level tax outcomes. We find no evidence for tax department centralization being associated with the overall level of tax planning. However, firms with more centralized tax departments engage in greater cross-border profit shifting, respond less to local tax incentives, and face higher tax risk. These findings suggest that tax department design shapes the means rather than the intensity of corporate tax planning. Our study extends the emerging literature on tax department design and provides insights for managers responsible for corporate tax strategies as well as for policymakers anticipating organizational responses to international tax reforms.

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5m Neighborhoods
affiliations: World Bank Development Research Group (DECRG), , Dartmouth College - Department of Economics, University of Chicago and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards, and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the U.S. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities-at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy.

title: From Interpretive Trust to Execution Authority: Runtime Epistemic Governance in Autonomous Systems

detail.title: From Interpretive Trust to Execution Authority: Runtime Epistemic Governance in Autonomous Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript is a conceptual and theoretical analysis and does not involve human participants, animals, or personal data.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces runtime execution authority as the conceptual successor to interpretive epistemic governance in autonomous systems. Building on recent scholarship that reframes trust as an epistemic and institutional achievement under uncertainty, the paper argues that interpretive governance becomes insufficient once computational systems acquire executional agency. The contribution is intentionally conceptual rather than prescriptive. It does not propose technical architectures, enforcement mechanisms, or regulatory instruments. Instead, it clarifies a governance distinction that becomes unavoidable as systems move from advising to acting: the separation of intelligence, which proposes actions, from authority, which permits them. The paper is intended for readers in AI governance, law, public policy, and institutional oversight. It aims to support scholarly dialogue on trust, accountability, and governance at the execution boundary without over-disclosure or implementation detail.

title: ESG Preferences, Returns, and Risk: A Utility-Based Theory of ESG Investment
affiliations: Burgundy School of Business and CEREN EA 7477, Burgundy School of Business, Université Bourgogne Franche-Comté, Dijon, France

detail.title: ESG Preferences, Returns, and Risk: A Utility-Based Theory of ESG Investment
detail.abstract: We develop a portfolio-choice theory of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investing that integrates ESG-related return beliefs, risk considerations, and intrinsic ESG preferences. ESG investment is modeled as a continuous portfolio tilt away from a baseline allocation, affecting expected returns, portfolio risk, and investor utility within a mean-variance framework. ESG tilts interact with baseline risk exposures and generate convex diversification costs. The model delivers a closed-form solution for optimal ESG exposure that depends on ESG return beliefs, intrinsic preferences, investor risk aversion, and the return covariance structure. ESG investment can be optimal even without positive ESG return premia when ESG tilts hedge portfolio risk or provide direct utility. The framework explains heterogeneous ESG adoption and reconciles mixed empirical evidence on ESG returns.

title: Product Life Cycle Heterogeneity in the Transmission of Uncertainty
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Economics

detail.title: Product Life Cycle Heterogeneity in the Transmission of Uncertainty

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: I show that firms at different stages of the product life cycle respond differently to increases in economic uncertainty, and that this heterogeneity matters for understanding the aggregate implications of uncertainty for the economy. In response to higher uncertainty, early-stage firms increase investment, leading to greater innovation output (e.g., product patents). In contrast, late-stage firms reduce both investment and innovation. Using highly granular product-level data, I find that when uncertainty rises, early-stage firms increase product entry and exit, shifting their portfolios toward newer products, whereas late-stage firms scale back portfolio adjustments by reducing entry and exit activity. A real-options model with product life-cycle heterogeneity rationalizes these patterns: uncertainty boosts investment, innovation, and product experimentation when firms hold valuable growth options but discourages such activity when projects are mature and less scalable. My findings reconcile mixed results in the literature and provide the first evidence that a firm's product life cycle stage plays a central role in shaping how economic uncertainty affects corporate investment and product markets.

title: The Evaluation Paradox: Cognitive Atrophy and the Erosion of Human Oversight in Agentic Workflows

detail.title: The Evaluation Paradox: Cognitive Atrophy and the Erosion of Human Oversight in Agentic Workflows
