detail.abstract: As organizations transition from Generative AI as a tool to autonomous "coworkers" (Agentic AI), a structural socio-technical risk emerges-the Evaluation Paradox. This paper argues that by automating foundational "routine" tasks, organizations unintentionally dismantle the "cognitive musculature" required for high-stakes verification and exception handling. Drawing on Bainbridge's (1983) Ironies of Automation and Sweller's (1988) Cognitive Load Theory, I analyse the empirical evidence from Microsoft and McKinsey to demonstrate a growing gap in human capital resilience. I propose a framework of Cognitive Load Balancing (CLB) to mitigate this atrophy through Socio-Technical Observability and "Business Telemetry.

title: Law, Conflict, and Hybrid Warfare: A Teaching Imperative for a Changing World
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law and Yeshiva University - Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law

detail.title: Law, Conflict, and Hybrid Warfare: A Teaching Imperative for a Changing World

publicationDetails.detailsText: Washington University Journal of Law & Policy, Vol. 79, No. 1, pp. 1-20, 2026
Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Lawyers increasingly find themselves at the frontlines of the battlefield, just not in the traditional sense. Hybrid warfare is a conflict form that combines traditional military offensive measures with nontraditional methods, including the harnessing of legal systems to achieve strategic goals. Lawyers have always been at the frontline of typical legal risk assessment, thinking about a client's risk of liability or regulation costs generally. Now, lawyers must stand at the ready for a lot more: lawyers must be prepared for cyber-attacks, disinformation campaigns using artificial intelligence, the use of court systems to suppress reporting or shield bad actors, and so much more. Gone are the days where traditional lawyering is the sole line of support that lawyers can offer. A lawyer's negotiation and mediation skills must be honed and trained in hybrid warfare to be an asset to clients experiencing these events. This Essay explains what hybrid warfare is, its evolution, and how it is going to appear before public and private sector lawyers across the globe. It will cover the goals and missions of the first course seeking to train lawyers in hybrid warfare. As the world changes, as methods of combat evolve, and as client needs change accordingly, lawyers must do the same.

title: Activating the Green Transition: Regional Absorptive Capacity and the Heterogeneous Effects of Industrial Policy
affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University, , Chongqing University and Thayer School of Engineering, Dartmouth College

detail.title: Activating the Green Transition: Regional Absorptive Capacity and the Heterogeneous Effects of Industrial Policy
detail.abstract: Green industrial policies are critical for driving technological transitions, yet empirical evaluations often yield weak or insignificant average effects. We argue this apparent ineffectiveness is not a policy failure but a failure to account for a critical contingency: a region's capacity to absorb and leverage policy signals. To investigate this, we develop a novel design combining machine learning-based text analysis with a causal machine learning framework, applied to the universe of Chinese municipal electric vehicle policies (EV). While baseline machine learning estimates show no significant average impact on EV adoption, an instrumental variable approach addressing endogeneity reveals a strong, positive causal effect. Crucially, we find this effect is not universal but is strictly activated by regional absorptive capacity (technological complementarity). The causal machine learning estimate for this interaction is substantial (Interaction estimate=12.951 log-points, p < 0.01), indicating that policy impact is negligible in low-capacity regions but powerful in high-capacity ones. Mechanism decomposition highlights a striking asymmetry: while demand-side infrastructure provides a necessary physical foundation, the policy's causal effect is overwhelmingly mediated by supply-side industrial restructuring-specifically innovation and firm entry. Regional absorptive capacity acts as a selective catalyst that primarily activates these demand-side administrative measures. This finding explains the aggregate ineffectiveness of demand-side policies, showing their efficacy is latent and conditional. Our study recasts the debate from if policy works to where and how, demonstrating that the efficacy of green transitions hinges on the co-evolution of industrial policy with local technological capabilities.

title: Climate of Trust in Russian Business
affiliations: SKOLKOVO Moscow School of Management, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Institute for National Projects, Institute for National Projects, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Moscow State University, Lomonosov Moscow State University - Faculty of Economics and Lomonosov Moscow State University - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Climate of Trust in Russian Business
detail.abstract:
Recent studies emphasize the high importance of trust for economic development. There is a positive relationship between trust & economic growth, investment activity, the volume of venture investments, and much more. The research is aimed at determining the level of trust and social capital in Russian business, factors for choosing
a counterparty, common mechanisms for ensuring the reliability of obligations & transaction management mechanisms, and the specifics of transaction costs. Based on an analysis of Russian and international reports, statistical studies, and scientific articles, a number of hypotheses were formulated and subsequently tested in the framework of qualitative and quantitative social studies.

title: Convex Tail Risk Dominates Poor Man's Covered Call Outcomes Despite High Win Rates
affiliations: New York University (NYU)

detail.title: Convex Tail Risk Dominates Poor Man's Covered Call Outcomes Despite High Win Rates
detail.abstract:
The Poor Man's Covered Call (PMCC) strategy is widely promoted as a capital-efficient alternative to traditional covered calls, combining a long-dated deep-in-the-money call option with repeated sales of short-dated out-of-the-money calls. Empirical discussions typically emphasize its high win rate and attractive risk-adjusted performance, but rarely account for margin-induced forced liquidation risk arising from the short call leg.

Using daily SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) option data from 2007-2025, we decompose PMCC performance into its constituent components and explicitly price liquidation risk using a transparent, rule-based stress proxy. Over the sample, SPY buy-and-hold, excluding dividends, achieves 8.2% CAGR with-56.5% maximum drawdown, while a standalone deep-in-the-money long-term equity anticipation securities (LEAPS) position delivers 14.9% CAGR and higher Sharpe but materially larger drawdowns (-87.8%). When forced liquidation risk is ignored, the PMCC exhibits a similar CAGR (14.9%) with an improved drawdown profile (-84.2%) and an 86.3% short-call win rate. Incorporating forced liquidation losses, however, fundamentally alters the strategy's risk profile: CAGR falls to 11.9% and maximum drawdowns deepen to-93.5% despite an unchanged win rate.

We document multiple liquidation stress episodes outside of the Global Financial Crisis, driven primarily by convex losses in low-premium short calls during sustained upward price movements. Overall, the apparent robustness of PMCC strategies is largely an artifact of ignoring convex tail risk; once liquidation risk is priced, performance and drawdowns deteriorate materially. These findings underscore the importance of explicitly modeling liquidation risk when evaluating option strategies that combine leveraged long exposure with short-volatility positions.

title: Modeling, Simulation and Stability Analysis of Traffic Flow
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Bangladesh University of Business and Technology and Jahangirnagar University

detail.title: Modeling, Simulation and Stability Analysis of Traffic Flow
detail.abstract: In our modern era, traffic congestion has become endemic with the rapid growth of population throughout the world. Every big city in the world has traffic jams at certain times of the day, especially our city of Dhaka. Traffic jams can cause many problems, like breathing problems and headaches from pollution and noise, tension, anxiety, and road rage, as well as big economic and societal expenses from missed production and time. So proper steps should be taken for a new solution on the traffic management system. To solve this traffic congestion problem, we try to model this. There have been three major approaches in mathematical modelling of traffic flow, which describes situations due to different assumptions, amplifications, and modifications. An example of a traffic flow model that makes use of macroscopic diffusion is shown in this present work. Here we simulate this model applying different numerical approaches using numerous density-velocity relations. We also present an analysis of traffic flow stability by comparing numerical and analytical results.

title: Program Simulation Prompting: Designing Interactive, Stateful Systems Using Large Language Models
affiliations: CirroLytix Research Services

detail.title: Program Simulation Prompting: Designing Interactive, Stateful Systems Using Large Language Models
detail.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as interactive systems rather than single-turn text generators. However, most prompt engineering paradigms remain oriented toward linear or reactive interactions and offer limited support for persistent state, structured workflows, or explicit user control. This paper introduces program simulation prompting, a prompting paradigm in which an LLM is instructed to simulate the behavior of a structured software program using natural language interaction alone. In this approach, the model adopts a persistent program identity, presents menu-driven interaction modes, manages explicit task state, and constrains behavior to a bounded domain.
We analyze three domain-diverse program simulation prompts—spanning startup ideation, culinary recipe development, and creative writing—using a qualitative comparative methodology. Across these case studies, we identify recurring design patterns, including main menu abstractions, explicit separation between creating new and continuing existing artifacts, progressive elaboration, summarization-based state compression, and transparent signaling of memory constraints. Based on these findings, we propose a general, reusable framework for program simulation prompting that decomposes prompt design into five layers: initialization, interaction, state management, output constraints, and user control mechanisms.
Our results demonstrate that program simulation prompting enables interactive, stateful, and user-controlled LLM behavior without fine-tuning, external tools, or autonomous agents. This paradigm bridges conversational AI and traditional software affordances, offering a lightweight and transparent alternative to agent-based systems.
We conclude by discussing implications for LLM usability, system design, and future hybrid approaches.

title: Enhancing Entrepreneurial Behavioral Strategies to increase Well-being and Work Performance: An Online Self-Training Intervention
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tilburg University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Syracuse University

detail.title: Enhancing Entrepreneurial Behavioral Strategies to increase Well-being and Work Performance: An Online Self-Training Intervention
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of an online intervention aimed at enhancing entrepreneurial strategies to optimize business demands, utilize the business-environment, and safeguarding personal needs. Using a quasi-experimental design (intervention group, N = 45, control group, N = 53), we assessed the impact of proactive strategies on entrepreneurs’ well-being and work performance. The intervention included six modules featuring instructional videos, assignments, and reflection exercises. Entrepreneurs in the intervention group showed increased levels of seeking resources, optimizing demands, idea generation, and environmental exploration, leading to improved well-being and work performance. These findings highlight the potential of online interventions for entrepreneurs.

title: Spatial Staffing
affiliations: University of Toronto and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Spatial Staffing
detail.abstract: We study the problem of staffing sizing for an on-demand ride-hailing platform over a d-dimensional service region for d ≥ 2. The decisions include a one-time capacity-investment decision on the number of servers to deploy at the beginning of the planning horizon, as well as real-time server-customer matching and serverrouting/repositioning decisions during the horizon. The objective is to minimize the long-run average cost per unit time, consisting of servers' staffing costs and customers' waiting costs. We show that the optimal staffing level can be written as the sum of a nominal load (the absolute minimum number of servers needed to prevent the system from exploding) and a safety capacity, and characterize how the staffing rule responds to several key factors, including the dimensionality d, the probability distribution(s) of customers' origins and destinations, and the car-pooling capacity q (the maximum number of customers allowed in a vehicle). Specifically, we show that (i) when q = 1, the safety capacity is proportional to the constant-demand arrival rate to the power of d/(d + 1), a result that holds broadly across distributional assumptions and mirrors earlier findings under stylized spatial models. (ii) When q ≥ 2, the scaling becomes 2d/(2d + 1), which, to our knowledge, was not discovered in the past. Critically, we derive these results by analyzing exact vehicle routing without relying on stylized assumptions and by developing provably near-optimal policies for general spatial matching settings beyond those in prior work. We provide quantitative guidance for fleet deployment and operational design in large-scale on-demand platforms and highlight how geometry, strategic delay, and repositioning jointly determine the appropriate notion of "safety capacity" in spatial systems.

title: Qualification Migration: A Structured Model for Coordinated Human Capital Investment and Temporary Labour Mobility

detail.title: Qualification Migration: A Structured Model for Coordinated Human Capital Investment and Temporary Labour Mobility
detail.abstract:
Contemporary migration and training regimes struggle to reconcile three competing objectives: meeting labour shortages in advanced economies, preventing brain drain from developing states, and ensuring the ethical treatment and eventual reintegration of migrant workers. Existing approaches—such as guest-worker programmes, circular migration, and Global Skill Partnerships—have achieved partial success but remain limited by weak return incentives, asymmetric benefit distribution, and the absence of enforceable institutional frameworks linking migration to long-term development outcomes.

This paper proposes a qualification migration model that reframes cross-border labour mobility as a state-backed human-capital investment regime rather than a labour-market adjustment mechanism. Under this model, destination states finance the education and training of foreign workers within their marginal institutional capacity, while origin states secure the structured return and reintegration of these workers into designated strategic industries. Trade unions or professional guilds act as financial custodians and governance intermediaries, administering salary deposits, coordinating employer participation, and enforcing repatriation incentives through non-coercive contractual mechanisms.

The model introduces a layered return structure combining worker contributions, employer co-financing, and temporary fiscal instruments to enable recovery of training costs within realistic time horizons, followed by a dividend phase in which destination states receive stable, low-risk returns linked to post-return productivity. Using illustrative case studies involving Thailand as an origin country and European and Middle Eastern destination states, the paper develops quantitative feasibility conditions for human-capital surplus, educational absorption capacity, and industry scale, demonstrating that qualification migration can be implemented without displacing domestic workers or students.

By treating migration as an additive investment process embedded in treaty-based coordination, the proposed framework converts brain drain into brain gain, aligns state, employer, and worker incentives, and mitigates the political, social, and ethical tensions associated with permanent settlement. The paper contributes to political economy, labour policy, and development economics by offering a scalable institutional architecture for ethically governed, development-oriented labour mobility.

title: Nokia’s Failure of Becoming a Software and Service Company: Unfolding the Black Box of Organizational Learning Trap
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Vaasa and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Nokia’s Failure of Becoming a Software and Service Company: Unfolding the Black Box of Organizational Learning Trap
detail.abstract: Nokia, formerly the world’s leading smartphone manufacturer, fell into an organizational learning trap when the US-based software and Internet companies disrupted smartphone market. This extended longitudinal single-case study scrutinizes how Nokia was unable to adapt to a new type of competition because of several endogenous factors that hindered Nokia from renewing itself strategically. The present study opens up the black box of organizational learning trap by conceptualizing three distinct yet interconnected organizational rigidities that hinder organization’s strategic learning and renewal, namely 1) organizational myopia (inability to scan the exogenous changes beyond existing competition), 2) organizational indecision (inability to make strategic decisions because of inherent tensions within the corporation), and 3) organizational paralysis (inability to deliberately realign organizational capabilities to address to a new type of a competition). The present study extends theoretical understanding of root causes of organizational non-learning and contributes to dynamic capability and strategic learning literatures by unraveling the path-dependent sources of organizational learning inertia. For business executives and managers, this study helps to understand potential sources of organizational capability rigidity and avoid falling into strategic learning traps in disrupted business markets.

title: VIA Triangulation in Education
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title: VIA Triangulation in Education
detail.abstract: Educational enquiry has long been characterized by fragmented epistemologies that privilege either causal inference, interpretive understanding, or experiential attunement, rarely holding all three in productive tension. This article presents VIA Triangulation as an integrative epistemological framework designed to address this fragmentation. The framework triangulates three essential lenses: Veritas (the pursuit of warranted causal claims), Inquiry (the cultivation of disciplined interpretive understanding), and Aesthesis (the attunement to lived aesthetic experience). Drawing on Dewey's theory of inquiry, Habermas's knowledge-constitutive interests, and Denzin's methodological triangulation, the article articulates how each lens addresses characteristic pathologies of the others, Veritas guards against impressionism, Inquiry guards against technocracy, and Aesthesis guards against sterile compliance. The article develops a five-step practitioner protocol that operationalizes VIA Triangulation for educational settings, demonstrating how educators can systematically collect and integrate evidence across all three dimensions. By making philosophical commitments explicit and operational, VIA Triangulation provides practitioners with a principled framework for justifying curriculum decisions, evaluating improvement, and ensuring that educational enquiry remains grounded in the full complexity of teaching and learning.

title: The Payoffs of Higher Pay: Labor Supply and Productivity Responses to a Voluntary Firm Minimum Wage
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and University of Virginia - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Payoffs of Higher Pay: Labor Supply and Productivity Responses to a Voluntary Firm Minimum Wage

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1182
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: What are the returns to firms of paying more? We study a Fortune 500 firm's voluntary firm-wide $15/hour minimum wage, which affected some warehouses more than others. Using a continuous difference-indifferences design, we find that a $1/hour pay increase (5.5 percent) halves worker departures, reduces absenteeism by 18.6 percent, and increases productivity (boxes moved per hour) by 5.7 percent. These productivity gains fully defrayed increased labor costs, offsetting the firm's incentive to mark down wages. We develop a simple model that connects efficiency-wage incentives and monopsony power, showing how these forces can counterbalance each other to keep wages closer to workers' marginal revenues.

title: A Data Driven Approach for Surgical Case Assignment Problem
affiliations: Warwick University - University of Warwick, Durham University Business School and Warwick University - University of Warwick

detail.title: A Data Driven Approach for Surgical Case Assignment Problem
detail.abstract: Inaccurate estimates of surgery duration reduce operating room efficiency, leading to under - or overutilized time blocks, costly overtime, and prolonged patient waiting times. Current scheduling practices in the National Health Service (NHS) in England rely on fixed duration benchmarks or clinician judgment, which fail to capture patient- and procedure-specific variability. We develop a data-driven framework that integrates machine learning predictions with deterministic and robust optimization models for surgical case assignment. Using three years of data from an NHS Foundation Trust, we compare alternative predictive models and show that our approach reduces the average error of duration estimates from 38 minutes to 11 minutes relative to NHS benchmarks. These predictions are embedded within a robust optimization formulation solved via a column-and-constraint generation algorithm to construct schedules that maximize utilization while hedging against uncertainty. Incorporating predictive inputs narrows the gap between expected and realized utilization from 25.8% to 1.5%, increases patient throughput by up to 45%, and reduces waiting list length by more than 70%. The proposed framework demonstrates that combining predictive analytics with robust optimization yields significant improvements in efficiency and service delivery. The approach is directly applicable to elective surgery scheduling and generalizable to other healthcare systems seeking data-driven, uncertainty-aware decision tools.

title: Credibility in Practice: A Channel-Based Framework for ESG Disclosure Reliability
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Credibility in Practice: A Channel-Based Framework for ESG Disclosure Reliability
detail.abstract: Global sustainability disclosure templates are converging, but semantic alignment does not guarantee that sustainability claims are reliable when challenged. This paper argues that disclosure reliability is partly an institutional outcome: it is produced by the accountability pathway that links a disclosure statement to feasible contestation and credible consequences. The paper develops a channel-based framework that treats the accountability channel as the unit of analysis and specifies four constitutive elements: (V) the legal vehicle rendering claims official; (A) the actors who verify, supervise, and adjudicate; (P) the procedural pathways that make claims challengeable (including access to evidence); and (S) the sanction set that makes misstatement costly, including rapid correction powers. Channel performance is assessed through a credibility triad namely tempo, visibility, and remedial bite, grounded in a deterrence logic (perceived probability × expected consequence, discounted by time). The framework is operationalised as a conservative 0-2 Accountability Channel Credibility Scorecard (ACCS) using publicly observable evidence within a bounded evidence window. Illustrative application to listed-issuer, ISSB-aligned climate disclosure channels in Singapore and Thailand shows how similar reporting headings can produce divergent credibility profiles when embedded in distinct domestic accountability architectures. The ACCS is offered as a practice-facing diagnostic for firms, regulators, and value-chain counterparties confronting rising sustainability due-diligence pressures in land-use-salient supply chains, where verification is structurally costly.

title: Decentralized Multi-product Pricing: Diagonal Dominance, Nash Equilibrium, and Price of Anarchy
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago - College of Business Administration, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - School of Engineering and

detail.title: Decentralized Multi-product Pricing: Diagonal Dominance, Nash Equilibrium, and Price of Anarchy
detail.abstract: Decentralized decision making in multi-product firms can lead to efficiency losses when autonomous decision makers fail to internalize cross-product demand interactions. This paper quantifies the magnitude of such losses by analyzing the Price of Anarchy in a pricing game in which each decision maker independently sets prices to maximize its own product-level revenue. We model demand using a linear system that captures both substitution and complementarity effects across products. We first establish existence and uniqueness of a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium under economically standard diagonal dominance conditions. Our main contribution is the derivation of a tight worst-case lower bound on the ratio between decentralized revenue and the optimal centralized revenue. We show that this efficiency loss is governed by a single scalar parameter, denoted by µ, which measures the aggregate strength of cross-price effects relative to own-price sensitivities. In particular, we prove that the revenue ratio is bounded below by 4(1-µ)/(2-µ) 2 , and we demonstrate the tightness of this bound by constructing a symmetric market topology in which the bound is exactly attained. We further refine the analysis by providing an instance-exact characterization of efficiency loss based on the spectral properties of the demand interaction matrix. Together, these results offer a quantitative framework for assessing the trade-off between centralized pricing and decentralized autonomy in multi-product settings.

title: Trust as a Binding Constraint Under Institutional Failure

detail.title: Trust as a Binding Constraint Under Institutional Failure
detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework for analyzing trust as an economic constraint rather than as a cultural trait, moral norm, or intrinsic preference. It argues that trust becomes economically binding when institutional conditions cause losses from coordination failure to be borne directly by individuals rather than absorbed through formal enforcement, insurance, or recovery mechanisms. Under such conditions, the absence of trust removes otherwise potentially beneficial exchanges from the feasible choice set by exposing individuals to losses that cannot be reliably mitigated or recovered within economically relevant time horizons. By locating trust within a framework of institutional capacity, risk allocation, and recoverability, the paper clarifies when trust constrains economic behavior and when it does not. The analysis relies on standard economic reasoning about constraints and feasibility and does not make claims about welfare, efficiency, or development outcomes. The contribution is conceptual, providing a disciplined economic definition of trust that explains its varying importance across institutional environments without appealing to cultural or normative explanations.

title: Bridging the Gap: Strengthening Agricultural Extension Services for Last-Mile Farmers – A Policy Brief
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Unaffiliated Authors and

detail.title: Bridging the Gap: Strengthening Agricultural Extension Services for Last-Mile Farmers – A Policy Brief
detail.abstract:
Agricultural extension services play a critical role in enhancing farm productivity, improving farmer incomes, and ensuring the diffusion of research-based knowledge across the agricultural supply chain. In India, however, extension systems continue to face persistent structural and operational challenges in reaching last-mile farmers, particularly small and marginal cultivators operating within highly fragmented, diverse, and climate-vulnerable agrarian contexts. This paper conceptualises agricultural extension as a wicked policy problem, shaped by the intrinsic heterogeneity of the agricultural sector and the deep interdependence across pre-harvest, production, post-harvest, and marketing stages.

Drawing on systems thinking and stakeholder analysis frameworks, the paper examines institutional capacity constraints, including adverse extension worker-to-farmer ratios, siloed programme design, behavioural resistance to innovation, and information asymmetries across the supply chain. It further highlights how socio-cultural factors, digital divides, and limited contextualisation of advisory services undermine the effectiveness of conventional top-down extension models.

The paper proposes an integrated reform architecture that combines bottom-up behavioural interventions with top-down technological and institutional innovations. Key recommendations include community-based peer learning groups, incentives for early adopters and para-extension workers, AI-enabled state-level dashboards for real-time decision support, strengthened forward and backward market linkages, and performance-linked incentives for extension personnel. By aligning stakeholder incentives and embedding data-driven feedback loops within existing administrative structures, the paper argues for a more resilient, inclusive, and scalable agricultural extension ecosystem.

The study contributes to policy discourse by offering a holistic, supply-chain-wide framework for reforming extension services, with implications for agricultural productivity, climate resilience, and rural livelihoods in developing agrarian economies.

title: When Search Starts with Generative AI: Content Licensing and Publisher Quality
affiliations: Chongqing University - School of Economics and Business Admininstration and

detail.title: When Search Starts with Generative AI: Content Licensing and Publisher Quality
detail.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly a first stop for information seeking. Acting as an answer engine, it delivers synthesized, self-contained responses that may incorporate publisher content through licensing agreements. These agreements are often viewed as win-win because AI platforms gain high-quality inputs and publishers receive compensation. However, this view overlooks a key structural feature: licensing makes AI answers derivative of publisher content within a sequential search process. As publisher quality improves, AI answers become more effective at satisfying consumers early, which cannibalizes direct engagement with publishers and may shrink the value created by licensing. As a result, even with licensing in place, AI can weaken publishers' incentives to invest in quality, despite always leaving them better off. Consumer welfare can also decline, even though AI expands the choice set with a more efficient option. Our analysis suggests that preserving publishers' quality incentives requires more than compensation through licensing; it also hinges on giving publishers control over how their content is incorporated into generative AI.

title: Constitutional Loyalty and the Limits of Institutional Transfer: A Framework for Recalibrating Integration Policy in Post-War Liberal Democracies

detail.title: Constitutional Loyalty and the Limits of Institutional Transfer: A Framework for Recalibrating Integration Policy in Post-War Liberal Democracies

detail.abstract: Current migration policy assumes that constitutional loyalty-the foundational commitment to legal norms, state legitimacy, and the rule of law-can be transmitted through integration courses and civic education. This paper argues that in postwar Germany, constitutional loyalty derives its normative weight from specific historical experience. For citizens, the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) is not merely a legal constraint but a collective response to catastrophe, carrying emotional and moral authority that no curriculum can replicate. This creates a structural asymmetry: newcomers may learn the content of constitutional norms while lacking access to the context that makes those norms feel binding rather than merely instrumental. Drawing on Fukuyama's distinction between high-trust and low-trust societies, Koopmans' empirical research on normative conflicts, and Tibi's concept of Leitkultur, this paper proposes that rather than demanding an assimilation that cannot occur or abandoning integration standards altogether, policy should acknowledge this asymmetry-calibrating expectations, timelines, and residency frameworks accordingly.

title: Rethinking Change Management Under Extreme Volatility: The ICASEMUS Model as an Integrative Framework for Executive Practice

detail.title: Rethinking Change Management Under Extreme Volatility: The ICASEMUS Model as an Integrative Framework for Executive Practice
detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations confront an operating environment defined by extreme volatility, where disruption is no longer episodic but structural. Traditional change management frameworks, while foundational, were largely conceived for conditions of relative environmental stability and planned, sequential transformation. This paper introduces the ICASEMUS model, an iterative, indicator-based change management framework designed to address the demands of sustained organizational adaptation under conditions of persistent uncertainty. The model operationalizes eight interdependent dimensions: Identification, Conscience, Acceptance, Strategy, Engagement, Movement, Urgency, and Stabilization. Each dimension functions simultaneously as both a process phase and a real-time performance indicator, enabling continuous recalibration as contexts shift. The paper situates the ICASEMUS framework within the established change management canon, including Lewin's three-step model, Kotter's eight-step process, the Prosci ADKAR model, and Bridges' Transition Model, offering integrative reflections rather than normative assessments of these contributions. A revised adaptation of the Kubler-Ross model is proposed to address the psychological and emotional dimensions of resistance to change within organizational settings. The ICASEMUS model is not presented as an empirically validated theory but as a normative framework for executive practice, derived from synthesis of established academic literature and repeated application in executive education and advisory contexts. Empirical validation is identified as a direction for future research.

title: Cognitive Integrity Under Pressure: A Theory-Informed Conceptual Framework for Executive Self-Regulation

detail.title: Cognitive Integrity Under Pressure: A Theory-Informed Conceptual Framework for Executive Self-Regulation
detail.abstract: Executives routinely operate in conditions where stress, time compression, and performance demands interact with self-regulatory capacity to affect judgment quality. This paper introduces the Dynamic Resonance Matrix, a theory-informed conceptual framework for executive development. The framework is practice-oriented and heuristic in nature, designed to support moment-to-moment self-regulation under pressure. It does not claim neuroscientific precision, empirical validation of discrete internal states, or universal applicability. The matrix integrates two continuous dimensions grounded in psychology and psychophysiology: physiological activation level and emotional valence. Their intersection is represented through six descriptive reference areas that characterize common experiential extremes observed in executive practice. These areas are not categorical states but rather reference points along continuous dimensions. Each area encompasses a range of intensities, and the matrix could be expanded into nine or more areas without altering its underlying logic. Drawing on research in stress psychophysiology, self-regulation, emotion regulation, and leadership behavior, the paper outlines how executives can recognize when internal conditions support or undermine judgment and engage rapid regulation practices compatible with ongoing performance. The contribution is not theoretical extension but provision of a shared language and navigational tool for developing cognitive integrity under pressure.

title: Strategic Team Composition Under Volatility: The PIKES Framework as an Integrative Model for Senior Hiring and Team Stewardship

detail.title: Strategic Team Composition Under Volatility: The PIKES Framework as an Integrative Model for Senior Hiring and Team Stewardship
detail.abstract: The failure rate of senior hires remains persistently high across industries, with estimates placing executive derailment between 30 and 50 percent within the first two years. The dominant explanations for this phenomenon have shifted over the past two decades from deficits in technical competence toward failures of cultural integration, political navigation, and relational alignment. Yet the frameworks available to hiring leaders for evaluating candidates at the strategic team level remain fragmented, oscillating between narrow competency assessments and broad person-organization fit heuristics that do not account for the systemic interdependencies within leadership teams operating under sustained environmental volatility. This paper introduces the PIKES framework, a five-dimensional model for strategic team composition and senior hiring developed through synthesis of established academic literature and refined through two decades of application in team management, executive hiring, advisory, and education contexts across industries. The five dimensions, Purpose, Integration, Knowledge, Ecosystem, and Self, function simultaneously as selection criteria and as ongoing diagnostic indicators for team stewardship. The framework's central proposition is that a team strong across four dimensions but structurally weak in one may still fail, because the dimensions operate as an interdependent system rather than as compensatory attributes. The paper situates PIKES within the established literatures on person-environment fit, organizational socialization, upper echelons theory, team effectiveness conditions, and emotional regulation at both individual and collective levels, offering integrative reflections on these contributions rather than normative assessments. A practical application section illustrates the framework's deployment in a restructuring scenario. Limitations are acknowledged: PIKES is presented as a normative decisionmaking framework for executive practice, not as an empirically validated theory. Empirical validation across organizational contexts and cultural settings is identified as a priority direction for future research.

title: Faith and Finance: The Impact of Religiosity on Bank Deposits
affiliations: , Texas A&M University-Kingsville and Texas A&M International University

detail.title: Faith and Finance: The Impact of Religiosity on Bank Deposits

declarations.funderStatement: This project is funded by the Presidential Research Development Grant Program at Texas A&M International University.

detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between county-level religiosity and bank deposit volumes using comprehensive U.S. bank branch-level data from 2000 to 2025. Controlling for market concentration, demographics, and county fixed effects, we find a robust negative association between religiosity and deposit volume. This relationship is more pronounced in urban areas, for large banks, and in high-income counties. Instrumental variable analysis using lagged religiosity confirms our findings. Denomination-level analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity, with the strongest effects for Orthodox traditions, moderate effects for Catholic, and the smallest for Protestant. These findings highlight how local cultural values shape household saving behaviors.

title: Rapid Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: A Decision Taxonomy for Time-Constrained Executive Contexts

detail.title: Rapid Decision-Making Under Uncertainty: A Decision Taxonomy for Time-Constrained Executive Contexts
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a decision taxonomy and structured methodology for executives facing the dual constraints of high uncertainty and severe time pressure. Building on Bezos' Type 1/Type 2 decision classification, the framework extends this binary model into a three-dimensional matrix incorporating reversibility, impact magnitude, and temporal constraints. Two complementary tools are introduced: the 4 Points of Tension (4PT) model for situational intelligence (SITUINT), and the Rapid High-Impact (RHI) Decision Framework for accelerated decision making in critical moments. These are normative tools derived from synthesis of established literature and refined through application in executive education and advisory contexts, not empirically validated theories. The contribution is specific and operational: a decision taxonomy for time-constrained executive contexts that improves decision quality and velocity when complete information is unavailable and delay carries significant cost. Empirical validation remains a direction for future research.

title: Organizational Environment: The Foundational Definition

detail.title: Organizational Environment: The Foundational Definition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author as part of HOWAR srl's research program.

detail.abstract:
We propose organizational environment as the unified system of features demonstrating effective influence on member experience, behavior, performance, and well-being. This definition is coherent with Lewin's effectiveness criterion—what is real is what has effects—applied systematically to organizational settings.

The criterion generates four operational requirements (influential, objective, trans-individual, homeostatic) that distinguish genuine environmental properties from ephemeral conditions. Applied comprehensively, these requirements yield a five-dimensional architecture comprising structural, processual, relational, physical-contextual, and cultural-normative features that integrate fragmented research traditions.

The framework produces a tripartite ontological distinction: organizational environment constitutes the objective substrate; organizational climate represents perceptual and affective responses to that substrate; organizational culture, rather than paralleling climate, constitutes one dimension within the environmental substrate itself.

This framework resolves three persistent contradictions that leading scholars acknowledge but have not addressed: the climate-culture conflation (Schneider et al., 2024), the measurement paradox (Oldham & Hackman, 2010), and the boundary ambiguity between organizational and individual characteristics.

The framework enables a paradigmatic transition: from individual adaptation to environmental optimization, from measuring member perceptions to specifying the features generating those perceptions, from holding individuals accountable for systemic conditions to holding organizations accountable for environmental design.

title: When Little's Law Fails as an Estimator: Finite-Sample Variance, Heavy-Traffic Pathology, and Reliability Diagnostics in Queueing Systems

detail.title: When Little's Law Fails as an Estimator: Finite-Sample Variance, Heavy-Traffic Pathology, and Reliability Diagnostics in Queueing Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests or conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Little's Law (L = λW) is exact, yet finite-sample estimation routinely exhibits 40–50% errors at high utilization. We argue these discrepancies reflect estimation pathology, not model failure, and develop a unified theory identifying three distinct failure modes. First, estimand mismatch: under non-stationary arrivals, time-average and arrival-average queue lengths diverge by up to 28%, causing systematic bias even with infinite samples. Second, variance explosion: estimator variance scales as Θ((1−ρ)⁻³/T)—approximately five orders of magnitude larger at ρ = 0.99 than at moderate utilization. We prove this scaling is fundamental via minimax lower bounds: no estimator can achieve better mean squared error than Ω((1−ρ)⁻³/T), regardless of construction. Third, distributional breakdown: heavy-tailed service causes CLT failure, with coefficient of variation exceeding 250%. We provide finite-sample concentration bounds with explicit constants, anytime-valid confidence sequences for adaptive stopping, and practical diagnostics (median-mean ratio, CV thresholds) to detect which pathology is operating. Extensive Monte Carlo validation confirms all predictions. The unifying insight is that apparent Little's Law violations are predictable and diagnosable—the law itself is exact; only estimation can be unreliable.

title: Geological Constraints on Bunker-Buster Penetration at Iran’s Fordow Facility

detail.title: Geological Constraints on Bunker-Buster Penetration at Iran’s Fordow Facility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzed publicly available geoscientific data, satellite imagery, and media reports. No experiments involving human subjects, animal subjects, or fieldwork requiring permits were conducted. The research adhered to principles of open science and transparency by relying solely on publicly accessible information.
declarations.funderStatement: Juntendo University

detail.abstract: Media reports on the U.S. strike against Iran's Fordow nuclear facility in June 2025 often cite the GBU-57 bunkerbuster's "200-foot penetration capability" without clarifying underlying geological assumptions. This study applies a geojournalistic approach-integrating satellite imagery, regional geological studies, and empirical rock strength data-to evaluate how local geology constrained penetration depth. Analysis shows that natural rock formations in the Qom area, dominated by sedimentary and igneous rocks with uniaxial compressive strengths commonly near or above 10,000 psi, likely present substantially greater resistance than the reinforced-concrete benchmarks typically cited. Strike-generated debris may add further resistance through regolith-like layers. While definitive damage assessment awaits classified disclosure or inspection, this study demonstrates that meaningful technical scrutiny is possible using open-source geoscientific data alone, and that uncontextualized penetration figures risk distorting public understanding and undermining informed discourse.

title: Survival Coefficient and Systemic Resilience: A Twin-Case Diagnosis of the "Kill Line" Phenomenon Among At-Risk Populations in China and the US -Toward a New Integrated Framework for Measuring Human Development

detail.title: Survival Coefficient and Systemic Resilience: A Twin-Case Diagnosis of the "Kill Line" Phenomenon Among At-Risk Populations in China and the US -Toward a New Integrated Framework for Measuring Human Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: 作者在作品创作过程中，没有收到过任何组织或个人的任何资助，作品也跟任何组织和个人没有任何经济或财务关系

detail.abstract: This study proposes the Survival Coefficient framework as a diagnostic tool for measuring household resilience deficits and applies it to six twin-case comparisons of at-risk households in China and the United States. Conventional development metrics—GDP per capita, poverty lines, and the Gini coefficient—share a fundamental paradigm flaw: they equate “poverty” with “misery” and tacitly assume that being “non-poor” means being “free from misery”. This misconception has rendered invisible the ALICE population—those statistically “counted” yet living one shock away from collapse. The Survival Coefficient framework integrates a Survival Pressure Index (localized essential cash expenditure calibrated by behavioral elasticity) and a Systemic Resilience Index (a five-layer depletion model: financial buffer, behavioral elasticity, social networks, spatial gradient resilience, and formal social protection), and establishes a two-stage dynamic diagnostic tool—the Warning Line and the Red Line. Methodologically, we employ a twin-case design: three U.S. and three Chinese at-risk households are matched by family structure and risk type, all sourced from authoritative media and official records, fully traceable and auditable. The empirical findings reveal a “falling” paradigm in the U.S.—credit scores alienated into a “social citizenship certification system”, welfare cliffs imposing de facto marginal tax rates exceeding 100%, medical debt remaining the leading cause of household bankruptcy, and spatial gradient resilience institutionally absent; red-line crossing typically leads to irreversible social death. China exhibits a “downgrading” paradigm—191 million urban-settled rural collective members retain statutory homestead rights (L4A), cross-city migration institutionally empowered by portable social security and mutual recognition of housing provident funds (L4B), and welfare decoupled from employment, imposing no penalty on income growth; red-line crossing usually results in reversible strategic downgrading. The theoretical contributions include: incorporating non-monetary resilience assets as core analytical categories parallel to income and welfare, operationalizing cultural habits as measurable resilience activation parameters, and for the first time distinguishing between the existence and the institutional thickness of spatial gradient resilience. The study calls for a policy paradigm shift from “poverty reduction” to “misery elimination”, and for integrating systemic resilience into the core indicator cluster of the “Beyond GDP” agenda.

title: Green Intervention and User Compliance: A Field Experiment on Smart A/C Controls
affiliations: Tsinghua University,  and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Green Intervention and User Compliance: A Field Experiment on Smart A/C Controls

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Smart automated control of energy use represents a promising and rapidly emerging approach to advancing carbon emissions reductions and resource conservation. However, its effectiveness can be limited when users do not comply with the interventions implemented by such systems. This research investigates how user behavior, specifically user compliance, influences the performance of smart control systems and how to design more effective strategies that address this behavioral challenge. We conduct a randomized controlled trial to test the impact of a smart airconditioning (A/C) control system implemented across 20 public office buildings and 390 office rooms in Hubei Province, China, during the summer of 2024. The smart control system periodically regulates the A/C's cooling energy use by automatically adjusting the temperature upward to a target limit when users set it below that limit. Users are allowed to override the control by setting the temperature back down, constituting a setting with centralized system management but decentralized user decision-making. Office rooms are randomly assigned to groups in which different control strategies are implemented, and we examine their respective impacts on electricity consumption. Our findings show that simply increasing the temperature limit does not yield significant energy savings, whereas control strategies that either adjust the temperature limit more frequently or adapt dynamically to user behavior achieve significant savings without compromising comfort. These results demonstrate the crucial role of user compliance in realizing the potential of smart control technologies and provide actionable guidance for designing more effective energy-saving strategies that better account for user behavior.

title: Power Asymmetries in BRICS: Serving the Global South or Entrenching Sino-Russian Interests?

detail.title: Power Asymmetries in BRICS: Serving the Global South or Entrenching Sino-Russian Interests?

keywords: Power Asymmetry; BRICS; Multipolarity; Global South; Interests; Russia & China; UN

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of BRICS Studies, volume 4, issue 2, 2026[10.36615/xw9mkn74]

detail.abstract: Since becoming a political bloc in 2009, BRICS has expanded to ten members. This paper interrogates the evolving role of this formation, which aspires to be a powerful voice for the Global South at the international level. This ambition evokes comparisons to the Non-Aligned Movement, which 'historically represented a collective voice of developing countries striving for independence, sovereignty, and international cooperation' during the pre-1990 bipolar world. However, the contemporary multipolar landscape presents distinct challenges to its efforts to be a counterweight to Western hegemony. This paper argues that the grouping increasingly entrenches Chinese economic primacy and Russian geopolitical interests, marginalising smaller members and the broader Global South. Empirical evidence from key UN bodies is used to highlight limited BRICS engagement at the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and divergent voting patterns within the UN Security Council (UNSC), underscoring institutional inertia. Financial and diplomatic asymmetries further enable Beijing and Moscow to dominate the bloc's agenda, weakening its credibility as a vehicle for Global South solidarity. These internal imbalances could also undermine the very concept of multipolarity that BRICS claims to champion. Through a structural realist lens, this paper analyses UN voting records, trade imbalances and case studies, including the Democratic Republic of Congo's cobalt supply chain, to reveal how disparities in representation, financial contributions and strategic priorities shape BRICS' trajectory. The paper concludes with policy recommendations.

title: Coding AI Finance: How Lawyers Shape Debt Capacity in the Innovation Economy

detail.title: Coding AI Finance: How Lawyers Shape Debt Capacity in the Innovation Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: TILEC Discussion Paper DP 2026-03

detail.abstract:
We are in the midst of an AI credit boom. In the AI sector, large-scale investments in computing infrastructure are being funded predominantly with debt, even though future revenues of AI firms depend on competitive arms-race dynamics and highly uncertain application-layer profitability. Standard corporate finance theory would predict that the combination of high capital intensity and unresolved uncertainty should constrain debt capacity and limit credit expansion. Yet such constraints have not materialized. Departing from standard predictions, this Article develops a Minskyan law-and-macro-finance framework revolving around the concept of “pledgeability”— —the extent to which the value of firms’ cashflows and assets can support debt finance. In our framework, credit booms are amplified by legal reconfigurations of pledgeability that push the debt frontier outward, enabling debt capacity to expand even as underlying technological and demand risk remains unresolved. The framework disaggregates the legal determinants of pledgeability into five core elements: contractability, enforceability, priority, transferability and separability. Together, these elements constitute what the Article terms the “code” of AI finance. On our account, transactional lawyers function as engineers of pledgeability—coding an expanding set of revenues and assets capable of supporting debt claims in response to growing investor demand for exposure to a booming sector.

Applying the framework to AI buildout in the United States, the Article traces the emergence of increasingly complex debt structures, ranging from project finance through private credit to securitization, each associated with a distinct configuration of pledgeability. Across these structures, transactional lawyers actively code pledgeability to transform uncertain future revenues (such as those arising from capacity reservations, take-or-pay commitments, and power purchase agreements) into cashflow streams and specialized assets (including equipment, facilities, and interconnection rights) into collateral capable of supporting fixed-claim capital. These complementary configurations of the code expand firms’ effective debt capacity beyond what prior legal configurations would have permitted, while increasing both aggregate leverage and the degree to which it becomes anchored to shared technological assumptions. The Article’s core contribution is to make explicit, for the first time, the legal infrastructure through which Minskyan dynamics operate, shaping how technological change is intermediated through credit markets and how innovation cycles interact with the broader financial system.

title: Carbon Transparency and Green Technology Adoption: Mandatory vs. Voluntary Disclosure
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) - Department of Information Systems and Management Engineering, Beijing Institute of Technology - BIT Zhuhai Campus, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Shanghai International Studies University

detail.title: Carbon Transparency and Green Technology Adoption: Mandatory vs. Voluntary Disclosure
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Over the past decade, governments worldwide have increasingly shifted from voluntary carbon disclosure initiatives to mandatory disclosure regimes. These mandates are intended to enhance carbon transparency and stimulate firms to adopt green technologies to reduce emissions. Yet, their effectiveness remains unclear, particularly as consumers are becoming more concerned about the carbon footprints of products. Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretical model to analyze a firm's decisions on green technology adoption, carbon information acquisition, and disclosure when selling to environmentally concerned consumers. Product emission level is uncertain, and greener technology generates fewer emissions in expectation. Under mandatory disclosure, a firm is required to disclose acquired emission information, whereas under voluntary disclosure, the firm can choose whether to disclose. Our analysis yields several key findings. First, under each disclosure regime, stronger consumer environmental concerns generally incentivize the firm to acquire and disclose emission information, but, counterintuitively, can discourage the firm to adopt green technology. Second, mandatory disclosure can be both economically and environmentally inferior to voluntary disclosure, leading to a multi-lose outcome by reducing firm profit and consumer surplus, impairing carbon transparency, and deterring green technology adoption. Third, this multi-lose outcome can be exacerbated as the cost of emission information acquisition decreases (e.g., through advances in emission tracking technologies such as blockchain and IoT tracking) and as consumer environmental concerns increases (e.g., via sustainability campaigns and educations by the governments and organizations). Managerial implications: Our results unravel the economic and environmental efficacy of mandatory and voluntary disclosure, providing important implications for policymakers regarding the ongoing implementation of disclosure mandates.

title: How to Disclose? Strategic AI Disclosure in Crowdfunding
affiliations: University of Connecticut - School of Business and University of Connecticut - School of Business

detail.title: How to Disclose? Strategic AI Disclosure in Crowdfunding
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly integrates into crowdfunding practices, strategic disclosure of AI involvement has become critical. Yet, empirical insights into how different disclosure strategies influence investor decisions remain limited. Drawing on signaling theory and Aristotle's rhetorical framework, we examine how mandatory AI disclosure affects crowdfunding performance and how substantive signals (degree of AI involvement) and rhetorical signals (logos/explicitness, ethos/authenticity, pathos/emotional tone) moderate these effects. Leveraging Kickstarter's mandatory AI disclosure policy as a natural experiment and four supplementary online experiments, we find that mandatory AI disclosure significantly reduces crowdfunding performance: funds raised decline by 39.8% and backer counts by 23.9% for AI-involved projects. However, this adverse effect is systematically moderated by disclosure strategy. Greater AI involvement amplifies the negative effects of AI disclosure, while high authenticity and high explicitness mitigate them. Interestingly, excessive positive emotional tone (a strategy creators might intuitively adopt to counteract AI skepticism) backfires and exacerbates negative outcomes. Supplementary randomized experiments identify two underlying mechanisms: perceived creator competence and AI washing concerns. Substantive signals primarily affect competence judgments, whereas rhetorical signals operate through varied pathways: either mediator alone or both in sequence. These findings provide theoretical and practical insights for entrepreneurs, platforms, and policymakers strategically managing AI transparency in high-stakes investment contexts.

title: Information Design in Omnichannel Services
affiliations: , Lingnan University and Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management

detail.title: Information Design in Omnichannel Services
detail.abstract: Omnichannel services are growing, allowing customers to choose between online orders and offline visits based on delay information in apps. Problem definition: We examine how an omnichannel service provider can utilize delay information disclosure to manage customer channel selection, improving throughput and customer experience. Methodology/results: Using an information design and queueing game framework, we analyze how information affects performance in an M/M/1 queue, where customers choose to join online or offline. We show that the throughput-maximizing disclosure policy follows a simple, implementable threshold structure. Furthermore, using threshold-structured policies, information design can increase both throughput and social welfare compared to the traditional offline system. This creates a win-win for customers and the service provider. We also analyze the case with non-app users who can only walk in. We reveal the cross-channel externality they create and caution against potential negative impacts on their welfare. Managerial implications: We propose delay information as a powerful and costless tool for synergizing service channels. Our findings guide the effective design of information disclosure in omnichannel service systems.

title: Dry weather, empty classrooms: How do rainfall shocks reduce schooling?
affiliations: Independent and Texas A&M University (TAMU), Central Texas

detail.title: Dry weather, empty classrooms: How do rainfall shocks reduce schooling?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We unpack the mechanisms through which rainfall shocks disrupt school enrollment in agrarian economies. We provide a simple theoretical model showing that income loss and labor constraints under imperfect markets mediate the effects of rainfall shocks on schooling. Empirically, we estimate the distributional impacts of rainfall shocks by combining micro-household panel data from Tanzania with high-resolution rainfall data and vegetation indices. Severe droughts (rainfall below the 10th percentile) reduce school enrollment by 10 percent, whereas moderate rainfall deficits or excess rainfall have no significant impact. The effects are concentrated among agricultural and asset-poor households and are largest for adolescents. Extreme droughts increase absenteeism by reducing agricultural yields, contracting hired labor, and cutting education spending significantly. Income shocks from high-value, water-intensive crops, not food staples, explain the negative impacts. Results clarify mixed evidence by identifying vulnerable groups and tracing the impact pathway. Findings underscore the need for targeted interventions to sustain schooling and build resilience in drought-prone regions.

title: Decision Integrity in Agentic Retail Banking
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Decision Integrity in Agentic Retail Banking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Retail banking has been at the forefront of AI adoption for the past three years or so. The industry is now well-established and is using artificial intelligence (AI) to carry out financial transactions under predetermined guidelines, known as "Agentic Banking."

To accomplish this at scale, banks have now created three essential capabilities for the Agentic Banking model: Rule-Based Cash Sweep Mechanisms, API-Enabled Financial Transparency, and Autonomous Portfolio Rebalancing. Nevertheless, these capabilities raise a significant structural governance concern: What happens if AI is not designed to protect but is given the ability to optimize?

The paper presents the idea of the Fiduciary Gap, which is defined as "the mismatch between what the AI system is optimized to do, and the broader responsibilities of the institution towards customers and balance sheet."

The structured case analysis of the AI-driven deposit optimization agent ("Opti") demonstrates how banks lose their economic partnerships through rule-based execution, which makes them more dependent on deposits and creates financial risks because they lack qualitative stewardship in their execution process. 

To address this risk, the paper proposes:

·       A Delegation Contract, which sets operational limits and conditions for escalating situations

·       A Fiduciary Hurdle Rate, which operates as an absolute execution stop

·       A pre-deployment simulation environment known as the Agentic Sandbox

·       Decision-level tracking, which operates through the Decision Integrity Chain™

·       The system establishes a conceptual framework that connects agentic penetration (ω) to deposit migration velocity

The paper presents Decision Engineering as a new governance discipline that establishes execution frameworks that implement fiduciary restrictions through automated systems. 

The paper states that fiduciary duty in programmable institutions must extend beyond mere policy to become an essential component of operational execution.

title: When Legal Preference Does Not Mean Utilization: Explaining Cooperative Marginalization in Philippine Government Procurement (2015-2025)

detail.title: When Legal Preference Does Not Mean Utilization: Explaining Cooperative Marginalization in Philippine Government Procurement (2015-2025)
detail.abstract: This study explains why long-standing legal procurement preferences for cooperatives in the Philippines have failed to translate into meaningful contract utilization. Despite constitutional mandates, statutory exemptions under Republic Act No. 9520, negotiated procurement modalities under Republic Act No. 9184, and sector-specific mandates such as the Sagip Saka Act, analysis of PhilGEPS award data from 2015 to 2025 shows that cooperatives consistently received only 0.07 to 0.22 percent of national procurement spending. Rather than attributing this gap to deficiencies in legal design, the study develops a threelevel explanatory model of utilization barriers: (1) supplier-side capacity constraints among cooperatives, (2) risk-averse behavior and familiarity bias among procuring entities, and (3) systemic monitoring and data design failures that render preferences invisible in practice. Using documentary analysis of legal frameworks and reproducible extraction of PhilGEPS open data, the paper demonstrates how legal preference without institutional, behavioral, and system support produces persistent marginalization. The findings contribute to public administration and procurement scholarship by showing that social procurement objectives require more than statutory accommodation; they require active alignment of institutional behavior, data systems, and capacity development. The transition to the New Government Procurement Act (RA 12009) is examined as a critical test of whether efficiency-driven reform further entrenches or can potentially correct this long-standing utilization gap.

title: A Unified 2D and 3D Publication Format Using a Two-Sided Digital Page and Real-Time Page-Turn Simulation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Unified 2D and 3D Publication Format Using a Two-Sided Digital Page and Real-Time Page-Turn Simulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

detail.abstract: Digital publishing has remained fundamentally two-dimensional for decades, even as computing environments have expanded into immersive 3D spaces. Existing formats such as PDF, EPUB, and HTML treat pages as flat, single-sided surfaces, while page-turn effects in commercial systems rely on 2D illusions, mirrored textures, or CPU-driven spline approximations. These approaches lack geometric identity, physical intuition, and extensibility to AR, VR, and spatial computing environments. This monograph introduces a unified 2D and 3D publication format based on a two-sided digital page primitive and a real-time page-turn simulation executed entirely on the GPU. The system models a page as a single 3D mesh with independent front and back surfaces, enabling true two-sided geometry and simultaneous visibility of both sides during deformation. A closed-form conic deformation equation, driven solely by elapsed time and evaluated in the vertex shader, bends the page into a quarter-elliptical cylinder. A five-mesh choreography and a minimal flag-driven state machine coordinate identity, visibility, and texture routing without CPU/GPU synchronization. The architecture operates as a continuous, refresh-driven simulation rather than a precomputed animation, scaling naturally across devices from mobile phones to AR/VR headsets. The result is a new digital "paper" primitive capable of hosting text, images, media, and interactive elements, and a publication format that unifies 2D flat-screen presentation with immersive 3D environments. This work establishes a foundation for next-generation digital documents and introduces a computational model aligned with the future of spatial computing.

title: A Population Perspective on the Beneficiaries of Public and Private Assistance Immediately and over the Long-term After a Major Disaster
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill, SurveyMETER and Duke University

detail.title: A Population Perspective on the Beneficiaries of Public and Private Assistance Immediately and over the Long-term After a Major Disaster

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Natural disasters undermine economic development, destroying lives, livelihoods, the built and natural environment. Public assistance programs follow, but knowledge of their reach, impact and evolution is limited. We address this gap, analyzing population-representative longitudinal survey data collected in Indonesia before and for two decades after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami which was followed by a large recovery program involving multiple major actors.  Those who lived, at the time of the tsunami, in communities that were badly damaged, were far more likely to receive aid and received larger amounts than residents of other areas immediately after the tsunami. Those gaps were small and insignificant four years post-tsunami. Conditional on exposure, individual attributes also shaped receipt which reached the vulnerable, particularly poor and female-headed households. Housing assistance, distributed several years post-tsunami to those who lost homes, was critical in the eyes of recipients, playing a key role as they rebuilt livelihoods.
